one_way_hebrew: Uses וְשׁוּם (ve-shum — 'and any/no') — a distinctly Mishnaic Hebrew word. Biblical Hebrew would use אִישׁ (ish) or אֶחָד (echad) alone for 'anyone.' The word שום in the sense of 'any' is post-biblical (cf. Mishnah Berachot 1:1 etc.). No back-translator from Greek οὐδείς ('no one') would produce this Mishnaic form.

Uses לִרְאוֹת בּוֹ (lir'ot bo — 'to see INTO it') — the preposition ב implies looking inside, examining the contents. Greek has βλέπειν αὐτό ('to look AT it') — merely seeing the exterior. The Hebrew implies the scroll's contents are what matters; the Greek implies even beholding it is impossible.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'in the heavens and in the earth' (two realms). Greek: 'in heaven, nor on earth, nor under the earth' (ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ, οὐδὲ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, οὐδὲ ὑποκάτω τῆς γῆς — three realms). Greek adds 'under the earth.'
Hebrew: 'to see into it' (לראות בו). Greek: 'to look at it' (βλέπειν αὐτό). Different prepositions, different meaning.
translation_notes: 'To see into it' preserves the Hebrew preposition ב (be — 'in/into'), which implies examining the contents rather than merely beholding the scroll's exterior.

one_way_hebrew: Uses כֵּיוָן שֶׁ (keiwan she- — 'since/seeing that') — a distinctly Mishnaic Hebrew causal conjunction not found anywhere in the biblical Hebrew canon. Biblical Hebrew uses כִּי (ki), יַעַן (ya'an), or עַל אֲשֶׁר (al asher) for 'because/since.' The Greek ὅτι (hoti — 'because') would be rendered as כי by any back-translator. The use of כיון ש is a fingerprint of authentic Hebrew composition in the Second Temple / early rabbinic period.

Uses בוֹכֶה אֲנִי (bocheh ani — 'weeping [am] I') — participle + pronoun word order, placing the emotional state first for emphasis. This is natural Hebrew syntax. Greek ἐγὼ ἔκλαιον ('I was weeping') uses standard Greek word order. The Hebrew emphasis pattern is natural in Hebrew but would not be produced by translation from Greek.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'worthy for this matter' (לזה הדבר — vague reference). Greek: 'worthy to open the scroll and to look at it' (ἄξιος ἀνοῖξαι τὸ βιβλίον οὐδὲ βλέπειν αὐτό — specific reference). The Hebrew uses the general דבר ('matter/thing'); the Greek spells out the specific action.
Greek adds 'nor to look at it' (οὐδὲ βλέπειν αὐτό) — absent from Hebrew.
translation_notes: 'Matter' for davar (H1697) captures the Hebrew's deliberate vagueness — the word encompasses word, thing, matter, affair, legal case. The Hebrew sees this as a legal matter (matching the deed-scroll imagery); the Greek narrows it to a physical action.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses מִמִּשְׁפַּחַת (mi-mishpachat — 'from the CLAN/FAMILY of', H4940). Greek has ἐκ τῆς φυλῆς ('from the TRIBE of'). In the OT social hierarchy, שֵׁבֶט/מַטֶּה (shevet/matteh — 'tribe') is the largest unit, while מִשְׁפָּחָה (mishpachah — 'clan/family') is a subdivision within the tribe (Josh 7:14 — Israel narrows by tribe, then clan, then household). A back-translator from Greek φυλή ('tribe') would use שבט, never the smaller-unit word משפחה. The Hebrew author uses the more precise kinship term — Yehudah's royal CLAN, not the entire tribe.

The manuscript has a lacuna: מִמִּשְׁפַּחַת [  ] יוּדָא — a visible gap between 'clan of' and 'Yehudah.' This physical gap in the Hebrew text is evidence of a manuscript tradition, not a translation — back-translations don't have lacunae.

The spelling יוּדָא (Yuda) rather than the standard יְהוּדָה (Yehudah) is the Aramaic-influenced form found in Ezra 5:1,8 and the Aramaic portions of Daniel. This spelling is characteristic of the Second Temple period and would not be produced by a Greek-to-Hebrew translator, who would use the standard biblical spelling.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'from the clan' (ממשפחת). Greek: 'from the tribe' (ἐκ τῆς φυλῆς). Different social unit.
Hebrew: 'to break' (לשבר) the seals. Greek: 'to loose' (λῦσαι) the seals — same deviation as verse 2.
translation_notes: 'Clan' for mishpachah preserves the distinction from 'tribe' (shevet). The lion comes from the specific ruling clan within Judah, not from the tribe generically.

'Overcome' for nitsach (H5329) — the root נצח means to prevail, be victorious. The same root appears in the Psalm titles as מְנַצֵּחַ (menatseach — 'choirmaster/director'), connecting victory to worship leadership. The victor is also the worship leader.
textual_notes: Genesis 49:9-10 — 'Judah is a lion's whelp (גּוּר אַרְיֵה יְהוּדָה)... The scepter shall not depart from Judah.' The 'lion from the clan of Yehudah' directly quotes Jacob's blessing. Isaiah 11:1,10 — 'A shoot from the stump of Jesse... the root of Jesse (שֹׁרֶשׁ יִשַׁי) shall stand.' The Hebrew naturally combines these two messianic prophecies.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses רוּחוֹת יַהְוֶה (ruchot YHWH — 'spirits of YHWH') with the divine name. Greek has τοῦ Θεοῦ πνεύματα ('spirits of God'). A back-translator from Greek θεός ('God') would write אלהים (Elohim), not the tetragrammaton YHWH. The Hebrew connects directly to Zechariah 4:10 — 'These seven are the EYES OF YHWH (עֵינֵי יְהוָה), ranging through the whole earth (מְשׁוֹטְטִים בְּכָל הָאָרֶץ).' The Hebrew author quotes Zechariah's language; the Greek translator replaced YHWH with the generic θεός.

Uses שֶׂה (seh, H7716) — the specific Passover lamb word from Exodus 12:3-5 (שֶׂה לְבֵית אָבוֹת — 'a lamb per household'). Greek ἀρνίον is a generic diminutive 'little lamb.' A back-translator would more likely use כֶּבֶשׂ (keves — 'young ram') or טָלֶה (taleh — 'young lamb'). The consistent use of seh throughout this chapter (vv. 6, 8, 12, 13) ties the Lamb directly to the Passover sacrifice.

Uses נֶהֱרַג (neherag — 'slain', niphal of הרג, H2026) — a general verb for killing. Greek ἐσφαγμένον (from σφάζω — 'to slaughter/butcher') specifically means ritual or sacrificial slaughter. Notably, the Hebrew does NOT use שָׁחַט (shachat — 'to slaughter'), which is the specific OT verb for slaughtering the Passover lamb (Ex 12:6). The Hebrew author chose the general 'killed' rather than the sacrificial 'slaughtered' — implying the lamb was murdered, not merely ritually processed.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'spirits of YHWH' (רוחות יהוה). Greek: 'spirits of God' (τοῦ Θεοῦ πνεύματα). Divine name vs. generic title.

Hebrew: one בְּתוֹךְ (betoch — 'in the midst of') governing throne, living-ones, and elders together. Greek: repeats ἐν μέσῳ ('in the midst') twice — 'in the midst of the throne and of the four living creatures, AND in the midst of the elders.' Hebrew is more concise.
translation_notes: 'Living-ones' for chayyot (H2416) — the same word as the living creatures in Ezekiel 1:5-22. The Hebrew author uses the Ezekiel term naturally; the Greek ζῷα ('living beings/animals') is a standard translation.
'Sent out' for nishlach (H7971, niphal) — from the root שלח, the same root as שלוחים (sheluchim — 'sent-ones/apostles' in Rev 21:14). The spirits are 'apostled' into all the earth.
textual_notes: Zechariah 4:10 — 'These seven are the eyes of YHWH, which range through the whole earth.' Also Zechariah 3:9 — 'Upon one stone are seven eyes.' The seven-eyed lamb merges the stone of Zechariah 3 with the eyes of Zechariah 4. Isaiah 11:2 lists the spirit of YHWH in sevenfold description upon the shoot of Jesse — connecting to the 'root of David' in verse 5.

greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'from the right hand of this one who sits' (מיד ימינו מזה שיושב). Greek: ἐκ τῆς δεξιᾶς τοῦ καθημένου ('from the right of the one sitting'). Close parallel — one of the few verses where Hebrew and Greek substantially agree.
translation_notes: The Hebrew uses the demonstrative מִזֶּה (mi-zeh — 'from THIS one') emphasizing the immediacy and specificity of the one on the throne. Greek simply says τοῦ καθημένου ('the one sitting').

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL — STRONGEST ONE-WAY MARKER IN THE CHAPTER: Uses מַחְתּוֹת (machtot — 'fire-pans/censers', H4289) — the specific Tabernacle/Temple implements for carrying burning coals. These appear in: Lev 10:1 (Nadab and Abihu took their machtah), Lev 16:12 (High Priest on Yom Kippur fills his machtah with coals from the altar), Num 16:6,17-18 (Korah's rebellion — each takes his machtah), Num 16:38-39 (rebel fire-pans hammered into altar covering), 1 Kings 7:50 (Solomon's Temple had golden machtot). Greek has φιάλας χρυσᾶς ('golden BOWLS/vials'). A back-translator from Greek would write קְעָרוֹת זָהָב ('golden bowls'), NOT the Levitical fire-pan term. The Hebrew describes an exact Tabernacle scene: fire-pans filled with incense before the divine presence — this is Yom Kippur in heaven.

Uses כִּינּוֹר (kinnor — 'lyre', H3658) — David's specific instrument (1 Sam 16:16,23; 2 Sam 6:5; Ps 33:2, 43:4, 49:4, 71:22, 81:2, 92:3, 98:5, 108:2, 147:7, 149:3, 150:3). This is the instrument of the Levitical Temple worship orchestrated by David (1 Chr 15:16, 25:1-6). Greek κιθάρας ('harps') is a standard translation but the Hebrew naturally reaches for the Davidic worship instrument. Note Hebrew SINGULAR כינור vs. Greek PLURAL κιθάρας — one lyre shared, not individual harps.

Uses תְּפִילַּת הַקְּדוֹשִׁים ('the PRAYER of the holy ones', H8605) — singular תפילה (tefillah), treating the collective prayers as one unified prayer. Greek has αἱ προσευχαί ('the PRAYERS', plural) τῶν ἁγίων ('of the saints'). A back-translator would use the plural תפילות. The Hebrew singular implies a unified liturgical offering.

Uses וּבְשָׁעָה שֶׁ (u-ve-sha'ah she- — 'and in the moment that') — a distinctly Mishnaic Hebrew temporal construction (cf. Mishnah Berachot 1:1). Biblical Hebrew would use כַּאֲשֶׁר (ka'asher — 'when') or בְּ + infinitive. Greek ὅτε ('when') is neutral. No back-translator would produce this Mishnaic idiom.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: מַחְתּוֹת ('fire-pans/censers'). Greek: φιάλας χρυσᾶς ('golden bowls'). Entirely different implements — Levitical fire-pans vs. libation bowls.
Greek adds χρυσᾶς ('golden') — absent from Hebrew. The Hebrew doesn't specify the material.
Hebrew: singular כינור ('a lyre'). Greek: plural κιθάρας ('harps'). Different number.
Hebrew: singular תפלת ('prayer'). Greek: plural προσευχαί ('prayers'). Different number.
translation_notes: 'Fire-pans' for machtot preserves the Tabernacle connection. These are not bowls for holding liquids but metal implements for carrying burning coals and incense — the same implements used on Yom Kippur when the High Priest enters the Holy of Holies (Lev 16:12-13).
'Lyre' for kinnor — David's instrument, the instrument of Levitical worship. Not a harp (nevel) but a smaller stringed instrument played with a plectrum.
textual_notes: Leviticus 16:12-13 — 'He shall take a fire-pan (מַחְתָּה) full of burning coals from the altar... and two handfuls of finely ground incense (קְטֹרֶת)... He shall put the incense on the fire before YHWH, so that the cloud of incense covers the mercy seat.' Revelation 5:8 describes the identical Yom Kippur scene: fire-pans full of incense before the divine presence.
Psalm 141:2 — 'Let my prayer (תפלתי) be counted as incense (קטרת) before you.' The Hebrew connection between prayer and incense is explicit in both Psalm and Revelation.

one_way_hebrew: Uses שִׁיר חָדָשׁ (shir chadash — 'a new song') — the EXACT phrase from Psalms 33:3, 40:4, 96:1, 98:1, 144:9, 149:1, and Isaiah 42:10. This is one of the most distinctive Psalm phrases in the Hebrew Bible. Greek ᾠδὴν καινήν is a standard translation, but the Hebrew naturally quotes the Psalms. The verb זִמְּרוּ (zimmeru — 'they sang/made music', H2167) is specifically the Psalm-singing verb, used dozens of times in Psalms (Ps 9:12, 18:50, 27:6, 30:5, 47:7, 57:8, 66:2,4, 68:5,33, 98:4-5, 105:2, 108:2, 135:3, 147:1,7, 149:3).

Uses וְקָנִיתָ (ve-qanita — 'and you acquired/purchased', H7069) from קָנָה (qanah). This verb carries a dual meaning in Hebrew: (1) to purchase/acquire (Gen 25:10, 33:19, 47:20), and (2) to create/bring forth (Gen 4:1 — Eve says 'I have acquired/created a man'; Gen 14:19,22 — 'God Most High, creator/acquirer of heaven and earth'; Deut 32:6 — 'Is he not your father who acquired/created you?'; Ps 139:13 — 'You created/acquired my inward parts'). Greek ἠγόρασας ('you bought in the marketplace', from ἀγοράζω) is purely commercial. A back-translator from Greek would use a simpler commercial verb. The Hebrew qanah implies both purchase AND creation — the lamb bought the holy ones and thereby created them anew.

Hebrew: בְּדָמֶיךָ (be-dameicha — 'with your BLOODS', PLURAL). Hebrew דם (dam — 'blood') in its plural form דמים (damim) specifically connotes violently shed blood, bloodguilt, or blood-price (Gen 4:10-11, 2 Sam 3:27-28, Ps 51:16, Isa 1:15). The plural form implies blood shed by violence. Greek ἐν τῷ αἵματί σου uses singular 'blood.' A back-translator would use singular דמך.
greek_deviations: Greek adds τῷ Θεῷ ('to God') after 'you purchased us' — absent from Hebrew. The Hebrew says simply 'you acquired us'; the Greek specifies 'you purchased us to God.'

Greek adds ἐκ πάσης φυλῆς καὶ γλώσσης καὶ λαοῦ καὶ ἔθνους ('from every tribe and tongue and people and nation') — the fourfold universal formula is entirely absent from the Hebrew. The Hebrew has only 'you acquired US' — intimate and unqualified.
translation_notes: 'Acquired' for qanita rather than 'bought' or 'purchased' — preserving the Hebrew verb's dual creation/purchase semantics. The redeemer both purchases and creates.
'Sang' for zimmeru — the specific Hebrew verb for making music, especially psalm-singing. This is not merely 'saying' or 'chanting' but musical worship.
textual_notes: Psalm 40:4 — 'He put a new song (שיר חדש) in my mouth, a praise to our God.' Psalm 98:1 — 'Sing to YHWH a new song (שיר חדש), for he has done marvelous things; his right hand and his holy arm have worked salvation for him.' The new song in the Psalms is always a response to YHWH's saving acts — matching the context here where the song celebrates the lamb's redemptive act.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Hebrew order is כֹהֲנִים (kohanim — 'priests') BEFORE מְלָכִים (melachim — 'kings'). Greek order is βασιλεῖς ('kings') BEFORE ἱερεῖς ('priests') — reversed. The Hebrew order matches Exodus 19:6 — מַמְלֶכֶת כֹּהֲנִים ('a kingdom of priests') — where priesthood is the defining role and kingship is the framework. A back-translator from Greek, seeing 'kings and priests,' would preserve that order. The Hebrew author instinctively follows the Torah's priority of priesthood over kingship.

Uses כֹהֲנִים (kohanim, H3548) — the specific OT priestly class descended from Aaron. This is not a generic 'priest' word but the title of the Aaronic/Levitical priesthood with all its duties of sacrifice, intercession, and teaching Torah (Lev 1-7, Deut 33:10, Mal 2:7). The scene in verse 8 (fire-pans, incense, lyres) has already established the priestly setting.
greek_deviations: Hebrew order: priests then kings. Greek order: kings then priests. Reversed priority.
Greek adds τῷ Θεῷ ἡμῶν ('to our God') — 'you made us kings and priests to our God.' This phrase is absent from Hebrew.
Greek: βασιλεύσομεν ('we shall reign'). Hebrew: נִהְיוּ מְלָכִים ('we shall be kings'). The Hebrew uses a stative (being kings), the Greek uses an active verb (reigning).
translation_notes: 'Priests' before 'kings' follows the Hebrew text's order, which reflects the Torah's theological priority. Israel's identity is priestly before it is royal.
textual_notes: Exodus 19:6 — 'And you shall be to me a kingdom of priests (ממלכת כהנים) and a holy nation.' This foundational covenant declaration shapes the Hebrew author's word order. The redeemed are first and foremost a priesthood.

one_way_hebrew: Uses אַלְפַּיִם רְבָבוֹת (alpayim revavot — 'two-thousand myriads' = 20,000,000) — a SPECIFIC number. Greek has μυριάδες μυριάδων καὶ χιλιάδες χιλιάδων ('myriads of myriads and thousands of thousands') — a poetic, indefinite multiplication. A back-translator from Greek's indefinite expression would write רבבות רבבות ואלפי אלפים (revavot revavot ve-alfei alafim), mirroring the Greek pattern. No back-translator would collapse this into the specific number 'two-thousand myriads.'
Uses קוֹלוֹת (qolot — 'voices', PLURAL). Greek has φωνήν (singular 'voice/sound'). Hebrew hears multiple distinct voices; Greek hears one unified sound.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: specific number 'two-thousand myriads' (20 million). Greek: indefinite 'myriads of myriads and thousands of thousands.'
Hebrew: mentions only messengers around the throne. Greek adds 'and the living creatures and the elders' (καὶ τῶν ζῴων καὶ τῶν πρεσβυτέρων).
Hebrew: 'voices' (plural). Greek: 'voice' (singular).
translation_notes: אַלְפַּיִם (alpayim) is the DUAL form of אֶלֶף (elef — 'thousand'), meaning specifically 'two thousand.' Combined with רבבות (revavot — 'myriads/ten-thousands'), the total is 2,000 × 10,000 = 20,000,000.
textual_notes: Daniel 7:10 — 'A thousand thousands (אֶלֶף אַלְפִין) served him, and ten thousand times ten thousand (רִבּוֹ רִבְבָן) stood before him.' The Hebrew Revelation's specific number may derive from a tradition of calculating Daniel's indefinite numbers into a specific total. Deuteronomy 33:2 — 'YHWH came from Sinai... from the myriads of holiness (מֵרִבְבֹת קֹדֶשׁ).' Myriads of heavenly beings is a Torah concept.

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew has FOUR attributes: כֹחַ (koach — 'strength'), כָבוֹד (kavod — 'glory'), תִפְאֶרֶת (tiferet — 'splendor'), תְּהִילֹּת (tehillot — 'praises'). Greek has SEVEN: δύναμιν (power), πλοῦτον (riches), σοφίαν (wisdom), ἰσχύν (strength), τιμήν (honor), δόξαν (glory), εὐλογίαν (blessing). The lists share almost no vocabulary overlap. The Hebrew four-fold doxology uses terms from priestly worship; the Greek seven-fold list appears independently composed. No back-translator would reduce seven distinct Greek terms to four different Hebrew terms.

Uses תִפְאֶרֶת (tiferet — 'splendor/beauty', H8597) — the word for the beauty of the priestly garments (Ex 28:2,40 — לְכָבוֹד וּלְתִפְאָרֶת 'for glory and for splendor'). The Hebrew doxology echoes the priestly garment description. Greek has no equivalent in its list — the closest is τιμή ('honor'), which is a different concept.

Uses תְּהִילֹּת (tehillot — 'praises', H8416) — from the root הלל, the same root as the book of Psalms (תְּהִלִּים / Tehillim). Greek has εὐλογίαν ('blessing') — a different concept entirely (praise vs. blessing). A back-translator from εὐλογία would use בְּרָכָה (berachah — 'blessing'), not תהילה.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: four attributes (strength, glory, splendor, praises). Greek: seven attributes (power, riches, wisdom, strength, honor, glory, blessing). Substantially different lists with different counts.
Greek adds πλοῦτον ('riches'), σοφίαν ('wisdom'), τιμήν ('honor') — all absent from Hebrew.
Hebrew: תפארת ('splendor'). No Greek equivalent. Hebrew: תהילות ('praises'). Greek: εὐλογίαν ('blessing'). Different words.
translation_notes: 'Splendor' for tiferet — the priestly garment word, linking this doxology to the priesthood theme that runs through the chapter.
'Praises' for tehillot — connecting to the Psalms (Tehillim). The lamb receives the praise that the Psalms direct to YHWH.
textual_notes: Exodus 28:2 — 'You shall make holy garments for Aaron your brother, for glory (כבוד) and for splendor (תפארת).' The exact pair כבוד + תפארת appears in both the priestly garments and this heavenly doxology, reinforcing the priestly character of the scene.

one_way_hebrew: Uses הַבְּרִיאוֹת (ha-bri'ot — 'the creatures/creations') — from the root ברא (bara — 'to create'), the Genesis 1:1 creation verb. This is a post-biblical Hebrew noun derived from the most theologically loaded verb in the Torah. Greek κτίσμα ('created thing') is a standard word. A back-translator could use various words; the specific choice of the ברא root ties this doxology to the creation narrative — all that God CREATED now praises the Creator and the Lamb.

CRITICAL: Uses the doxology formula מֵעוֹלָם וְעַד עוֹלָם ('from everlasting to everlasting') — the signature closing of the Psalm books: Ps 41:14 (closing Book I), Ps 72:19 (Book II), Ps 89:53 (Book III), Ps 106:48 (Book IV). Also 1 Chr 16:36, Neh 9:5. Greek has εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων ('unto the ages of the ages') — a different formula. A back-translator from Greek would write לְעוֹלְמֵי עוֹלָמִים (le-olmei olamim — 'unto ages of ages'), mirroring the Greek genitive construction. No back-translator would produce the Psalm doxology formula me-olam ve-ad olam.

Hebrew has THREE attributes: כָבוֹד (kavod — 'glory'), תְּהִילּוֹת (tehillot — 'praises'), שֶׁבַח (shevach — 'commendation'). Greek has FOUR: εὐλογία (blessing), τιμή (honor), δόξα (glory), κράτος (dominion). Again the lists differ substantially. Hebrew שֶׁבַח (shevach, H7623) is especially common in Aramaic/late Hebrew (Dan 2:23, 4:34,37; Neh 9:5). Greek κράτος ('dominion/might') is an entirely different concept from 'commendation.'
greek_deviations: Hebrew: three attributes (glory, praises, commendation). Greek: four attributes (blessing, honor, glory, dominion). Different lists, different counts.
Hebrew: me-olam ve-ad olam ('from everlasting to everlasting' — Psalm doxology). Greek: εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων ('unto the ages of the ages'). Different formulae.
Greek adds 'and all things in them' (καὶ τὰ ἐν αὐτοῖς πάντα) — absent from Hebrew.
translation_notes: 'Creatures' for bri'ot — preserving the creation (ברא) connection. Everything that God spoke into being in Genesis now speaks praise back to him.
'Commendation' for shevach — this word emphasizes verbal praise and laudatory speech, distinguished from tehillah (song-praise) and kavod (weighty glory).
'From everlasting to everlasting' preserves the Psalm doxology formula that Hebrew readers would immediately recognize.
textual_notes: Psalm 106:48 — 'Blessed be YHWH, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting (מן העולם ועד העולם). And let all the people say: Amen!' This final Psalm doxology is echoed here — and the 'Amen' follows immediately in verse 14.

Nehemiah 9:5 — 'Stand up and bless (ברכו) YHWH your God from everlasting to everlasting. Blessed be your glorious name (שם כבודך), which is exalted above all blessing and praise (ברכה ותהלה).' The same vocabulary cluster (kavod, tehillah, me-olam ve-ad olam) appears in both texts.

one_way_hebrew: Uses עוֹנִים (onim — 'answering/responding', H6030) — the specific Hebrew liturgical verb for responsive worship. In Deuteronomy 27:14-26, the Levites speak and all Israel 'answers' (ענה) 'Amen.' In 1 Chronicles 16:36, 'all the people said Amen and praised (הלל) YHWH.' In Nehemiah 5:13, 8:6, the people 'answered' Amen. Greek ἔλεγον means simply 'were saying.' A back-translator from Greek would use אומרים (omerim — 'saying'), NOT the liturgically loaded ענה ('to answer'). The Hebrew implies a responsive liturgy — the living-ones ANSWER the universal doxology of verse 13 with the liturgical Amen.

Uses מִתְפַּלְּלִים (mitpallelim — 'praying', H6419, hitpael of פלל) — the specific Hebrew verb for intercessory/liturgical prayer (Gen 20:7, 1 Sam 1:10,26-27, 1 Kings 8:28-30, Dan 9:4,20). Greek has προσεκύνησαν ('they worshipped/bowed down'). Prostration and prayer are different actions. A back-translator from Greek would use השתחווה (hishtachaveh — 'bowed down/worshipped'), NOT the prayer verb התפלל. The Hebrew sees the elders engaged in PRAYER — active intercession — not mere prostration.

Again uses מֵעוֹלָם וְעַד עוֹלָם ('from everlasting to everlasting') — the Psalm doxology formula, now describing the eternal life of the one on the throne. This formula was used for the doxology in verse 13; now it describes the one who receives it.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'answering' (עונים — responsive liturgy). Greek: 'were saying' (ἔλεγον). Different verbs with different liturgical implications.
Hebrew: 'praying' (מתפללים — active prayer). Greek: 'worshipped' (προσεκύνησαν — prostration). Different actions.

Hebrew: 'to this one who lives from everlasting to everlasting' (לזה שחי מעולם ועד עולם). Greek: 'the one living unto the ages of the ages' (ζῶντι εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων). Different formulae, and Greek omits the 'from' — only saying 'into' the ages.
translation_notes: 'Answered' for onim — preserving the responsive liturgical sense. The living-ones do not merely speak; they respond to the creation-wide praise with the covenantal affirmation 'Amen.'

'Prayed' for mitpallelim — the hitpael of פלל carries a reflexive/intensive sense, implying earnest, whole-being prayer. This is the same verb Hannah uses (1 Sam 1:10), Solomon uses at the Temple dedication (1 Kings 8:28), and Daniel uses in exile (Dan 9:4).
textual_notes: 1 Chronicles 16:36 — 'Blessed be YHWH the God of Israel from everlasting to everlasting (מן העולם ועד העולם). And all the people said Amen (ויאמרו כל העם אמן) and praised YHWH (והלל ליהוה).' This scene — the Psalm doxology formula followed by the congregational Amen — is the precise liturgical pattern reproduced in Revelation 5:13-14.

Nehemiah 8:6 — 'And Ezra blessed YHWH the great God, and all the people answered (ויענו) Amen, Amen, lifting their hands; and they bowed their heads and worshipped (וישתחוו) YHWH with their faces to the ground.' The Hebrew Revelation's sequence (answering Amen + falling down + praying) follows this Nehemiah worship pattern.

6.summary:
Revelation 6 in Hebrew is saturated with OT prophetic quotations and Mishnaic Hebrew features that could not arise from back-translation of the Greek text. The chapter contains at least 20 clear one-way translation markers.

The strongest one-way markers are: (1) VERBATIM QUOTE of Isaiah 34:4 in v.13, where the Hebrew matches the OT word-for-word while the Greek paraphrases freely; (2) VERBATIM QUOTE of Isaiah 2:19 in v.15, using the distinctly Isaiah 'tunnels of dust' (מחילות עפר) where Greek has generic 'rocks of the mountains'; (3) מלאך המות (Malakh ha-Mavet — 'Messenger of Death') vs. Greek 'Death' — the Hebrew names the Jewish angelic figure; (4) גיהנם (Gei-Hinnom) vs. Greek Hades — a geographic Hebrew location vs. the Greek mythological underworld; (5) היכל (heikhal — 'sanctuary') vs. Greek 'altar' — entirely different sacred architecture; (6) קדושת יהוה (kedushat YHWH — 'sanctification of YHWH') — the technical kiddush ha-Shem martyrdom concept vs. Greek 'word of God'; (7) פנים (panim — 'faces') for currency vs. Greek 'denarius'; (8) ברד (barod — 'spotted') vs. Greek chloros ('pale'), connecting to Zechariah's horse visions; (9) חרון אפו ('burning of his nostril') — the OT anthropomorphic wrath formula vs. Greek 'the great day of his wrath'; (10) רוזנים (rozenim — 'rulers') from Psalm 2:2.

Mishnaic Hebrew features pervade the text: כיון ש (keivan she — 'as soon as', vv.3,7), בשעה ש (be-sha'ah she — 'in the hour that', v.5), בשביל (bishvil — 'for the sake of', v.9), רשות (reshut — 'authority', v.8), זמן (zeman — 'time', v.11), דרים (darim — 'dwelling', v.10), and consistent masculine-for-feminine gender relaxation in participles. These are living Hebrew speech patterns that no Greek back-translator would produce.

The four horsemen sequence draws systematically from Zechariah 1:8 and 6:1-8 (colored horses), Ezekiel 14:21 (sword, famine, pestilence, beasts — the four judgments), and the Isaiah 2/34 Day of YHWH tradition. The fifth seal introduces specifically Jewish martyrdom theology (kiddush ha-Shem). The sixth seal weaves Joel 2:31, Isaiah 34:4, Isaiah 2:19, Hosea 10:8, Nahum 1:6, and Malachi 3:2 into a unified vision of cosmic judgment — all using the OT Hebrew source texts directly.

one_way_hebrew: Uses חֲתִימוֹת (chatimot — 'sealings', from חתם H2856), the verbal-noun plural denoting the ACT of sealing. The OT uses חוֹתָם (chotem, H2368 — 'seal/signet ring') for the physical object. Greek σφραγίδων ('seals') is ambiguous. A back-translator from Greek would use חותמות (chotamot — the concrete noun plural), not the verbal-noun form chatimot. The Hebrew distinguishes the sealed-ness of the scroll from the object used to seal it.

Hebrew says ALL FOUR living-creatures speak together 'as one voice' (כקול אחד). Greek says 'one of the four living-creatures' (ἑνὸς ἐκ τῶν τεσσάρων ζώων) — only one speaks. These are incompatible narratives: a unified chorus vs. a single speaker. A back-translator from Greek would never change 'one of the four' to 'all four as one voice.'
Hebrew: 'as one voice' (כקול אחד). Greek: 'as a voice of thunder' (ὡς φωνὴ βροντῆς). Entirely different simile. The Hebrew emphasizes UNITY of the creatures; the Greek emphasizes POWER of the voice.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: all four creatures speak in unison. Greek: one of the four creatures speaks.
Hebrew: 'as one voice.' Greek: 'as a voice of thunder.' Different imagery.
translation_notes: Note gender mismatch: חיות (feminine plural noun) with אומרים (masculine plural participle). This is characteristic of spoken/Mishnaic Hebrew where masculine plurals serve as default for groups. A careful back-translator would maintain grammatical agreement.
שׂה (seh, H7716) — the specific Passover lamb word from Exodus 12:3-5. See note on Revelation 21:9.

one_way_hebrew: Uses כֶּתֶר (keter, H3804 — 'diadem/royal crown'). This is the crown of Esther (Est 1:11, 2:17, 6:8) and of God (Job 31:36). Greek στέφανος ('wreath/garland') is a victory wreath, NOT a royal diadem. A back-translator from Greek would use עטרה (atarah — 'wreath/garland', the Hebrew equivalent of stephanos), not the royal keter. The Hebrew author assigns a ROYAL diadem; the Greek translator downgraded it to a victor's wreath.

Hebrew: וְנִצַּח (ve-nitsach — 'and he conquered', perfect tense) — the conquest is COMPLETED, a done event. Greek: ἵνα νικήσῃ ('in order that he might conquer', subjunctive) — the conquest is PURPOSE/INTENT, not yet accomplished. A back-translator from a Greek subjunctive would use כדי שינצח ('so that he may conquer'), not the Hebrew perfect ve-nitsach. The Hebrew sees the conquest as already accomplished; the Greek sees it as pending.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'diadem' (כתר — royal crown). Greek: 'wreath' (στέφανος — victor's garland). Different type of headwear entirely.
Hebrew: 'he went forth to conquer AND conquered' (completed). Greek: 'he went forth conquering AND in order to conquer' (ongoing + purposive). Different aspect.
translation_notes: 'Diadem' for keter rather than 'crown' to distinguish it from the Greek stephanos (wreath). The keter is the royal crown of Persian and Israelite monarchy.
Hebrew has בידו (be-yado — 'in his hand') specifying the bow's location. Greek ἔχων τόξον ('having a bow') is less specific.
textual_notes: Zechariah 1:8 and 6:1-8 describe horses of different colors in visions. The white horse connects to Zechariah's white horses (Zech 6:3,6). The Hebrew author draws from the same prophetic horse-vision tradition.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses כֵּיוָן שֶׁ (keivan she — 'as soon as/when'). This is a quintessential MISHNAIC Hebrew conjunction, appearing extensively in the Mishnah and Talmud but NEVER in the OT. Greek simply has ὅτε ('when'). A back-translator from Greek ὅτε would use כאשר (ka'asher), בעת (be-et), or כ (ke-) — standard biblical Hebrew forms. NO back-translator would produce the Mishnaic keivan she. This is a living Hebrew speech pattern.

Hebrew uses PASSIVE נפתח (niftach — 'was opened') — the seal opens by itself / is opened without a named agent. Greek uses ACTIVE ἤνοιξε ('he opened') with the Lamb as agent. A back-translator from the Greek active would write שפתח השה ('that the lamb opened'), preserving the agent. The Hebrew passive reflects a Semitic preference for divine passives.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: passive 'was opened' (no agent named). Greek: active 'he [the Lamb] opened.' Different voice.
Note: the Mishnaic conjunction כיון ש recurs in vv. 3, 7 — a consistent authorial pattern.
translation_notes: Gender mismatch continues: חיה (feminine) with אומר (masculine singular participle). Same Mishnaic pattern as verse 1.

one_way_hebrew: Uses אָדֹם (adom, H122 — 'red'), sharing the consonantal root א-ד-ם with אָדָם (adam — 'man'), אֲדָמָה (adamah — 'ground'), and דָּם (dam — 'blood'). The war-horse is blood-colored — a Hebrew wordplay impossible in Greek where πυρρός ('fiery/flame-colored') has no connection to αἷμα ('blood') or ἄνθρωπος ('man'). A back-translator from πυρρός would use a fire-related word like אדמדם or אש-צבע, not the blood/earth root adom.

Hebrew says הַשָּׁלוֹם (ha-shalom — 'THE peace') with the definite article. Shalom in Hebrew encompasses wholeness, completeness, welfare, and covenant faithfulness — not merely the absence of war. Greek τὴν εἰρήνην ('the peace') is narrower. The Hebrew definite article suggests THE established shalom — the covenant order — is being removed.

Hebrew: הלך לחוץ (halakh la-chuts — 'went to the outside'). This decomposes the motion into verb + spatial adverb, a characteristically Hebrew construction. Greek ἐξῆλθεν is a single verb ('went out'). A back-translator would not decompose the Greek compound verb into this Hebrew spatial expression.
greek_deviations: Greek adds 'that they should slay one another' (ἵνα ἀλλήλους σφάξωσιν) — entirely absent from the Hebrew.
Hebrew: 'red' (adom — blood-colored). Greek: πυρρός ('fiery/flame-colored'). Different color associations.
translation_notes: חֶרֶב (cherev, H2719) — the standard Hebrew sword, the weapon of war throughout the OT (Gen 3:24, 27:40, Ex 5:21, Deut 32:25). Greek μάχαιρα can mean a knife or short sword.
textual_notes: Zechariah 1:8 and 6:2 — red horses appear in Zechariah's visions. In Zech 6:2, the red horses are paired with the first chariot. The Hebrew author draws from the same prophetic tradition.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses בְּשָׁעָה שֶׁ (be-sha'ah she — 'in the hour that'). שָׁעָה in biblical Hebrew (H8159) means 'to gaze/look.' The meaning 'hour/time' is EXCLUSIVELY post-biblical/Mishnaic. This temporal expression is quintessentially Mishnaic — appearing constantly in Talmudic narrative. Greek ὅτε ('when') is simply a conjunction. A back-translator from Greek would use כאשר or בעת, not this Mishnaic time idiom. Like כיון ש in v.3, this proves living Hebrew composition.

Uses מֹאזְנַיִם (moznayim, H3976 — 'scales/balance'). This is a dual-form noun (the two pans of a balance), used in Leviticus 19:36 for just scales (מאזני צדק) and in Job 31:6 (ישקלני במאזני צדק — 'let him weigh me in just scales'). Greek ζυγόν (zygon) means 'yoke' and only secondarily 'balance beam.' A back-translator from Greek 'yoke' would not produce the specifically commercial/judicial Hebrew moznayim.
translation_notes: 'Scales' for moznayim — the dual form reflects the two-pan balance, an instrument of justice and commerce in the OT.
Gender mismatch persists: החיה (feminine) with השלישי (masculine ordinal). Consistent Mishnaic pattern throughout the chapter.
textual_notes: Black is the color of famine and mourning (Lam 4:8 — 'their appearance is blacker than soot'; Lam 5:10 — 'our skin was hot as an oven because of the burning heat of famine'). The scales indicate rationed food — famine conditions.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Hebrew uses פָּנִים (panim — 'faces', H6440) as the unit of price/currency. Greek uses δηναρίου ('a denarius' — a Roman coin). A back-translator from Greek would transliterate as דינר (dinar), NEVER produce פנים. The Hebrew author calls the coin denomination by its 'face' — because coins bear faces/images. This is a uniquely Semitic monetary idiom: the 'face' of the coin IS the coin. Compare how English preserves 'face value.' No translator going Greek→Hebrew would independently create this idiom.

Uses מִדָּה (middah, H4060 — 'measure') — a standard Hebrew volume/capacity measure. Greek χοῖνιξ (choinix) is a specific Greek dry measure (about a quart). A back-translator from Greek would transliterate the Greek unit, not substitute the generic Hebrew middah.

Uses אַל תַּעֲשֶׂה רַע (al ta'aseh ra — 'do not do evil') — the Hebrew moral vocabulary of רע (ra, H7451 — 'evil'). Greek μὴ ἀδικήσῃς ('do not act unjustly') uses the legal concept of ἀδικέω ('to wrong/injure'). A back-translator from Greek would write אל תעשה עוול ('do not do injustice'), not the general moral term ra ('evil'). The Hebrew frames the command in moral-cosmic terms; the Greek in legal terms.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'two faces' (panim — a monetary term). Greek: 'a denarius' (a specific Roman coin). Entirely different denomination system.
Hebrew: 'do not do evil' (moral framing). Greek: 'do not act unjustly' (legal framing).
translation_notes: 'Faces' for panim is preserved literally to show the Hebrew monetary idiom. The meaning is 'coins' — called by the face/image they bear.

חטים (chittim, H2406 — 'wheat') and שעורים (se'orim, H8184 — 'barley') are standard OT agricultural vocabulary. The price ratio (1 measure wheat = 3 measures barley) indicates severe famine prices — roughly 8-16 times normal.
textual_notes: Leviticus 26:26 — 'When I break your staff of bread, ten women shall bake your bread in one oven, and they shall deliver your bread by weight, and you shall eat and not be satisfied.' The famine-seal echoes Levitical covenant curses.
2 Kings 7:1 — Elisha's prophecy: 'a measure of fine flour for a shekel and two measures of barley for a shekel.' Similar commercial language for food pricing in famine/siege conditions.

one_way_hebrew: כיון ש (keivan she) again — the same Mishnaic conjunction as v.3, forming a consistent authorial pattern. A back-translator would not independently reproduce this idiom in multiple verses.
greek_deviations: Greek adds φωνήν ('a voice') — 'I heard a voice of the fourth living creature.' Hebrew simply: 'I heard the fourth living-creature saying.' Hebrew is more direct.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses בָּרֹד (barod, H1261 — 'spotted/dappled') for the horse's color. Greek χλωρός (chloros — 'pale/greenish'). These are COMPLETELY different descriptions. Hebrew barod describes a mottled/speckled animal — the SAME word used in Genesis 31:10,12 for Jacob's spotted flocks and in Zechariah 6:3,6 for the dappled horses in the prophet's vision. A back-translator from Greek χλωρός would use ירקרק (yerakrak — 'greenish') or חִוֵּר (chiver — 'pale'). The use of barod ties this horse directly to Zechariah's four-horse vision.

Hebrew adds וְאַמֵּץ (ve-ametz — 'and strong', from אמץ H553). This word is entirely absent from Greek. It describes the horse's physical power/might — the word used when God tells Joshua 'be strong and courageous' (חזק ואמץ, Josh 1:6,7,9). No back-translator would add this.

CRITICAL: Uses מַלְאַךְ הַמָּוֶת (Malakh ha-Mavet — 'Messenger of Death', H4397 + H4194). This is the Angel of Death figure deeply embedded in Jewish tradition (2 Sam 24:16, Prov 16:14, Ps 78:49 traditions; extensively in Talmudic literature). Greek has simply Θάνατος ('Death'). A back-translator from Greek would write מָוֶת ('Death'), not the compound title 'Messenger of Death.' The Hebrew names a specific AGENT; the Greek names an abstract concept.

CRITICAL: Uses הַגֵּיהִנֹּם (ha-Geihinnom — 'Gei-Hinnom'). Greek has ᾍδης ('Hades'). Gei-Hinnom is the Valley of Hinnom — a REAL GEOGRAPHIC LOCATION south of Jerusalem (Josh 15:8, 18:16, 2 Kings 23:10, Jer 7:31-32, 19:2,6, 32:35) that became the site of child sacrifice to Molech and then the metaphor for divine judgment. Hades is the GREEK underworld. A back-translator from Greek ᾍδης would write שְׁאוֹל (Sheol — the Hebrew underworld equivalent), NEVER Gei-Hinnom. These are from completely different cultural-geographic frameworks.

Uses רְשׁוּת (reshut — 'authority/permission'). This is a quintessential MISHNAIC Hebrew term — the standard Talmudic word for legal authority/permission. It has no OT Hebrew equivalent (biblical Hebrew uses שלטון or ממשלה). Greek ἐξουσία ('authority') is standard. A back-translator would produce שלטון or ממשלה from ἐξουσία, not the Mishnaic reshut.

Uses the idiom עַל יַד (al yad — 'by the hand of', H5921 + H3027) for agency. This is a characteristically Hebrew expression for instrumentality. Greek ὑπό ('by/under') is a simple preposition. A back-translator would use ע״י or ב, not the fuller על יד.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'spotted and strong' (barod ve-ametz). Greek: 'pale/green' (chloros). Entirely different description. Greek lacks 'strong.'
Hebrew: 'Messenger of Death' (compound title). Greek: 'Death' (simple name).
Hebrew: 'Gei-Hinnom' (geographic). Greek: 'Hades' (mythological). Different conceptual worlds.

Hebrew: 'authority' (reshut — Mishnaic). Greek: 'authority' (exousia) + 'over a fourth of the earth' (ἐπὶ τὸ τέταρτον τῆς γῆς). Greek frames authority as 'over' territory; Hebrew frames it as authority 'to kill a fourth portion upon the earth.'
translation_notes: 'Pestilence' for mavet in the list (sword, famine, pestilence, beasts). In OT prophetic usage, mavet ('death') in a list of plagues means 'pestilence/plague' — see Jeremiah 15:2: 'those destined for pestilence (mavet), to pestilence; those destined for the sword, to the sword; those destined for famine, to famine' and Ezekiel 14:21.
'Spotted' for barod — following the Zechariah horse vision tradition rather than the Greek 'pale' interpretation.
textual_notes: Ezekiel 14:21 — 'my four deadly acts of judgment: sword, famine, wild beasts, and pestilence.' The Hebrew Revelation's four-fold judgment (sword, famine, pestilence, beasts) matches Ezekiel's four judgments EXACTLY in the same categories, though in different order. This is standard OT prophetic language that the Hebrew author naturally employs.

Zechariah 6:1-8 — four chariots with different-colored horses. The Hebrew Revelation's four horses echo Zechariah's four horse teams, with the 'spotted' (barod) horse directly matching Zechariah's ברדים (beruddim — 'dappled/spotted') horses.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses הֵיכָל (heikhal, H1964 — 'sanctuary/palace'). This is the specific word for the inner Temple — the nave of Solomon's Temple (1 Kings 6:3,5,17,33; 7:50), the heavenly temple (Ps 11:4, 18:6, Hab 2:20, Mic 1:2). Greek has θυσιαστηρίου (thysiasteriou — 'altar'). These are ENTIRELY DIFFERENT sacred spaces. The souls are beneath the SANCTUARY (the holy place where God dwells) in the Hebrew, but beneath the ALTAR (where sacrifices are offered) in the Greek. A back-translator from Greek would write מזבח (mizbeach — 'altar'), NEVER היכל. The Hebrew implies the souls dwell in God's heavenly palace; the Greek implies they are sacrificial offerings.

CRITICAL: Uses עַל קְדוּשַּׁת יַהְוֶה (al kedushat YHWH — 'for the sanctification of YHWH'). This is the concept of קִדּוּשׁ הַשֵּׁם (kiddush ha-Shem — 'sanctification of the Name') — THE specifically Jewish concept of martyrdom, dying to sanctify God's name. This concept pervades Rabbinic literature and became the standard term for Jewish martyrdom. Greek has διὰ τὸν λόγον τοῦ θεοῦ ('for the word of God'). A back-translator from Greek would write על דבר אלהים ('for the word of God'), NEVER produce the technical kiddush ha-Shem concept. This is one of the chapter's strongest one-way markers.

Uses נְשָׁמוֹת (neshamot — 'breaths/souls', H5397), from the root נשם ('to breathe'). This is THE word from Genesis 2:7 — נִשְׁמַת חַיִּים (nishmat chayyim — 'breath of life') that God breathed into Adam. Greek uses ψυχάς (psychas — 'souls'). A back-translator from Greek ψυχή would use נפשות (nefashot — from nephesh, the standard Hebrew equivalent of psyche). The use of neshamah rather than nephesh implies the divine-breath component of the soul — these are bearers of God's own breath.

Uses בִּשְׁבִיל (bishvil — 'for the sake of') — a quintessential MISHNAIC Hebrew preposition meaning 'because of/for the sake of.' It appears nowhere in the OT. Greek διά ('because of/for') is standard. A back-translator from Greek would use למען, בגלל, or בעבור — biblical Hebrew causal prepositions. The Mishnaic bishvil further confirms living Hebrew composition.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'beneath the sanctuary' (היכל — heavenly palace). Greek: 'beneath the altar' (θυσιαστηρίου). Different sacred architecture.
Hebrew: 'for the sanctification of YHWH' (kiddush ha-Shem martyrdom concept). Greek: 'for the word of God' (logos tou theou). Different reason for dying.
Hebrew: neshamot ('divine breaths/souls'). Greek: psychas ('souls'). Different anthropological term.
translation_notes: 'Breaths' for neshamot to preserve the Genesis 2:7 connection — these are bearers of God's own nishmat chayyim.
'Sanctification' for kedushat to capture the kiddush ha-Shem concept. These are martyrs who died to sanctify God's name.
עֵדוּת (edut, H5715 — 'testimony') — the same word for the Tablets of Testimony (לוחות העדות, Ex 31:18, 32:15, 34:29) and the Ark of the Testimony. The martyrs bore witness like the Torah tablets.
textual_notes: The location 'beneath the sanctuary' connects to the ancient Jewish concept that the souls of the righteous are stored 'under the throne of glory' (תחת כסא הכבוד — Shabbat 152b). The Hebrew naturally places martyred souls beneath God's heavenly dwelling.

one_way_hebrew: Uses צוֹעֲקִים (tso'akim — 'crying out', from צעק H6817). This is THE word for Israel's cry of distress from Egypt: וַיִּצְעֲקוּ ('and they cried out', Ex 2:23, 14:10). It recurs throughout Judges when Israel cries out under oppression (Judg 3:9, 3:15, 4:3, 6:6, 10:10). The martyrs' cry uses the Exodus vocabulary of oppression. Greek ἔκραξαν (from κράζω) is generic 'they shouted.' A back-translator would use זעק (za'aq) or קרא (qara), not specifically the Exodus-laden צעק.

Uses נֶאֱמָן (ne'eman — 'faithful/trustworthy', from אמן H539). Greek has ἀληθινός (alethinos — 'true/genuine'). A back-translator from Greek ἀληθινός would use אֲמִתִּי (amitti — 'true') or אֶמֶת (emet — 'truth'). The Hebrew ne'eman means 'faithful/reliable' — a DIFFERENT theological attribute from 'true.' God is called ne'eman in Deuteronomy 7:9 (הָאֵל הַנֶּאֱמָן — 'the faithful God'). The Hebrew invokes covenant faithfulness; the Greek invokes ontological truthfulness.

Hebrew: עד מתי תשפוט ואינה תנקם — 'until when will you judge and NOT avenge.' This implies God IS judging but has NOT YET avenged. Greek: Ἕως πότε... οὐ κρίνεις καὶ ἐκδικεῖς — 'until when do you NOT judge AND avenge.' Greek implies God is doing NEITHER. These are different theological claims about divine activity.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'faithful' (ne'eman — covenant loyalty). Greek: 'true' (alethinos — genuineness). Different divine attribute.
Hebrew implies God is judging but not yet avenging. Greek implies God is doing neither.
Hebrew: 'those who dwell' (דרים — Mishnaic present participle of דור). Greek: κατοικούντων ('inhabitants'). The Hebrew דרים (darim) is a Mishnaic form; biblical Hebrew would use ישבים (yoshvim).
translation_notes: 'Master' for adon (H113) — not YHWH but the title of sovereign authority. Psalm 12:4 and Psalm 114:7 use this form.

Blood vengeance (נקם דם) is a foundational OT concept: Genesis 4:10 — Abel's blood 'cries out from the ground'; Deuteronomy 32:43 — 'he avenges the blood of his servants'; Psalm 79:10 — 'let the avenging of the blood of your servants be known among the nations.'
textual_notes: The cry עד מתי ('until when/how long') echoes Psalm 13:1-2 — 'How long, O YHWH? Will you forget me forever?' and Psalm 79:5 — 'How long, O YHWH? Will you be angry forever?' and Habakkuk 1:2 — 'O YHWH, how long shall I cry and you will not hear?' The martyrs cry with the Psalms' vocabulary.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מַלְבּוּשֵׁי (malbushei — 'garments of', from לבש H3847, noun form H4403). This word emphasizes the act of being clothed — it is the garment-as-worn, used for royal garments (1 Kings 10:5, 2 Chr 9:4, Ezek 16:13). Greek στολαί ('robes') is a specific type of robe. A back-translator from Greek would use בגדים (begadim — 'garments') or כתנות (ketonot — 'tunics'), not the specifically royal/dignified malbushim.

Uses תִּשְׁקְטוּ (tishketu — 'be still/at rest', from שקט H8252). This is the word for the land being at rest after war: 'the land had rest (שקט) forty years' (Judg 3:11, 3:30, 5:31, 8:28). It implies CESSATION OF STRIFE — the martyrs should rest from their cry for vengeance as one rests from battle. Greek ἀναπαύσωνται ('rest/take repose') is generic rest. A back-translator from Greek would use ינוחו (yanuchu — 'rest', from נוח), not the war-ceasefire verb shaqat.

Uses זְמָן (zeman — 'a time'). This is a distinctly post-biblical/Mishnaic word for 'time/appointed time.' Biblical Hebrew uses עת (et) or מועד (mo'ed). Greek χρόνον ('time') is standard. A back-translator from Greek would use עת or זמן (less likely the latter, but the consistent use of Mishnaic vocabulary throughout confirms Hebrew composition).
greek_deviations: MAJOR: Greek adds an entire clause absent from Hebrew: ἕως πληρωθῶσιν καὶ οἱ σύνδουλοι αὐτῶν καὶ οἱ ἀδελφοὶ αὐτῶν, οἱ μέλλοντες ἀποκτέννεσθαι ὡς καὶ αὐτοί ('until their fellow servants and brothers who were about to be killed as they were should be complete'). This entire clause about future martyrs is absent from the Hebrew.
Hebrew: 'be still' (שקט — cease from agitation). Greek: 'rest' (ἀναπαύω — take repose). Different type of quietness.
translation_notes: 'Be still' for shaqat captures the military-rest nuance — these are warriors told to stand down, not sleepers told to nap.
'Garments' for malbushim — the dignified/royal garment, clothing the martyrs in honor.

one_way_hebrew: Uses רַעֲדוֹת הָאָרֶץ (ra'adot ha-aretz — 'trembling of the earth', from רעד H7460). The noun רַעֲדָה (re'adah, H7461) describes personal trembling from fear/awe: 'serve YHWH with fear and rejoice with trembling (רעדה)' (Ps 2:11); 'trembling (רעדה) seized the godless' (Isa 33:14). The Hebrew personifies the earth as TREMBLING IN FEAR. Greek σεισμὸς μέγας ('a great earthquake') is a technical geological term. A back-translator from Greek would use רעש גדול (ra'ash gadol — 'great earthquake'), using the standard Hebrew earthquake word רעש, not the fear-trembling word רעדה.

Hebrew: אדם כדם (adom ka-dam — 'red as blood'). The wordplay between אדם (adom — 'red') and דם (dam — 'blood') involves the same consonantal root א-ד-ם. The moon becomes 'blood-red' with the Hebrew pun embedded. Greek simply says ὡς αἷμα ('as blood') without the color word. The Hebrew is richer.
Hebrew lacks 'great' (μέγας) before the earthquake. Greek says 'a GREAT earthquake.' The Hebrew simply records 'a trembling of the earth' without magnifying it.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'trembling of the earth' (personified fear). Greek: 'a great earthquake' (geological event + adjective 'great').
Greek adds ὡς σάκκος τρίχινος ('like a hairy sackcloth') after 'the sun was black.' This simile is absent from Hebrew.
Hebrew: 'red as blood' (with adom/dam wordplay). Greek: simply 'as blood' (no color word).
translation_notes: 'Trembling' for ra'adot preserves the personification — the earth itself trembles, like a person trembling before God.
textual_notes: Joel 2:31 (Hebrew 3:4) — הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ יֵהָפֵךְ לְחֹשֶׁךְ וְהַיָּרֵחַ לְדָם ('The sun shall be turned to darkness and the moon to blood'). The Hebrew Revelation echoes Joel's cosmic signs. Joel says 'darkness' (חשך); the Hebrew Revelation says 'black' (שחור) — a related but different word. The moon-blood connection is preserved directly.
Isaiah 13:10 — 'The sun will be dark (חשך) at its rising, and the moon will not shed its light.' Cosmic darkening as a sign of YHWH's day of judgment.

one_way_hebrew: VERBATIM ISAIAH QUOTE: This verse is taken almost word-for-word from Isaiah 34:4b — וְכָל צְבָאָם יִבּוֹל כִּנְבֹל עָלֶה מִגֶּפֶן וּכְנֹבֶלֶת מִתְּאֵנָה ('and all their host shall wither as a leaf withers from a vine, and as a withered-fig from a fig-tree'). The match is EXACT. Greek has 'the stars of heaven fell to the earth, as a fig tree casts its unripe figs when shaken by a great wind' (οἱ ἀστέρες τοῦ οὐρανοῦ ἔπεσον εἰς τὴν γῆν, ὡς συκῆ βάλλει τοὺς ὀλύνθους αὐτῆς ὑπὸ ἀνέμου μεγάλου σειομένη). A back-translator from Greek would write כוכבי השמים נפלו ארצה כתאנה משלכת פגיה ברוח גדולה — bearing NO resemblance to Isaiah 34:4. The Hebrew PRESERVES the Isaiah source text; the Greek PARAPHRASES it.

Uses צְבָאָם (tseva'am — 'their host', H6635). Hebrew צבא is the cosmic-military term for the heavenly host — stars conceived as an army (Gen 2:1, Deut 4:19, Isa 34:4, 40:26). Greek has ἀστέρες τοῦ οὐρανοῦ ('stars of heaven'). The Hebrew author uses the OT cosmic-military term; the Greek translator made it explicit with 'stars of heaven.'

The verb יִבּוֹל (yibol — 'shall wither/fade', H5034) and כנבל (kinvol — 'as withers') and כנבלת (ke-novelet — 'as a withered-thing') all derive from the root נבל (navel — 'to wither/fade/fall'). This triple use of the same root creates alliterative emphasis impossible in the Greek, which uses three different verbs (ἔπεσον 'fell', βάλλει 'casts', σειομένη 'shaken').
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'all their host shall wither' (Isaiah 34:4 verbatim). Greek: 'the stars of heaven fell to the earth.' Different verb, different subject.

Hebrew: 'as a leaf withers from a vine, and as a withered-fig from a fig-tree' (Isaiah 34:4). Greek: 'as a fig-tree casts its unripe figs when shaken by a great wind.' Different imagery — Hebrew emphasizes withering; Greek emphasizes violent shaking.
Greek adds 'stars fell to the earth' and 'shaken by a great wind' — both absent from Hebrew.
translation_notes: 'Host' for tsava — preserving the military/cosmic nuance. The heavenly bodies are God's army.
'Withered-fig' for novelet — a feminine participial form meaning 'a withered/fallen thing,' specifically an overripe fig that drops from the tree.
textual_notes: Isaiah 34:4 (full verse): וְנָמַקּוּ כָּל צְבָא הַשָּׁמַיִם וְנָגֹלּוּ כַסֵּפֶר הַשָּׁמָיִם וְכָל צְבָאָם יִבּוֹל כִּנְבֹל עָלֶה מִגֶּפֶן וּכְנֹבֶלֶת מִתְּאֵנָה — 'And all the host of heaven shall waste away, and the heavens shall be rolled up like a scroll, and all their host shall wither as a leaf withers from a vine and as a withered-fig from a fig-tree.' The Hebrew Revelation quotes the second half verbatim. This is one of the strongest one-way markers in the chapter.

one_way_hebrew: Uses הָרִים וּגְבָעוֹת (harim u-geva'ot — 'mountains and hills'). This is standard OT prophetic pairing: Isaiah 2:14 ('upon all the high mountains and upon all the lifted hills'), Isaiah 40:4 ('every mountain and hill shall be made low'), Isaiah 54:10 ('though the mountains depart and the hills be shaken'), Micah 6:1 ('arise, contend before the mountains, and let the hills hear your voice'). Greek has ὄρος καὶ νῆσος ('mountain and island'). A back-translator from Greek would write הר ואי ('mountain and island'), NEVER substitute 'hills' (גבעות) for 'islands' (νῆσος). The Hebrew preserves the OT prophetic pairing; the Greek transforms hills into islands.

The verb נִדַּעֲזוּ (nid'azu — 'were shaken') appears to be a rare or dialectal Hebrew form. It may derive from a root related to זעזע (za'aza — 'to shake violently') with an infixed ד, or from an otherwise unattested root דעז. Its rarity suggests genuine Hebrew composition rather than back-translation, where a translator would use the common biblical word נמוטו (namotu — 'were shaken') or הוזזו (huzazu — 'were moved').
greek_deviations: MAJOR: Hebrew lacks the entire clause: ὁ οὐρανὸς ἀπεχωρίσθη ὡς βιβλίον ἑλισσόμενον ('the heaven departed as a scroll rolled up'). This is present in Greek but absent from Hebrew.
Hebrew: 'mountains and hills' (הרים וגבעות). Greek: 'mountain and island' (ὄρος καὶ νῆσος). Different second element.
translation_notes: נדעזו is a hapax or extremely rare form. 'Were shaken' captures the evident meaning from context. The form may reflect dialectal or colloquial Hebrew.
textual_notes: Isaiah 54:10 — כִּי הֶהָרִים יָמוּשׁוּ וְהַגְּבָעוֹת תְּמוּטֶינָה ('though the mountains depart and the hills be shaken'). The Hebrew Revelation uses the same mountain-hill pair in the same context of cosmic upheaval.

Note that Isaiah 34:4a (the first half of the verse partially quoted in v.13) says 'the heavens shall be rolled up like a scroll' (ונגלו כספר השמים). The Hebrew Revelation omits this; the Greek preserves it. This suggests the Hebrew author selectively quoted Isaiah 34.

one_way_hebrew: VERBATIM ISAIAH QUOTE: בִּמְעָרוֹת צֻרִים וּבִמְחִלּוֹת עָפָר ('in caves of rocks and in tunnels of dust') is taken directly from Isaiah 2:19 — וּבָאוּ בִּמְעָרוֹת צֻרִים וּבִמְחִלּוֹת עָפָר מִפְּנֵי פַּחַד יְהוָה וּמֵהֲדַר גְּאוֹנוֹ ('and they shall go into caves of rocks and tunnels of dust from before the terror of YHWH and the splendor of his majesty'). The Hebrew preserves Isaiah's EXACT phrasing. Greek has εἰς τὰ σπήλαια καὶ εἰς τὰς πέτρας τῶν ὀρέων ('into the caves and into the rocks of the mountains'). A back-translator from Greek would write במערות ובסלעי ההרים ('in caves and in the rocks of the mountains'), NOT the Isaiah-specific 'tunnels of dust' (מחילות עפר).

Uses רוֹזְנִים (rozenim — 'rulers/dignitaries', H7336). This is an archaic/poetic Hebrew word appearing in Judges 5:3, Psalm 2:2, Proverbs 8:15, 31:4, Isaiah 40:23, Habakkuk 1:10. The pairing מלכי ארץ ורוזנים ('kings of the earth and rulers') directly echoes Psalm 2:2 — יִתְיַצְּבוּ מַלְכֵי אֶרֶץ וְרוֹזְנִים ('the kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers'). Greek μεγιστᾶνες ('great men/magnates') is generic. A back-translator from Greek would use גדולים or שרים, not the archaic Psalm 2 term rozenim.

Uses שׁוֹטְרִים (shotrim — 'officers', H7860). This is a specifically Israelite administrative term for foremen/officials (Ex 5:6,10,14; Deut 1:15, 16:18, 20:5,8,9; Josh 1:10). These are the officers who organized Israel's tribal administration. Greek χιλίαρχοι ('commanders of a thousand') is a Greco-Roman military rank. A back-translator from Greek would write שרי אלפים ('captains of thousands') to mirror the Greek term, not the Torah-specific shotrim.
greek_deviations: Hebrew list: kings, rulers, wealthy, officers, servants, free (6 categories). Greek list: kings, great men, commanders, rich, strong, every slave, every free (7 categories). Greek adds 'strong' (ἰσχυροί) absent from Hebrew.
Hebrew: 'caves of rocks and tunnels of dust' (Isaiah 2:19 verbatim). Greek: 'caves and rocks of the mountains.' Different hiding places.
Hebrew: 'rulers' (rozenim — archaic/Psalm 2). Greek: 'great men' (megistanes). Different social category.
translation_notes: 'Rulers' for rozenim — preserving the Psalm 2 connection and the archaic Hebrew dignity of the term.
'Officers' for shotrim — the Israelite tribal administrative officials, not Roman military commanders.
'Tunnels of dust' for mechilot afar — underground passages in the dry earth, distinct from rocky caves.
textual_notes: Isaiah 2:19-21 is the direct source: 'And they shall go into caves of rocks and tunnels of dust, from before the terror of YHWH and from the splendor of his majesty, when he rises to terrify the earth.' The Hebrew Revelation quotes this passage and then extends it in verses 16-17.

Psalm 2:2 — 'The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers (rozenim) take counsel together against YHWH and against his anointed.' The Psalm 2 language of kings and rulers rebelling against God's authority frames the entire passage.

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew adds הַמַּרְאֶה (ha-mar'eh — 'the appearance/vision', H4758) — entirely absent from Greek. In Ezekiel, God's presence is repeatedly described as a מַרְאֶה (mar'eh — 'appearance/vision'): Ezekiel 1:26-28 ('the appearance of the likeness of the glory of YHWH'), Ezekiel 8:2 ('the appearance of fire'), Ezekiel 10:1. This is an Ezekiel-specific term for theophany. A back-translator from Greek, which has simply ἀπὸ προσώπου τοῦ καθημένου ('from the face of the one sitting'), would not add this Ezekiel technical term.

Uses חֲרוֹן (charon, H2740 — 'burning-wrath'), specifically the fierce/burning anger of God. This word appears 40+ times in the OT (Ex 32:12, Num 25:4, Deut 13:17, Josh 7:26, 2 Kings 23:26, Jer 4:8). Greek ὀργῆς (orges — 'anger/wrath') is generic. A back-translator from Greek would use אף (af), חמה (chemah), or עברה (evrah), not the specific charon which typically pairs with af as חרון אף ('burning of anger') in the OT. The use of charon alone is theologically loaded — it is the BURNING quality of divine wrath.

The phrase מפני ('from the face of') used twice — מפני המראה של זה היושב... ומפני חרון — echoes Isaiah 2:19,21 where the same preposition frames divine terror: מפני פחד יהוה ('from the face of the terror of YHWH'). The Hebrew Revelation continues the Isaiah 2 quotation begun in v.15.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'from the face of the APPEARANCE of the one sitting' (adds mar'eh — theophany term). Greek: 'from the face of the one sitting' (no 'appearance').
Hebrew: 'burning-wrath' (charon — specific burning anger). Greek: 'wrath' (orge — generic anger).
translation_notes: 'Burning-wrath' for charon — this is not merely anger but the burning/fierce quality of divine anger, a technical prophetic term.
'Appearance' for mar'eh — the theophanic vision, how God manifests visibly. These people flee not from God directly but from the visible manifestation of his presence.
textual_notes: Hosea 10:8 — וְאָמְרוּ לֶהָרִים כַּסּוּנוּ וְלַגְּבָעוֹת נִפְלוּ עָלֵינוּ ('and they shall say to the mountains: Cover us, and to the hills: Fall on us'). The Hebrew Revelation echoes Hosea but uses סלעים ('rocks') where Hosea has גבעות ('hills'). Yeshua quotes this Hosea passage in Luke 23:30.

The combined quotation of Isaiah 2:19 (v.15) + Hosea 10:8 (v.16) shows the Hebrew author weaving OT prophetic texts together — a technique characteristic of Hebrew literary composition, not translation.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses חֲרוֹן אַפּוֹ (charon apo — 'the burning of his nostril', H2740 + H639). This is THE standard OT expression for God's fierce anger — an anthropomorphism of God's nostrils flaring with burning wrath. It appears in: Exodus 32:12 ('turn from the burning of your anger'), Numbers 25:4, Deuteronomy 13:17, Joshua 7:26, 2 Kings 23:26, Isaiah 13:9,13, Jeremiah 4:8, 12:13, 25:37, 30:24, 51:45, Lamentations 1:12, 2:1,3, Nahum 1:6, Zephaniah 2:2-3, 3:8, and many more. Greek has ἡ ἡμέρα ἡ μεγάλη τῆς ὀργῆς αὐτοῦ ('the great day of HIS WRATH'). A back-translator from Greek would write יום חרון אפו or more likely יום הגדול של זעמו — but the Hebrew construction 'the day of the burning of his nostril' is the deeply embedded OT prophetic formula that a translator would not independently reconstruct from the Greek. The anthropomorphism (God's nostrils) is uniquely Hebrew.

Hebrew lacks 'great' (μεγάλη). Greek says 'the GREAT day of his wrath.' Hebrew simply says 'the day of his burning-nostril.' The Hebrew is more intimate and visceral; the Greek adds an adjective of magnitude.

Uses מִי יוּכַל לַעֲמוֹד לְפָנָיו ('who is able to stand before him') — the OT idiom עמד לפני (amad lifnei — 'to stand before') denoting being in someone's presence/service (Gen 41:46, 1 Sam 16:22, 1 Kings 1:2, Jer 15:19). This echoes Nahum 1:6: מִי יַעֲמוֹד לִפְנֵי זַעְמוֹ ('who can stand before his fury?') and Malachi 3:2: וּמִי הָעֹמֵד בְּהֵרָאוֹתוֹ ('who can stand when he appears?'). The Hebrew weaves Nahum and Malachi together naturally. Greek σταθῆναι is simply 'to stand' without the interpersonal 'before his face' nuance.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the day of the burning of his nostril' (anthropomorphic — God's nostrils flare). Greek: 'the great day of his wrath' (abstract — magnitude of anger + 'great').
Hebrew: no adjective modifying 'day.' Greek: adds 'great' (μεγάλη).

Greek: τῆς ὀργῆς αὐτοῦ ('of his wrath'). But whose wrath? Greek is ambiguous — it could refer to the one on the throne or the lamb. Hebrew: אפו ('his nostril') with singular suffix, naturally referring to the one on the throne.
translation_notes: 'Burning of his nostril' preserves the Hebrew anthropomorphism. אף (af, H639) literally means 'nose/nostril' and by extension 'anger' (because nostrils flare in anger). חרון אף is literally 'the burning of the nose' — God's nostrils are hot with fury.
'To stand before him' — the language of royal audience. Who can maintain their standing (position/status/courage) in the presence of such wrath?
textual_notes: Nahum 1:6 — לִפְנֵי זַעְמוֹ מִי יַעֲמוֹד וּמִי יָקוּם בַּחֲרוֹן אַפּוֹ ('Before his rage who can stand, and who can rise up against the burning of his anger?'). The Hebrew Revelation combines Nahum's חרון אפו with his מי יעמוד in a single sentence.

Malachi 3:2 — וּמִי מְכַלְכֵּל אֶת יוֹם בּוֹאוֹ וּמִי הָעֹמֵד בְּהֵרָאוֹתוֹ ('And who can endure the day of his coming? And who can stand when he appears?'). The 'day + coming + who can stand' structure is preserved in the Hebrew Revelation.
Zephaniah 2:2-3 — בְּטֶרֶם לֹא בָּא עֲלֵיכֶם חֲרוֹן אַף יְהוָה ('before the burning of YHWH's anger comes upon you'). The same charon af + bo (come) construction.

7.summary: Revelation 7 in Hebrew contains some of the most decisive one-way translation markers in the entire book. The chapter quotes Isaiah 49:10 VERBATIM in v16, preserving the exact word order, the rare vocabulary שָׁרָב (sharav — appearing only in Isa 35:7 and 49:10), and the precise phrasing that the Greek rearranges and expands. It quotes Isaiah 25:8 in v17, preserving 'from upon all faces' (מֵעַל כָּל פָּנִים) where the Greek shifts to 'from their eyes.' The Ezekiel 9:4 תָּו (tav-mark) in v3 is among the strongest one-way markers in all of Revelation — the Hebrew uses the specific prophetic term for the forehead-mark rather than the generic 'sealing' of the Greek. The Psalm 3:9 quotation in v10 (לְיַהְוֶה הַיְשׁוּעָה) is a concise Psalm formula that the Greek expands into a full descriptive clause. The Aramaic חַבְרוּתָה (chavruta — 'fellowship', v9), the Daniel 6:27 paired expression חַי וְקִיֵּים (v2), the priestly-service verb שֵׁרְתוּ (v15), the metallurgical verb זִקְּקוּ ('refined', v14), the generic עֲנָפִים ('branches', v9 — pointing to a Sukkot setting), the distinction between מִשְׁפְּחוֹת (clans, v4) and שֵׁבֶט (tribe, vv5-8), and the feminine verb תָּדוּר (v15 — implying the Shekhinah) all demonstrate Hebrew concepts that could not derive from the Greek text. Multiple Mishnaic Hebrew forms (בִשְׁבִיל, לְהַזִּיק, מֵאֵיזֶה, שׁוּם, חַבְרוּתָה, אֵילּוּ) coexist with biblical Hebrew and Aramaic, consistent with a text composed in the late Second Temple period. The Sukkot imagery of v9 (branches, Psalm-quoting cry of deliverance, standing before the throne) connects to Zechariah 14:16's prophecy that all nations will celebrate Sukkot in the age to come.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מִתְאַפְּקִים (mit'apqim, H662 — hitpael of אפק, 'restraining/holding back'). The hitpael implies the messengers are straining to restrain forces that resist them — holding themselves firm against the winds' pressure. Greek κρατοῦντας ('holding/seizing') is simple active. A back-translator from Greek would use מַחֲזִיקִים (machzikim — 'holding') or אוֹחֲזִים (ochazim — 'grasping'), not the reflexive-intensive hitpael form. Compare Gen 43:31 and 45:1 where Joseph 'restrained himself' (וַיִּתְאַפַּק) — the same root conveying forceful self-control.

Uses הַמַּיִם (ha-mayim — 'the waters', H4325) in v1 but הַיָּם (ha-yam — 'the sea', H3220) in vv2-3. Greek uses θάλασσα ('sea') in all three verses. The Hebrew author DISTINGUISHES: the wind affects all 'waters' (rivers, lakes, seas), but the messengers' commission to 'harm' targets specifically 'the sea.' A back-translator seeing θάλασσα three times in Greek would use יָם three times. The Hebrew variation is deliberate and meaningful.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the waters' (הַמַּיִם). Greek: 'the sea' (τῆς θαλάσσης). Hebrew is broader — all water surfaces.
translation_notes: 'Holding back' for mit'apqim — the hitpael of אפק conveys forceful restraint against resistance, not merely passive holding.
שׁוּם (shum — 'any') is a post-biblical Hebrew word, characteristic of Mishnaic usage.

one_way_hebrew: Uses חוֹתָם (chotam, H2368 — 'seal/signet ring') — the specific OT word for a personal signet used for authentication and identity. Judah's chotam (Gen 38:18), the priestly breastplate engravings 'like the engravings of a chotam' (Ex 28:11,21), and Haggai 2:23 where YHWH makes Zerubbabel 'like a chotam.' Greek σφραγῖδα is a generic 'seal.' The Hebrew word carries the weight of personal identity and covenant authorization.

Uses the paired expression חַי וְקִיֵּים (chai v'qayyem — 'living and enduring'). This matches Daniel 6:27 (Aramaic: חַי וְקַיָּם) where Daniel declares God is 'the living and enduring God.' Greek ζῶντος has only 'living' — omitting the distinctly Aramaic/Daniel term קַיָּם entirely. A back-translator from Greek, seeing only ζῶντος, would write חַי alone, never independently adding the Daniel-specific formula.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'living and enduring' (חַי וְקִיֵּים — paired expression). Greek: 'living' (ζῶντος) only. The Aramaic pair is reduced to a single adjective.
translation_notes: 'From the rising of the sun' (מִמִּזְרַח הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ) is a standard OT phrase for 'from the east' (Deut 4:41, Josh 1:15, Mal 1:11). It is more vivid than a simple directional word.
קִיֵּים (qayyem — 'enduring/established') is a post-biblical/Aramaic form from the root קום. No standard Strong's number.
לְהַזִּיק (lehazziq — 'to harm/damage') is a Mishnaic Hebrew causative form, characteristic of post-biblical Hebrew.
textual_notes: Daniel 6:27 (Aramaic): 'He is the living God and enduring forever' (אֱלָהָא חַיָּא וְקַיָּם לְעָלְמִין). The Hebrew Revelation preserves this Danielic divine description.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses תָּו (tav, H8420 — 'a mark/sign') — the specific word from Ezekiel 9:4 where YHWH commands: 'Pass through Jerusalem and put a תָּו upon the foreheads of the men who sigh and groan over all the abominations.' The Hebrew תָּו is the name of the last letter of the Hebrew alphabet, which in ancient paleo-Hebrew script was written as a cross-mark (×/+). Greek σφραγίσωμεν ('we shall seal') uses a generic sealing verb. A back-translator from Greek would write נַחְתֹּם (nachtom — 'we shall seal') from חתם (H2856), NEVER the Ezekiel-specific תָּו. The Hebrew author sees this scene as the fulfillment of Ezekiel 9.

Uses first person SINGULAR אֶתֵּן (eten — 'I shall place', H5414). Greek has first person PLURAL σφραγίσωμεν ('we shall seal'). The Hebrew presents the messenger acting with sole authority; the Greek implies collective action. A back-translator from the Greek plural would write נחתום ('we shall seal'), not the singular 'I shall place.'

Uses עַבְדֵי יַהְוֶה (avdei YHWH — 'servants of YHWH') with the Tetragrammaton. Greek: τοὺς δούλους τοῦ θεοῦ ἡμῶν ('the servants of our God'). A back-translator from Greek would write עַבְדֵי אֱלֹהֵינוּ ('servants of our Elohim'), not the covenant name YHWH.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: singular 'the tree' (לָעֵץ). Greek: plural 'the trees' (τὰ δένδρα).
Hebrew: 'I shall place a mark' (first singular, action = placing a tav). Greek: 'we shall seal' (first plural, action = sealing). Different person, different verb, different concept.
Hebrew: 'servants of YHWH' (Tetragrammaton). Greek: 'servants of our God' (τοῦ θεοῦ ἡμῶν).
translation_notes: 'Mark' for tav — preserving the Ezekiel 9:4 connection. The tav-mark is not a generic seal but a specific prophetic sign.

The Hebrew distinguishes three concepts across vv2-4: the חוֹתָם (chotam — the seal instrument, v2), the תָּו (tav — the mark placed, v3), and the verb חתם (chatam — the action of sealing, v4). Greek σφραγίς/σφραγίζω collapses all three into one concept.
textual_notes: Ezekiel 9:4,6 — 'Go through the city, through Jerusalem, and put a mark (תָּו) upon the foreheads of the men who sigh and groan over all the abominations... but touch no one upon whom is the mark.' The tav-mark is explicitly a sign of protection from judgment, exactly as in this context.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses מִשְׁפְּחוֹת (mishpechot — 'clans/families', H4940) — the specific Israelite kinship unit BELOW the שֵׁבֶט (tribe) in the biblical hierarchy: tribe → clan → household (see Josh 7:14-18, Num 1:2). Greek ἐκ πάσης φυλῆς ('from every tribe') uses the generic 'tribe' and adds 'every' (πάσης) which is absent from Hebrew. A back-translator from Greek φυλή would use שֵׁבֶט (shevet — 'tribe'), not the more specific mishpachah. The Hebrew author preserves the nuanced Israelite social structure: the sealing penetrates to the clan level within each tribe.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'from the clans' (מִמִּשְׁפְּחוֹת — without 'every'). Greek: 'from every tribe' (ἐκ πάσης φυλῆς — adds 'every' and uses 'tribe' not 'clan').
translation_notes: 'Clans' for mishpechot preserves the Hebrew social hierarchy. The next four verses (5-8) then enumerate by שֵׁבֶט (tribe), showing the Hebrew author uses both terms precisely: sealed at the clan level, listed by tribal identity.
אֵילּוּ (eilu — 'those') is a distinctly post-biblical/Mishnaic Hebrew demonstrative pronoun.
textual_notes: The Hebrew number expression 'a hundred and four and forty thousands' (מֵאָה וְאַרְבַּע וְאַרְבָּעִים אֲלָפִים) = 144,000, following standard Hebrew number order.

one_way_hebrew: Verse 4 uses מִשְׁפְּחוֹת (mishpechot — 'clans') but the enumeration in vv5-8 switches to שֵׁבֶט (shevet — 'tribe'). The Hebrew preserves a distinction between the kinship level of the sealing (clan) and the identity marker of the listing (tribe). Greek uses φυλή ('tribe') throughout, collapsing this distinction.
translation_notes: יְהוּדָא (Yehuda) is spelled with final aleph (א) instead of the standard Hebrew final he (ה) in יְהוּדָה. This Aramaic-influenced spelling appears in Ezra's Aramaic sections (Ezra 5:1,8). This spelling is characteristic of Hebrew/Aramaic manuscript tradition, not a feature a Greek back-translator would introduce.
textual_notes: Dan is absent from this twelve-tribe list; Levi (normally excluded from tribal land allotments) is included. Joseph replaces his son Ephraim. The list begins with Judah (the royal/messianic tribe) rather than Reuben (the firstborn). These rearrangements reflect deliberate theological choices rooted in Hebrew tribal traditions.

translation_notes: Levi's inclusion is notable — Levi is normally excluded from tribal land allotments (Num 18:20-24, Deut 10:9) because 'YHWH is their inheritance.' The inclusion of Levi in this sealing list suggests a priestly identity for the entire sealed community.

יוֹסֵף (Yosef) appears rather than his son אֶפְרַיִם (Ephraim). Since Menasheh (Joseph's other son) is listed separately in v6, Joseph here effectively stands in for Ephraim. This preserves the patriarchal name rather than the tribal subdivision.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses חַבְרוּתָה (chavruta — 'fellowship/company') — a distinctly Aramaic/Mishnaic term for an intimate communal group, later the standard word for a Torah study partnership in rabbinic literature. Greek ὄχλος πολύς ('a great crowd') describes an anonymous mass. A back-translator from Greek would use הָמוֹן (hamon — 'multitude') or קָהָל (qahal — 'assembly'), never the Aramaic-flavored chavruta. The Hebrew envisions this innumerable company as a fellowship, not a crowd.

CRITICAL: Uses עֲנָפִים (anafim — 'branches', H6057) — the GENERIC word for branches of any tree. Greek φοίνικες (phoinikes) specifically means 'palm branches.' A back-translator from Greek would use תְּמָרִים (temarim — 'palms') or כַּפּוֹת תְּמָרִים (kappot temarim — 'palm fronds', as in Lev 23:40). The Hebrew author uses the general word, evoking the Sukkot (Feast of Tabernacles) lulav bundle which includes palm, willow, and myrtle branches (Lev 23:40). The Greek translator narrowed this to palms alone.

Hebrew: מִכָּל הָעַמִּים (mikol ha-amim — 'from all the peoples', one collective term). Greek: ἐκ παντὸς ἔθνους καὶ φυλῶν καὶ λαῶν καὶ γλωσσῶν ('from every nation and tribes and peoples and tongues' — fourfold list). A back-translator from Greek would reproduce the fourfold list. The Hebrew uses a single comprehensive term, the standard OT expression for gentile nations (Deut 7:7, 14:2).
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'a great fellowship' (חַבְרוּתָה גְּדוֹלָה). Greek: 'a great crowd' (ὄχλος πολύς). Different social concept.
Hebrew: 'from all the peoples' (one term). Greek: 'from every nation and tribes and peoples and tongues' (fourfold list). Greek adds 'tribes' and 'tongues' absent from Hebrew.
Hebrew: 'branches' (עֲנָפִים — generic). Greek: 'palm branches' (φοίνικες — specific).
translation_notes: 'Fellowship' for chavruta — this Aramaic term carries connotations of intimate association absent from 'crowd.'

'Branches' for anafim is deliberately generic. In the Sukkot context (Lev 23:40), the commanded set includes 'fruit of goodly trees, branches of palm trees (כַּפֹּת תְּמָרִים), boughs of thick trees (עֲנַף עֵץ עָבוֹת), and willows of the brook.' The word עֲנָף itself appears in the Sukkot passage for the thick-tree boughs.
textual_notes: The Sukkot (Feast of Tabernacles) imagery is unmistakable: a multitude holding branches before YHWH's throne, crying out declarations of salvation. During Sukkot, worshippers wave the lulav bundle and cry הוֹשַׁעְנָא (hoshana — 'save now!'). Zechariah 14:16 prophesies that in the age to come, all nations will go up to Jerusalem to celebrate Sukkot. This scene appears to be its fulfillment.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: לְיַהְוֶה הַיְשׁוּעָה (la-YHWH hayeshu'ah — 'To YHWH belongs the deliverance') is a DIRECT QUOTE from Psalm 3:9 [8]: לַיהוָה הַיְשׁוּעָה ('To YHWH belongs the salvation'). The Hebrew preserves this concise Psalm declaration and extends it: 'and to the lamb.' Greek expands this to Ἡ σωτηρία τῷ θεῷ ἡμῶν τῷ καθημένῳ ἐπὶ τοῦ θρόνου, καὶ τῷ ἀρνίῳ ('Salvation to our God who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb'). A back-translator from the expanded Greek would write הַיְשׁוּעָה לֵאלֹהֵינוּ הַיֹּשֵׁב עַל הַכִּסֵּא, not the compact Psalm 3 quote. The Hebrew is shorter, more elegant, and scripturally rooted; the Greek is a theological expansion.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'To YHWH the deliverance, and to the lamb' (7 words, Psalm quotation). Greek: 'Salvation to our God who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb' (expanded with throne description). The Hebrew is a concise Psalm quote; the Greek is a descriptive expansion.
Hebrew uses the Tetragrammaton (יַהְוֶה). Greek has 'our God' (τῷ θεῷ ἡμῶν).
translation_notes: 'Deliverance' for yeshu'ah (H3444) — the word contains the root of the name Yeshua (ישוע). The Hebrew naturally carries this wordplay; the Greek σωτηρία does not.
The cry structure (l'+dative + noun) is a Hebrew declaration of attribution: 'To X belongs Y.' See also Jonah 2:10 [9]: יְשׁוּעָתָה לַיהוָה ('Deliverance is YHWH's').
textual_notes: Psalm 3:9 [8]: לַיהוָה הַיְשׁוּעָה עַל עַמְּךָ בִרְכָתֶךָ סֶּלָה ('To YHWH belongs the salvation; upon your people your blessing. Selah.'). The Revelation text quotes the first clause and extends it to include the lamb as co-recipient of the declaration.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מִתְפַּלְּלִים (mitpallelim — 'praying', H6419, hitpael of פלל) — the definitive Hebrew word for prayer/intercession (Gen 20:7, 1 Sam 1:10, 1 Kings 8:30, Dan 9:4). Greek: προσεκύνησαν ('worshipped/prostrated'). These are fundamentally different acts — prayer vs. prostration. A back-translator from Greek would write הִשְׁתַּחֲווּ (hishtachavu — 'bowed down/worshipped'), the standard LXX equivalent of προσκυνέω, NOT the prayer verb mitpallelim.

Uses חַיּוֹת (chayyot — 'living-creatures', H2416) — Ezekiel's specific term for the throne-bearing creatures (Ezek 1:5,13-15,19-22; 3:13; 10:15,17,20). This is not a generic word for 'animals' but a technical Ezekiel term. Greek ζῷα ('living beings') is close but lacks the specific Ezekiel resonance.
