Uses מַיִם חַיִּים (mayim chayyim — 'living waters') — a specific Hebrew idiom for flowing spring water (Jer 2:13, 17:13; Zech 14:8; Gen 26:19). Greek has τῆς πηγῆς τοῦ ὕδατος τῆς ζωῆς ('the fountain of the water of life'). A back-translator from Greek would write מעין מים החיים ('fountain of the waters of life'), not the idiomatic mayim chayyim.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the first and the last' (Isaiah quote). Greek: 'the Alpha and the Omega' (Greek letter metaphor). Entirely different expressions.
Hebrew: 'living waters' (two words). Greek: 'the fountain of the water of life' (expanded phrase).
translation_notes: תְּחִילַּת (techilat — 'beginning') lacks a standard Strong's number; it's a later Hebrew form from the root חלל.

'Living waters' is the idiomatic English rendering of mayim chayyim — water that flows (as opposed to stagnant cistern water). See Jeremiah 2:13 where YHWH calls himself 'the fountain of living waters.'
textual_notes: Isaiah 44:6 — 'Thus says YHWH, the King of Israel and his Redeemer, YHWH of hosts: I am the first and I am the last; besides me there is no god.' The speaker on the throne uses YHWH's own self-declaration from Isaiah.

translation_notes: אֶהְיֶה (ehyeh — 'I shall be') appears in brackets [אֶהְיֶה] in the source text, suggesting editorial restoration. This is the same form God uses in Exodus 3:14 (אֶהְיֶה אֲשֶׁר אֶהְיֶה — 'I will be what I will be').
'Heir' for yoresh (H3423) — the root ירש means to possess/inherit, used of Israel inheriting the Promised Land.
textual_notes: Echoes 2 Samuel 7:14 — 'I will be his father, and he shall be my son.' The Davidic covenant promise extended to all overcomers.

one_way_hebrew: Uses שְׂכָרָם (secharam — 'their wages', H7939). Greek has τὸ μέρος αὐτῶν ('their portion/part'). A back-translator from Greek would use חֵלֶק (cheleq — 'portion'), not שָׂכָר (sachar — 'wage'). The Hebrew implies payment earned by deeds; the Greek implies an allotted share.

CRITICAL: Uses מֵאֵשׁ הַשְּׁאוֹל ('from the fire of Sheol', H7585). Greek has ἐν τῇ λίμνῃ τῇ καιομένῃ ('in the lake that burns'). Sheol (שאול) is the Hebrew underworld — a deeply rooted OT concept (Gen 37:35, Num 16:30, Deut 32:22, Ps 16:10, 86:13, Isa 14:9). A back-translator from Greek 'lake' (λίμνη) would write אֲגַם אֵשׁ ('lake of fire'), NOT 'fire of Sheol.' The 'lake of fire' is a Greek concept; 'fire of Sheol' is a Hebrew one.
greek_deviations: Hebrew list: unbelievers, murderers, fornicators, sorcerers, liars (5 categories). Greek list: cowardly, unbelieving, abominable, murderers, fornicators, sorcerers, IDOLATERS, all liars (8 categories). Greek adds cowardly (δειλοῖς), abominable (ἐβδελυγμένοις), and idolaters (εἰδωλολάτραις).
Hebrew: 'fire of Sheol.' Greek: 'lake of fire.' Entirely different imagery.
translation_notes: כַּזְבָנִים (kazbanim — 'liars') is a later Hebrew agentive form from כזב (kazav — to lie). No standard Strong's number.
'Wages' for sechar captures the Hebrew concept of earned recompense — you labored in evil, here is your pay.
textual_notes: Deuteronomy 32:22 — 'For a fire is kindled in my anger, and it burns to the depths of Sheol.' The Hebrew concept of fire in Sheol has deep OT roots. The Greek 'lake of fire' concept appears to be a reinterpretation.

one_way_hebrew: Uses נְגָעִים (nega'im — 'plagues/afflictions', H5061) — the specific Levitical word for plagues of Egypt (Ex 11:1) and skin diseases requiring priestly inspection (Lev 13-14). Greek πληγῶν ('blows/plagues') is generic. A back-translator could use מַכּוֹת (makot — 'blows/plagues') but the author specifically chose the Levitical term.

Uses שֶׂה (seh — 'lamb', H7716) — the specific Passover lamb word from Exodus 12:3-5 (שֶׂה לְבֵית אָבוֹת — 'a lamb per household'). Greek ἀρνίον is a generic diminutive 'little lamb.' A back-translator would more likely use כֶּבֶשׂ (keves) or טָלֶה (taleh). The use of seh ties the Lamb directly to the Passover.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the woman, the bride' (אשה then כלה). Greek: 'the bride, the woman' (νύμφην then γυναῖκα). Reversed order.
translation_notes: 'Plagues' for nega'im — preserving the Levitical/Exodus connection.
'Lamb' for seh — the Passover-specific term, distinguishing it from generic words for sheep.

greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'he led me' (ונהג אותי). Greek: 'he carried me away in the spirit' (ἀπήνεγκέ με ἐν πνεύματι). Greek adds 'in the spirit' which is absent from Hebrew.
Hebrew: 'from heavens to the earth.' Greek: 'from heaven from God' (ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ ἀπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ). Again, Greek adds 'from God.'
translation_notes: נִהַג (nihag, H5090) means 'to lead/drive/guide' — used of leading flocks (Gen 31:18, Isa 11:6) and driving chariots. Concrete and physical, unlike the Greek 'carried away in spirit.'
textual_notes: Echoes Ezekiel 40:2 — 'he brought me to the land of Israel and set me on a very high mountain, on which was a structure like a city.' The great and high mountain vision is an Ezekiel pattern.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מְאוֹרָהּ (me'orah — 'her luminary', H3974) — the SAME word from Genesis 1:14-16 for the sun, moon, and stars (מְאֹרֹת). The New Jerusalem's light is described using creation language. Greek φωστήρ could be translated several ways; a back-translator would more likely use אוֹר (or — 'light') or נֵר (ner — 'lamp').

Uses אֶבֶן טוֹבָה ('goodly stone') — the standard OT term for precious gems (Gen 2:12, 1 Kings 10:2). Greek has λίθῳ τιμιωτάτῳ ('most precious stone'). A back-translator would use אבן יקרה ('precious stone'), not the OT-specific אבן טובה.
greek_deviations: Greek adds κρυσταλλίζοντι ('crystal-clear/sparkling') which is absent from Hebrew.
translation_notes: 'Luminary' for ma'or preserves the Genesis creation connection — the same word for the heavenly lights.
'Splendor' for tiferet (H8597) captures the beauty/glory/ornamental nuance that 'glory' alone misses.

greek_deviations: Greek adds 'and high' (καὶ ὑψηλόν) to describe the wall — absent from Hebrew.
Hebrew: 'of Yisrael.' Greek: 'of the sons of Israel' (τῶν υἱῶν Ἰσραήλ). Greek adds 'sons of.'
Greek: names 'inscribed/written' (ἐπιγεγραμμένα). Hebrew just says 'names' without specifying they were written.
translation_notes: Note the gender mismatch: חוֹמָה (feminine) with גְּדוֹלִים (masculine plural). This may indicate 'great walls' as a composite structure, or it may be a textual peculiarity.
textual_notes: Echoes Ezekiel 48:30-35 which describes gates named after the twelve tribes.

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew order: East, West, North, South. Greek order: East, North, South, West. The Hebrew follows a Hebrew-centric orientation where East (mizrach — 'place of rising') is primary, then its opposite West, then North-South. A back-translator from Greek would preserve the Greek order.
greek_deviations: Direction order differs: Hebrew E-W-N-S vs. Greek E-N-S-W.
textual_notes: Matches Ezekiel 48:30-34 which lists gates by direction, though Ezekiel's order is also different (N-E-S-W).

one_way_hebrew: Uses שְׁלוּחִים (sheluchim — 'sent-ones', from shalach H7971) — a native Hebrew word meaning 'emissaries/delegates.' Greek has ἀποστόλων ('apostles'). If the Hebrew were a back-translation from Greek, the translator would almost certainly transliterate as אפוסטולים. The use of the native Hebrew sheluchim strongly suggests Hebrew priority.
translation_notes: 'Sent-ones' for sheluchim — preserving the Hebrew meaning without importing the Greek loanword 'apostle.'

greek_deviations: Hebrew: city, wall, gates. Greek: city, gates, wall. Different order.
translation_notes: קָנֶה (qaneh, H7070 — 'reed') — the same word used for Ezekiel's measuring reed (Ezek 40:3,5). The vision deliberately parallels Ezekiel's temple measurement.
textual_notes: Ezekiel 40:3 — 'a man whose appearance was like bronze, with a linen cord and a measuring reed (קנה) in his hand.' Same tool, different material (gold here vs. unspecified in Ezekiel).

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses קִבְרוֹת הַשָּׂדֶה ('field-plots') as the unit of measurement. Greek has σταδίων ('stadia' — a Greek unit). A back-translator from Greek would transliterate as סטאדיון or use a standard Hebrew measure like אמה (cubit). The Hebrew uses a uniquely Hebraic land-measurement idiom that has no connection to the Greek unit. The Greek translator converted the unfamiliar Hebrew unit to a familiar Greek one.

Uses מוּנָּח (munach — 'resting/placed', from nuach H5117 — to rest). This is the root of Noah's name and carries connotations of sabbath rest. Greek κεῖται ('lies/is situated') is neutral. A back-translator from Greek would use שוכב (shochev) or מונח is possible but the nuach/rest theological layer would be accidental.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'twelve thousand field-plots' (קברות השדה). Greek: 'twelve thousand stadia' (σταδίων). Entirely different measurement unit.
translation_notes: קִבְרוֹת (qivrot) — possibly related to measured burial plots (from קבר, qever — 'grave/plot') used as a land-area unit. Compare Kibroth-hattaavah (Num 11:34). The meaning is 'measured field sections.'
'Lay at rest' for munach captures the nuach/rest theology.

greek_deviations: Greek adds ὅμοιον ὑάλῳ καθαρῷ ('like clear glass') — absent from Hebrew. The Hebrew is more concise.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: The text explicitly marks קאלקידניר as בְּלַעַז ('in a foreign tongue'). A Hebrew author encountering a stone without a Hebrew name self-consciously flags it as foreign. A back-translator from Greek would simply transliterate without this meta-linguistic awareness. This is one of the strongest proofs of Hebrew authorship in the entire chapter.

Uses נֹפֶךְ (nofech, H5306) for the fourth stone — the High Priest's breastplate stone from Exodus 28:18 and 39:11. Greek has σμάραγδος ('emerald'). A back-translator would transliterate σμάραγδος, not reach back to the Torah's priestly gemstone vocabulary.
greek_deviations: Stone identifications differ between Hebrew and Greek for several positions, suggesting independent traditions rather than translation.
translation_notes: Preserving '(in foreign tongue)' as it appears in the Hebrew — this is part of the original text's self-awareness about borrowing non-Hebrew terms.
'Goodly stones' (אבנים טובים) rather than 'precious stones' — the Hebrew uses טוב ('good') not יקר ('precious'), matching OT usage (Gen 2:12).
textual_notes: The use of Torah breastplate stone names (Exodus 28:17-20) shows the author connecting the New Jerusalem's foundations to the priestly garments — the city itself becomes a priestly structure.

one_way_hebrew: ALL stone names are from the High Priest's breastplate (Exodus 28:17-20): אֹדֶם (odem), שֹׁהַם (shoham), אַחְלָמָה (achlamah), תַּרְשִׁישׁ (tarshish), פִּטְדָה (pitdah), שְׁבוֹ (shevo), לֶשֶׁם (leshem). These are Torah-specific gemstone vocabulary. A back-translator from Greek would transliterate the Greek names (σαρδόνυξ, σάρδιος, χρυσόλιθος, βήρυλλος, τοπάζιον, χρυσόπρασος, ὑάκινθος), not independently reconstruct the Exodus breastplate vocabulary.
Again marks the final stone בְּלַעַז ('in foreign tongue') — a second instance of the Hebrew author's meta-linguistic self-awareness.
greek_deviations: Stone identifications do not match Greek 1:1. E.g., Hebrew 5th = אדם (ruby/carnelian); Greek 5th = σαρδόνυξ (sardonyx). Hebrew 6th = שהם (onyx); Greek 6th = σάρδιος (sardius/carnelian). This suggests independent tradition.
translation_notes: Stone name identifications follow the standard OT identifications from Exodus. The exact modern mineral correspondence is debated for several of these.
textual_notes: The full breastplate stone list in Exodus 28:17-20: Row 1: אדם, פטדה, ברקת. Row 2: נפך, ספיר, יהלם. Row 3: לשם, שבו, אחלמה. Row 4: תרשיש, שהם, ישפה. The Hebrew Revelation redistributes these across twelve foundations.

one_way_hebrew: Uses רְחוֹבוֹת (rechovot — 'plazas/broad places', H7339, PLURAL). Greek has πλατεῖα (singular 'street'). The Hebrew naturally uses plural for a city's public spaces.

Uses צְלוֹחִית (tselochit — 'flask/vial') where Greek has ὕαλος ('glass'). A back-translator from Greek would use זכוכית (zechuchit — 'glass'), not the Hebrew word for a vessel/flask. Different metaphor entirely.
translation_notes: זַךְ (zach, H2134 — 'pure/clear') is an OT word (Job 8:6, Prov 16:2, 20:11, Lam 4:7).

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses TWO different terms: בֵּית הַתְּפִילָּה ('house of prayer', H8605) for what was NOT seen, and בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ ('house of the sanctuary', H4720) for what YHWH IS. Greek uses ναός ('temple') for both. A back-translator from Greek, seeing the same word ναός twice, would use the same Hebrew word both times. The Hebrew author distinguishes between a prayer house (synagogue-type) and the actual sanctuary (mikdash).

Uses יַהְוֶה צְבָאוֹת (YHWH Tsevaot — 'YHWH of Hosts/Armies', H6635) — a specific compound divine name occurring 285 times in the OT. Greek has κύριος ὁ θεὸς ὁ παντοκράτωρ ('Lord God Almighty'). A back-translator from Greek would write אֲדֹנָי אֱלֹהִים שַׁדַּי or similar, NOT the specific OT name YHWH Tsevaot.
translation_notes: 'House of prayer' echoes Isaiah 56:7 — 'my house shall be called a house of prayer (בֵּית תְּפִלָּה) for all peoples' — which Yeshua quotes in Matt 21:13.
'House of the sanctuary' (beit hamikdash) is the standard Hebrew term for the Temple.

greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'its light is the lamb' (אורה — 'light'). Greek: 'its lamp (λύχνος) is the Lamb.' Hebrew uses אוֹר (elemental light); Greek uses λύχνος (a household lamp). Different scale of imagery.
translation_notes: מָאוֹר (ma'or, H3974) again — the Genesis 1:14-16 creation word. YHWH's glory replaces the sun and moon as the city's luminary, just as the luminaries served in the original creation.
textual_notes: Isaiah 60:19-20 — 'The sun shall be no more your light by day, nor for brightness shall the moon give you light; but YHWH will be your everlasting light, and your God will be your glory.' The Hebrew preserves this Isaiah connection directly.

one_way_hebrew: Uses הָעַמִּים הַקְּדוֹשִׁים ('the holy peoples', H6918). Greek has τὰ ἔθνη τῶν σωζομένων ('the nations of those being saved'). 'Holy peoples' (amim kedoshim) echoes the OT concept of a 'holy nation' (goy kadosh, Ex 19:6) extended to plural peoples. A back-translator from Greek would write העמים הנושעים ('the saved peoples'), not 'the holy peoples.'

Uses חֵילָם (cheilam — 'their resources/wealth/strength', H2428). Greek has δόξαν καὶ τιμήν ('glory and honor'). The Hebrew חיל encompasses wealth, military might, and productive capacity — an untranslatable Hebrew concept. A back-translator from Greek would use כבוד ויקר ('glory and honor').
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'holy peoples.' Greek: 'saved nations.' Different qualifying attribute.
Hebrew: 'their resources' (one word — חיל). Greek: 'glory and honor' (two words). Different concepts entirely.
translation_notes: 'Resources' for chayil — this word covers wealth, military strength, valor, and productive capability. It's the word used in Proverbs 31:10 for the 'woman of chayil.'
textual_notes: Isaiah 60:3,5 — 'Nations shall come to your light, and kings to the brightness of your rising... the wealth (חיל) of the nations shall come to you.' The Hebrew Revelation quotes Isaiah 60 with the same word חיל.

one_way_hebrew: VERBATIM QUOTE from Isaiah 60:11 — וּפִתְּחוּ שְׁעָרַיִךְ תָּמִיד יוֹמָם וָלַיְלָה לֹא יִסָּגֵרוּ. The Hebrew preserves Isaiah's exact words INCLUDING the 2nd person address שְׁעָרַיִךְ ('YOUR gates' — feminine singular suffix). Greek has αὐτῆς ('HER gates' — 3rd person). A back-translator from Greek, which has 3rd person 'its/her gates,' would NEVER switch to 2nd person 'your gates.' This is perhaps the single clearest one-way translation marker in the entire chapter.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'your gates' (2nd person, quoting Isaiah). Greek: 'its gates' (3rd person).
Hebrew: 'day and night they shall not be shut' (preserving Isaiah's full phrase). Greek: only 'by day' (ἡμέρας) — drops 'and night.'
translation_notes: Translated in 2nd person to preserve the Isaiah quotation: 'your gates shall be open continually.'
textual_notes: Isaiah 60:11 (exact source text): וּפִתְּחוּ שְׁעָרַיִךְ תָּמִיד יוֹמָם וָלַיְלָה לֹא יִסָּגֵרוּ לְהָבִיא אֵלַיִךְ חֵיל גּוֹיִם — 'And your gates shall be open continually; day and night they shall not be shut, to bring to you the wealth of nations.' The next verse (v26) fulfills the second half of this Isaiah prophecy.

greek_deviations: Hebrew: תפארת וכבוד ('splendor and glory'). Greek: δόξαν καὶ τιμήν ('glory and honor'). Different word pair. Hebrew tiferet ('splendor/beauty') ≠ Greek doxa ('glory'); Hebrew kavod ('glory/weight') ≠ Greek time ('honor').
textual_notes: Continues the Isaiah 60:11 fulfillment — the wealth/glory of nations being brought into the city.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses זָר (zar — 'stranger/unauthorized one', H2114). This is the specific Torah term for someone not authorized to approach holy space — used in Numbers 1:51, 3:10, 3:38, 18:4, 18:7 for non-priests approaching the Tabernacle ('the stranger who comes near shall be put to death'). Greek has πᾶν κοινοῦν ('anything defiled/common'). A back-translator from Greek would write כל טמא ('anything unclean') or כל חול ('anything common'), NOT the Levitical-priestly term zar. The Hebrew author sees the New Jerusalem as sacred priestly space where the 'unauthorized' may not approach.

Uses יִקְרַב (yiqrav — 'shall come near/approach', H7126) — the specific priestly term for approaching the altar/holy place (Lev 1:3, 9:7, 16:1, Num 16:40, 18:3). Greek εἰσέλθῃ means simply 'enter.' A back-translator from Greek would use יבוא (yavo — 'enter'), not the priestly-approach verb qarav.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'a stranger shall not come near to HIM' (אליו — masculine singular, possibly YHWH). Greek: 'anything defiled shall not enter into IT' (εἰς αὐτήν — feminine, the city). Different subject restriction (unauthorized person vs. defiled thing) and different referent (him vs. it).
Greek adds 'doing abomination and lying' (ποιοῦν βδέλυγμα καὶ ψεῦδος) — an expanded list absent from the concise Hebrew.
Hebrew: 'the scroll of life' (ספר החיים). Greek: 'the book of life of the Lamb' (βιβλίῳ τῆς ζωῆς τοῦ ἀρνίου). Greek adds 'of the Lamb.'
translation_notes: 'Stranger' for zar — this is NOT a xenophobic term but a priestly/Levitical concept about authorization to enter holy space. The New Jerusalem is the ultimate Holy of Holies.
'Come near' for yiqrav — the specific priestly approach verb, distinguishing this from merely 'entering.'
textual_notes: Psalm 69:28 (Hebrew) — 'Let them be blotted out of the book of the living (ספר חיים).' The Hebrew phrase 'sefer hachayyim' connects to this OT precedent.
The masculine אליו ('to him') may refer to YHWH rather than the city, making this a statement about approaching God's presence — consistent with the Levitical zar restriction.

22.summary: Revelation 22 in Hebrew is saturated with verbatim OT quotations and Torah-specific vocabulary that could not plausibly derive from the Greek text. The chapter contains at least 20 clear one-way translation markers. The most decisive are: (1) Verse 5 — VERBATIM Isaiah 60:19, word for word, including 2nd person feminine address (לָךְ, אלהיִךְ, תפארתֵּךְ), where the Greek is a complete 3rd-person rephrasing with zero Isaiah vocabulary. (2) Verse 2 — VERBATIM Ezekiel 47:12, preserving the prophet's exact syntax (ועל הנחל יעלה על שפתו מזה ומזה כל עץ מאכל... פריו למאכל ועלהו לתרופה), PLUS the insertion of Genesis 2:9's 'tree of life' — merging two OT streams. (3) Verse 17 — Isaiah 55:1 quotation (לכו למים חיים... בלוא כסף ובלוא מחיר). (4) Verse 13 — 'the first and the last' (Isaiah 44:6) instead of 'Alpha and Omega.' (5) Verse 3 — חרם (cherem, the sacred ban — Zechariah 14:11 verbatim) instead of 'curse.' (6) Verses 18-19 — the יוסיף/יגרע (add/diminish) verb pair from Deuteronomy 4:2, with verse 19 using Exodus 32:33's מחה (blot out) language. (7) Verse 21 — חסד (covenant loyalty) closing the book instead of χάρις (grace). The systematic differences — prayer vs. worship (vv. 8-9), holy vs. blessed (vv. 7, 14), pious vs. righteous (v. 11), living waters vs. water of life (vv. 1, 17), YHWH of Hosts vs. 'God of the spirits of the prophets' (v. 6), edah vs. churches (v. 16), cherem vs. curse (v. 3), and the blotting-out of the NAME vs. removal of a PORTION (v. 19) — reveal two texts with fundamentally different theological vocabularies. The Hebrew thinks in Levitical categories (tamei/kadosh, chasid, cherem, nega'im, sharat), quotes the prophets verbatim, and uses priestly terminology throughout. The Greek operates with its own conceptual framework. The direction of dependence is clear: the Hebrew is the source.

one_way_hebrew: Uses נַחַל (nachal, H5158 — 'wadi/torrent-stream') — a seasonal watercourse carved into rock, fed by rain or springs (Gen 26:19, Deut 2:13, Ps 110:7). Greek has ποταμόν ('river' — a permanent, major waterway). A back-translator from Greek would use נָהָר (nahar — 'river'), not nachal. The wadi is a distinctly Semitic landscape feature; the Greek translator upgraded it to a river.

Uses מַיִם חַיִּים (mayim chayyim — 'living waters') — the Hebrew idiom for flowing spring water (Gen 26:19, Jer 2:13, 17:13, Zech 14:8). Greek has ὕδατος ζωῆς ('water of life'). 'Living waters' in Hebrew means water that MOVES (as opposed to stagnant cistern water); 'water of life' in Greek means water that grants eternal life. A back-translator from Greek would write מֵי הַחַיִּים ('waters of THE life'), not the idiomatic mayim chayyim.

Uses כְּאַחְלָמָה (ke-achlamah, H306 — 'like crystal/amethyst') — a High Priest breastplate stone from Exodus 28:19 and 39:12. Greek has ὡς κρύσταλλον ('like crystal'). A back-translator from Greek would write כבדולח or כקרח ('like ice/crystal'), not the Torah's priestly gemstone vocabulary.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: nachal ('wadi'). Greek: ποταμόν ('river'). Different watercourse entirely.
Hebrew: 'full of living waters' (מלא ממים חיים). Greek: 'pure/clean water of life' (καθαρὸν ὕδατος ζωῆς). Hebrew emphasizes abundance and flow; Greek emphasizes purity and eternal life.
Hebrew: 'like achlamah' (breastplate stone). Greek: 'like crystal' (κρύσταλλον). Different comparison.
translation_notes: 'Wadi' for nachal preserves the specific Semitic landscape term — a torrent that flows through a rocky channel, often seasonal but here perpetually fed from the throne.
'Living waters' for mayim chayyim is the standard English rendering of this Hebrew idiom. See Jeremiah 2:13 where YHWH calls himself 'the fountain of living waters' (מְקוֹר מַיִם חַיִּים).
textual_notes: Zechariah 14:8 — 'And on that day living waters (מַיִם חַיִּים) shall go out from Yerushalayim.' The Hebrew Revelation preserves the prophetic idiom verbatim.
Ezekiel 47:1-12 describes water flowing from the threshold of the Temple eastward. The Hebrew nachal in Revelation connects to the nachal in Ezekiel's vision.

one_way_hebrew: VERBATIM QUOTE from Ezekiel 47:12: וְעַל הַנַּחַל יַעֲלֶה עַל שְׂפָתוֹ מִזֶּה וּמִזֶּה כָּל עֵץ מַאֲכָל... וְהָיָה פִרְיוֹ לְמַאֲכָל וְעָלֵהוּ לִתְרוּפָה. The Hebrew preserves Ezekiel's exact phrasing word for word — nachal, ya'aleh, sefato, mizzeh umizzeh, kol ets ma'achal, piryo lema'achal, alehu litrupah. Greek Revelation completely restructures this: ξύλον ζωῆς ποιοῦν καρποὺς δώδεκα ('tree of life bearing twelve fruits'). A back-translator from Greek would NEVER reconstruct Ezekiel 47:12 verbatim.

CRITICAL: Hebrew has BOTH כָּל עֵץ מַאֲכָל ('every tree of food') AND עֵץ הַחַיִּים ('the tree of life'). Greek has ONLY ξύλον ζωῆς ('tree of life'). The Hebrew merges Ezekiel's 'every food tree' with Genesis 2:9's 'tree of life' — two OT streams flowing together. A back-translator from Greek, which has only 'tree of life,' would never add 'every tree of food.'
Uses רְחוֹבוֹת (rechovot — 'plazas/broad places', H7339, PLURAL). Greek has τῆς πλατείας (singular 'street'). Same plural usage as 21:21.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: Ezekiel 47:12 verbatim with the tree of life added. Greek: restructured into its own syntax.
Hebrew: 'every tree of food AND the tree of life.' Greek: only 'tree of life.' Hebrew has both; Greek dropped the Ezekiel food-trees.
Greek adds κατὰ μῆνα ἕνα ἕκαστον ἀποδιδοῦν τὸν καρπὸν αὐτοῦ ('each month yielding its fruit') — the monthly cycle detail absent from Hebrew.
Hebrew: 'its leaf for healing' (singular leaf, unqualified). Greek: τὰ φύλλα τοῦ ξύλου εἰς θεραπείαν τῶν ἐθνῶν ('the leaves of the tree for healing of the nations'). Greek adds 'of the nations.'
translation_notes: 'Bank' for sefat (H8193 — literally 'lip') — the standard Hebrew word for a riverbank (Gen 41:3, Ex 2:3, Ezek 47:7).
תְּרוּפָה (terupah, H8644 — 'healing/medicine') from the root רפא (to heal). This word occurs in Ezekiel 47:12 and nowhere else in the OT — its appearance here confirms the direct Ezekiel quotation.
textual_notes: Ezekiel 47:12 (source text): וְעַל הַנַּחַל יַעֲלֶה עַל שְׂפָתוֹ מִזֶּה וּמִזֶּה כָּל עֵץ מַאֲכָל לֹא יִבּוֹל עָלֵהוּ וְלֹא יִתֹּם פִּרְיוֹ לָחֳדָשָׁיו יְבַכֵּר כִּי מֵימָיו מִן הַמִּקְדָּשׁ הֵמָּה יוֹצְאִים וְהָיָה פִרְיוֹ לְמַאֲכָל וְעָלֵהוּ לִתְרוּפָה. The Hebrew Revelation quotes the beginning and ending of this verse nearly verbatim, inserting 'the tree of life' from Genesis 2:9.

Genesis 2:9 — 'And YHWH Elohim caused to grow every tree pleasant to sight and good for food, and the tree of life (עֵץ הַחַיִּים) in the midst of the garden.' The Hebrew author sees the New Jerusalem as Eden restored, merging Genesis 2 with Ezekiel 47.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses חֵרֶם (cherem, H2764 — 'the ban/devoted destruction'). This is the specific Torah term for total consecrated destruction — the annihilation of Jericho (Josh 6:17-18), the punishment for Achan's theft (Josh 7:1,11-12), the destruction of the Canaanites (Deut 7:2, 20:17). Greek has κατάθεμα ('curse'). A back-translator from Greek would use קְלָלָה (qelalah — 'curse') or אָלָה (alah — 'oath-curse'), NOT the weighty Torah concept of cherem. The Hebrew declares that the sacred ban — the mechanism of total destruction under YHWH's wrath — shall cease to exist.

Uses יִשְׁכּוֹן (yishkon, H7931 — 'shall dwell/tabernacle'), from the root שכן (shakan) — the root of שְׁכִינָה (Shekinah, the divine presence). Greek has ἔσται ('shall be'). The Hebrew says the throne TABERNACLES there — the Shekinah glory dwells. A back-translator from Greek would write יהיה ('shall be'), not the theologically loaded yishkon.

Uses יְשָׁרְתוּהוּ (yeshartuhu — 'shall minister to him', H8334) — the specific verb for Levitical/priestly ministry (Ex 28:35, Num 3:6, 1 Sam 2:11, Ezek 44:11). Greek has λατρεύσουσιν ('shall serve/worship'). The Hebrew specifies priestly liturgical service; the Greek uses generic worship. A back-translator from Greek would use יעבדו (ya'avdu — 'serve') or ישתחוו (yishtachavu — 'bow down'), not the priestly ministry verb sharat.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: חרם ('the ban/devoted destruction'). Greek: κατάθεμα ('curse'). Entirely different concepts — sacred total destruction vs. a pronouncement of curse.
Hebrew: 'shall tabernacle' (ישכון — Shekinah root). Greek: 'shall be' (ἔσται). The Hebrew adds the dwelling/tabernacle theology.
translation_notes: 'Ban' for cherem captures the Torah concept without the full phrase 'devoted to destruction.' The cherem is the most extreme form of YHWH's judgment — total, irrevocable destruction (cf. Zechariah 14:11 — 'there shall be no more cherem').
'Tabernacle' for yishkon makes the Shekinah connection explicit. The throne does not merely exist in the city — it dwells there as YHWH dwelt in the Tabernacle.
'Minister' for yeshartu distinguishes Levitical priestly service from generic worship or servitude.
textual_notes: Zechariah 14:11 — וְחֵרֶם לֹא יִהְיֶה עוֹד ('and the cherem shall not be anymore'). The Hebrew Revelation quotes Zechariah 14:11 verbatim. The Greek translator paraphrased this as 'no more curse' (κατάθεμα), losing the Zechariah source.

translation_notes: The promise 'they shall see his face' reverses Exodus 33:20 — 'You cannot see my face, for no man shall see me and live.' In the renewed creation, the barrier is removed.
מִצְחֵיהֶם (mitscheihem — 'their foreheads', H4696) — the same word used in Ezekiel 9:4 where the righteous are marked on the forehead (מֵצַח) for preservation.
textual_notes: Psalm 17:15 — 'As for me, I shall behold your face in righteousness; I shall be satisfied when I awake with your likeness.' The face-to-face vision of God is the ultimate hope of the Psalms.

one_way_hebrew: VERBATIM QUOTE from Isaiah 60:19: לֹא־יִהְיֶה־לָּךְ עוֹד הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ לְאוֹר יוֹמָם וּלְנֹגַהּ הַיָּרֵחַ לֹא־יָאִיר לָךְ וְהָיָה־לָךְ יְהוָה לְאוֹר עוֹלָם וֵאלֹהַיִךְ לְתִפְאַרְתֵּךְ. The Hebrew Revelation reproduces Isaiah 60:19 WORD FOR WORD, including: (1) the 2nd person address לָךְ ('to you'), (2) the specific word נֹגַהּ ('brightness', H5051), (3) the divine name YHWH, (4) אוֹר עוֹלָם ('everlasting light'), and (5) the final phrase וֵאלֹהַיִךְ לְתִפְאַרְתֵּךְ ('and your Elohim for your splendor'). Greek Revelation 22:5 says: καὶ νὺξ οὐκ ἔσται ἐκεῖ, καὶ χρείαν οὐκ ἔχουσιν λύχνου καὶ φωτὸς ἡλίου, ὅτι κύριος ὁ θεὸς φωτιεῖ αὐτούς ('and night shall not be there, and they have no need of lamp nor light of sun, for the Lord God will illuminate them'). The Greek is a COMPLETE REPHRASING — 3rd person, no Isaiah vocabulary, no נגה, no תפארת, no direct quotation whatsoever. This is among the single strongest one-way markers in all of Revelation.

The Hebrew preserves Isaiah's 2nd person feminine singular address (לָךְ, אלהיִךְ, תפארתֵּךְ) — speaking directly to Jerusalem. Greek uses 3rd person plural (αὐτούς — 'them'). A back-translator from Greek's 3rd person would NEVER switch to 2nd person feminine singular, let alone reproduce Isaiah 60:19 verbatim.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: VERBATIM Isaiah 60:19 in 2nd person feminine singular. Greek: entirely restructured paraphrase in 3rd person plural.

Hebrew: 'the sun shall not be anymore for light by day, nor for brightness shall the moon give light to you.' Greek: 'they have no need of lamp nor light of sun.' Greek drops the moon, adds 'lamp,' changes the syntax entirely.
Hebrew: 'and your Elohim for your splendor' (תפארתך). Greek: completely absent — no equivalent at all.
Greek adds 'and they shall reign forever and ever' (βασιλεύσουσιν εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων) — absent from the Hebrew.
translation_notes: Translated in 2nd person feminine singular to preserve the Isaiah quotation: 'to you,' 'your Elohim,' 'your splendor.' The city is addressed as a woman, consistent with Jerusalem-as-bride throughout.
'Splendor' for tiferet (H8597) — the same word used for the High Priest's garments (Ex 28:2, 28:40) meaning beauty/glory/ornamental splendor. YHWH himself becomes the city's adornment.
textual_notes: Isaiah 60:19 (exact source): לֹא־יִהְיֶה־לָּךְ עוֹד הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ לְאוֹר יוֹמָם וּלְנֹגַהּ הַיָּרֵחַ לֹא־יָאִיר לָךְ וְהָיָה־לָךְ יְהוָה לְאוֹר עוֹלָם וֵאלֹהַיִךְ לְתִפְאַרְתֵּךְ. Isaiah 60:20 continues: לֹא־יָבוֹא עוֹד שִׁמְשֵׁךְ וִירֵחֵךְ לֹא יֵאָסֵף כִּי יְהוָה יִהְיֶה־לָּךְ לְאוֹר עוֹלָם וְשָׁלְמוּ יְמֵי אֶבְלֵךְ ('Your sun shall not set anymore, and your moon shall not withdraw itself, for YHWH shall be to you an everlasting light, and the days of your mourning shall be completed'). The Hebrew Revelation quotes v19 verbatim; the concept of v20 (end of mourning) was fulfilled in 21:4.

This Isaiah 60:19 verbatim quote in a Hebrew text of Revelation is perhaps the most decisive evidence for Hebrew priority in the entire book. No back-translator from the Greek paraphrase could reconstruct the original Isaiah prophecy word for word.

one_way_hebrew: Uses יַהְוֶה צְבָאוֹת (YHWH Tsevaot — 'YHWH of Hosts/Armies', H6635) — the specific compound divine name occurring 285 times in the OT prophets (Isa 1:9, 6:3; Jer 7:3; Hag 1:2; Zech 1:3; Mal 1:4). Greek has κύριος ὁ θεὸς τῶν πνευμάτων τῶν προφητῶν ('the Lord God of the spirits of the prophets'). A back-translator from Greek would write אֲדֹנָי אֱלֹהֵי רוּחוֹת הַנְּבִיאִים ('Lord God of the spirits of the prophets'), NOT the specific OT title YHWH Tsevaot. The Greek translator apparently could not render the military-host concept and substituted a phrase about prophetic spirits.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: אמת ('truth' — one word). Greek: πιστοὶ καὶ ἀληθινοί ('faithful and true' — two words). Hebrew is more concise.
Hebrew: 'YHWH of Hosts' (יהוה צבאות). Greek: 'the Lord God of the spirits of the prophets' (κύριος ὁ θεὸς τῶν πνευμάτων τῶν προφητῶν). Completely different divine title.
textual_notes: The phrase YHWH Tsevaot is the signature title of the later prophets — Isaiah, Jeremiah, Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi use it extensively. Its appearance here anchors the text in the Hebrew prophetic tradition.

one_way_hebrew: Uses קָדוֹשׁ (kadosh — 'holy', H6918). Greek has μακάριος ('blessed/happy'). These are fundamentally different concepts — kadosh means 'set apart, consecrated, belonging to YHWH' while makarios means 'fortunate, blessed, happy.' A back-translator from Greek would use אַשְׁרֵי (ashrei — 'happy/blessed'), NOT kadosh. The Hebrew author declares the believer HOLY, not merely happy.

Uses מַאֲמִין (ma'amin — 'believes/trusts', H539, from the root אמן — amen). Greek has τηρῶν ('keeps/guards'). Believing and keeping are different activities — one is internal faith, the other external observance. A back-translator from Greek would use שׁוֹמֵר (shomer — 'keeper/guardian'), not the faith-verb ma'amin.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: קדוש ('holy'). Greek: μακάριος ('blessed'). Different attribute entirely.
Hebrew: שמאמין ('who believes'). Greek: ὁ τηρῶν ('who keeps/guards'). Different activity.
translation_notes: The word [אָבֹא] appears in brackets in the source, indicating editorial restoration of a damaged or unclear reading. The consonantal text supports אבוא (from בוא — 'to come').
בִּמְהֵרָה (bimherah — 'swiftly/hastily', H4120) — from the root מהר (to hasten). This is the standard Hebrew word for 'quickly' in a theological context (Ps 31:3, 79:8, 143:7).

one_way_hebrew: Uses וְהִתְפַּלַּלְתִּי (vehitpallalti — 'and I prayed', H6419, hitpa'el of פלל). Greek has προσκυνῆσαι ('to worship/prostrate'). הִתְפַּלֵּל is the reflexive verb specifically meaning 'to pray' — the standard Hebrew word for directing prayer (1 Kings 8:28, Dan 9:4, Neh 1:4). Greek προσκυνέω means 'to bow in worship.' A back-translator from Greek would write וָאֶשְׁתַּחֲוֶה (va-eshtachaveh — 'and I bowed in worship'), NOT the prayer verb hitpallel. The Hebrew says Yochanan PRAYED to the messenger; the Greek says he WORSHIPPED.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'I prayed to the messenger' (התפללתי). Greek: 'I fell to worship before the feet of the messenger' (ἔπεσα προσκυνῆσαι ἔμπροσθεν τῶν ποδῶν). Different activity (prayer vs. worship) and Greek adds 'before the feet.'
Hebrew: 'I fell to the ground' (נפלתי לארץ). Greek: ἔπεσα ('I fell'). Hebrew specifies 'to the ground/earth.'
translation_notes: כֵּיוָן (keivan) — a later Hebrew conjunction meaning 'when/since.' Not a standard OT term; common in Mishnaic Hebrew.

one_way_hebrew: Uses חַבְרוּתְךָ (chavrutecha — 'your fellowship/companionship', from the root חבר H2270 — 'companion/fellow'). Greek has σύνδουλός σου ('your fellow-servant'). The Hebrew חברות (chavrut) is a distinctly Semitic concept — a study partnership, companionship of equals. A back-translator from Greek σύνδουλος would write עֶבֶד כָּמוֹךָ ('a servant like you'), not the fellowship-companion word.

Uses הַמְּקַיְּימִים (hamequyemim — 'those who uphold/establish', H6965, from קום in the hiphil — 'to cause to stand/establish'). Greek has τηρούντων ('those who keep/guard'). The Hebrew implies actively ESTABLISHING and UPHOLDING the words — making them stand firm — while the Greek implies passively GUARDING them. Different postures toward the text.

Uses עֲשֵׂי תְּפִלָּתְךָ לְיַהְוֶה ('make your prayer to YHWH', H8605). Greek has τῷ θεῷ προσκύνησον ('worship God'). Again prayer vs. worship, and YHWH vs. generic 'God.' The Hebrew-Greek prayer/worship distinction is CONSISTENT across vv. 8-9, suggesting a systematic difference in the author's understanding.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'from your fellowship' (חברותך — fellowship of equals). Greek: 'your fellow-servant' (σύνδουλος — shared servitude). Different relational concept.
Hebrew: 'Make your prayer to YHWH.' Greek: 'Worship God.' Prayer vs. worship; YHWH vs. θεός.
translation_notes: 'Fellowship' for chavrutecha — the root חבר means 'to join/be united' and the noun describes a bond of companionship. In later rabbinic literature, chavruta becomes the technical term for a Torah study partner.
'Uphold' for mequyemim — distinguishing the active establishment of the words from mere passive guarding.

one_way_hebrew: Uses הֶחָזוֹן (hachazon — 'the vision', H2377). Greek has τοὺς λόγους τῆς προφητείας ('the words of the prophecy'). חָזוֹן is the specific prophetic-vision word — the opening word of Isaiah (חֲזוֹן יְשַׁעְיָהוּ, Isa 1:1), used for Daniel's sealed visions (Dan 8:26, 12:4). A back-translator from Greek 'words of the prophecy' would write דִּבְרֵי הַנְּבוּאָה, not chazon.

Uses תִּסְתֹּם (tistom — 'seal/stop up', H5640, from סתם). This is the EXACT verb from Daniel 8:26 — סְתֹם הֶחָזוֹן ('seal the vision') and Daniel 12:4 — סְתֹם הַדְּבָרִים ('seal the words'). The Hebrew Revelation deliberately REVERSES Daniel's command: Daniel was told TO seal; Yochanan is told NOT to seal. A back-translator from Greek σφραγίσῃς ('seal') could also use חתם (chatam), but the specific use of סתם ties this to Daniel's Hebrew, not to a Greek source.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the vision' (החזון — the prophetic vision). Greek: 'the words of the prophecy' (τοὺς λόγους τῆς προφητείας). Different object being left unsealed.
translation_notes: 'Vision' for chazon preserves the technical prophetic term — this is not generic 'words' but a seen revelation.
textual_notes: Daniel 8:26 — סְתֹם הֶחָזוֹן כִּי לְיָמִים רַבִּים ('seal the vision, for it is for many days'). Daniel 12:4 — סְתֹם הַדְּבָרִים וַחֲתֹם הַסֵּפֶר עַד עֵת קֵץ ('seal the words and close the scroll until the time of the end'). The Hebrew Revelation inverts Daniel: DO NOT seal, for the time is NEAR — not far off.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses חָסִיד (chasid — 'pious one', H2623) — the specific Hebrew term for one characterized by חֶסֶד (chesed — covenant loyalty/faithful love). Greek has δίκαιος ('righteous/just'). These are NOT the same concept: a chasid is defined by loyal love and covenant faithfulness; a dikaios is defined by justice and legal righteousness. A back-translator from Greek would use צַדִּיק (tsaddiq — 'righteous'), the standard Hebrew equivalent of δίκαιος, NOT chasid. The chasid is a uniquely Hebrew concept with no Greek equivalent.

Uses טָמֵא (tamei — 'unclean', H2931) — the specific Levitical purity term for ritual impurity (Lev 11-15, Num 19). Greek has ῥυπαρός ('filthy' — moral dirtiness). A back-translator from Greek would use מְלוּכְלָךְ or מְזוּהָם ('dirty/soiled'), not the priestly-ritual purity word tamei. The Hebrew frames the contrast in Levitical categories: clean/unclean (tahor/tamei), holy/profane.
Uses כָּל עֵת ('all time' — forever/perpetually). Greek has ἔτι ('still/yet'). The Hebrew declares a permanent, eternal state; the Greek suggests ongoing continuation. Different temporal scope.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: רע ('evil' — moral character). Greek: ὁ ἀδικῶν ('the unjust one' — one doing wrong). Character vs. action.
Hebrew: טמא ('unclean' — Levitical impurity). Greek: ῥυπαρός ('filthy' — moral dirt). Different conceptual framework.
Hebrew: חסיד ('pious' — covenant loyalty). Greek: δίκαιος ('righteous/just'). Different virtue.
Hebrew: כל עת ('all time' — permanent). Greek: ἔτι ('still/yet' — continuing).
translation_notes: 'Pious' for chasid — capturing the chesed/loyal-love dimension. The chasid in the Psalms is YHWH's faithful one (Ps 4:4, 12:2, 16:10, 32:6, 86:2, 149:1,5). It is the root of Hasidim — the 'pious ones.'
textual_notes: The four-fold contrast (evil/unclean vs. pious/holy) maps onto Levitical categories, not Greek ethical ones. The Hebrew author thinks in terms of purity and holiness (tahor/tamei, kadosh/chol), not in terms of Greek justice and moral virtue.

one_way_hebrew: Uses לְשַׁלֵּם (leshalem — 'to repay/recompense', H7999, from the root שלם — shalom/completeness). The Hebrew verb carries the connotation of making complete, restoring wholeness, fulfilling an obligation. Greek has ἀποδοῦναι ('to give back/render'). The Hebrew root connects repayment to SHALOM — the restoration of cosmic balance. A back-translator from Greek would use להשיב (lehashiv — 'to return/restore'), not the shalom-rooted leshalem.
greek_deviations: Greek adds ὁ μισθός μου μετ' ἐμοῦ ('my reward is with me') — absent from the Hebrew. This phrase echoes Isaiah 40:10 and 62:11 in the Greek tradition, but the Hebrew text here does not include it.
Hebrew: כמעשהו ('according to his deed' — singular). Greek: ὡς τὸ ἔργον αὐτοῦ ἔσται ('as his work shall be'). Hebrew refers to the completed deed; Greek to the work that shall be.
translation_notes: The word [אָבֹא] again appears in brackets in the source, as in v7.
'Repay' for leshalem captures the completion/wholeness nuance of the shalom root.
textual_notes: Psalm 62:13 — 'For you repay (תְשַׁלֵּם) to a man according to his deed (כְּמַעֲשֵׂהוּ).' The Hebrew Revelation uses the exact Psalm 62 phrasing. The Greek paraphrases differently.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses הָרִאשׁוֹן וְהָאַחֲרוֹן ('the first and the last') — a DIRECT QUOTE from Isaiah 44:6 and 48:12 where YHWH declares: 'I am the first and I am the last; besides me there is no god.' Greek has τὸ Α καὶ τὸ Ω, ἀρχὴ καὶ τέλος, ὁ πρῶτος καὶ ὁ ἔσχατος ('the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end, the first and the last'). If the Hebrew were a back-translation from Greek, the translator would write הָאָלֶף וְהַתָּו ('the Aleph and the Tav') for Alpha and Omega. Instead, the Hebrew preserves Isaiah's self-declaration of YHWH. The Greek translator converted the Hebrew theological concept to Greek letters and expanded two titles to three. This is the same decisive one-way marker seen in 21:6.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: TWO titles — 'the first and the last' + 'the beginning and the end.' Greek: THREE titles — adds 'the Alpha and the Omega.' Hebrew never mentions Greek letters.
Hebrew order: first/last, then beginning/end. Greek order: Alpha/Omega, beginning/end, first/last. Different sequence.
translation_notes: תְּחִילַּת (techilat — 'beginning') is a later Hebrew form from the root חלל. It lacks a standard Strong's number but is common in Mishnaic Hebrew.
textual_notes: Isaiah 44:6 — כֹּה אָמַר יְהוָה מֶלֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵל וְגֹאֲלוֹ יְהוָה צְבָאוֹת אֲנִי רִאשׁוֹן וַאֲנִי אַחֲרוֹן וּמִבַּלְעָדַי אֵין אֱלֹהִים ('Thus says YHWH, the King of Israel and his Redeemer, YHWH of Hosts: I am the first and I am the last; and besides me there is no god'). Isaiah 48:12 — אֲנִי הוּא אֲנִי רִאשׁוֹן אַף אֲנִי אַחֲרוֹן ('I am he; I am the first, indeed I am the last'). The speaker claims YHWH's exclusive self-identification from Isaiah.

one_way_hebrew: Uses קְדוֹשִׁים (kedoshim — 'holy ones', H6918). Greek has μακάριοι ('blessed/happy'). Same kadosh vs. makarios distinction as v7. The Hebrew frames commandment-keeping as a matter of holiness; the Greek frames it as a matter of blessedness.

Uses מִצְוֹתָיו (mitsvotav — 'his commandments', H4687) — the standard Torah term for divine commands (Ex 20:6, Deut 5:10, 6:2, 8:1). Greek also has ἐντολάς ('commandments'). Both traditions agree here.

Uses חֵלֶק (cheleq — 'portion/allotment', H2506) — the word for a tribal inheritance (Josh 19:9, Deut 10:9 — 'YHWH is their cheleq'). Greek has ἐξουσία ('authority/right'). A back-translator from Greek would use רְשׁוּת (reshut — 'permission/authority'), not the land-inheritance word cheleq. The Hebrew frames access to the tree of life as a COVENANT INHERITANCE, like a tribal allotment in the Promised Land.

Uses מֵהָעִיר ('from the city'). Greek has εἰσέλθωσιν εἰς τὴν πόλιν ('enter INTO the city'). OPPOSITE direction — the Hebrew says 'from/out of the city,' the Greek says 'into the city.' The Hebrew envisions the righteous as citizens of the city who go forth from it freely, while v15's outsiders cannot enter. The Greek envisions the righteous entering a city they are outside of.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: קדושים ('holy'). Greek: μακάριοι ('blessed'). Same deviation as v7.
Hebrew: חלק ('portion' — inheritance). Greek: ἐξουσία ('authority/right'). Different concept.
Hebrew: לילך מהעיר ('to go forth FROM the city'). Greek: εἰσέλθωσιν εἰς τὴν πόλιν ('enter INTO the city'). Opposite direction of movement.
translation_notes: 'Commandments' for mitsvotav — the Torah's specific term for divine commands, not generic moral precepts.
'Portion' for cheleq preserves the covenant-inheritance concept.

'Merit' for yizkeh (H2135, from זכה — 'to be clean/pure' → 'to merit/be worthy') — a word that develops its 'merit' meaning in later Hebrew. The idea is that keeping commandments PURIFIES one to be worthy.
textual_notes: Genesis 3:22-24 — man is expelled FROM the garden and barred from the tree of life. The Hebrew Revelation reverses this: the commandment-keepers regain their portion in the tree of life and their right to go forth from the city-garden. The direction 'from the city' may echo the Edenic going-forth.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מִבַּחוּץ עוֹמְדִים ('from outside, standing', H5975). Greek has only ἔξω ('outside'). The Hebrew adds the verb עמד ('to stand') — they are POSITIONED and STANDING outside, a concrete image of exclusion. This verbal specificity is characteristic of Hebrew narrative, not translation from Greek.

Uses הַזּוֹנוֹת (hazzonot — 'the harlots', H2181, FEMININE PLURAL). Greek has πόρνοι ('fornicators', MASCULINE). The Hebrew specifically means female harlots — women who sell sexual services. The Greek means male sexual sinners. A back-translator from Greek's masculine πόρνοι would use זוֹנִים (zonim — masculine) or מְנָאֲפִים (mena'afim — 'adulterers'), not the feminine זונות.

Uses כְּלָבִים (kelavim — 'dogs', H3611) — in Hebrew a term of profound contempt for the ritually impure and the spiritually worthless (1 Sam 17:43, 2 Sam 3:8, 2 Kings 8:13). In Deut 23:19 'dog' (כלב) is a term for a male cult prostitute. The Hebrew resonance is far richer than the Greek κύνες.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 5 categories (dogs, sorcerers, harlots, murderers, liars). Greek: 6 categories (dogs, sorcerers, fornicators, murderers, idolaters, liars). Greek adds εἰδωλολάτραι ('idolaters') which is absent from Hebrew.
Hebrew: הזונות (feminine harlots). Greek: πόρνοι (masculine fornicators). Different gender and shade of meaning.
Greek: πᾶς ὁ φιλῶν καὶ ποιῶν ψεῦδος ('everyone loving and practicing a lie'). Hebrew: הכזבנים ('the liars'). Hebrew is more concise.
translation_notes: כַּזְבָנִים (kazbanim — 'liars') is a later Hebrew agentive form from כזב (kazav — to lie). No standard Strong's number. Same form as in 21:8.
רַצְחָנִים (ratshanim — 'murderers') is a late Hebrew agentive from רצח (ratsach, H7523 — 'to murder'). The -an/-anim suffix is characteristic of Mishnaic Hebrew.

one_way_hebrew: Uses עֵדָה (edah — 'congregation', H5712) — the specific OT term for the assembled congregation of Israel (Num 1:2, 16:3, 27:17, Josh 22:16). Greek has ταῖς ἐκκλησίαις ('the churches' — plural). A back-translator from Greek would use קְהִלּוֹת (kehilot — 'assemblies') or transliterate ἐκκλησία. The Hebrew author uses the singular edah — THE congregation, as a unified body — not plural 'churches.' This reflects an Israelite assembly theology, not a diaspora church structure.

Uses שֹׁרֶשׁ מִמִּשְׁפְּחוֹת דָּוִד ('the root FROM the families of David'). Greek has ἡ ῥίζα καὶ τὸ γένος τοῦ Δαυΐδ ('the root AND the offspring of David'). The Hebrew says the root comes FROM David's families — a claim of Davidic origin. The Greek says he is BOTH root (source) AND offspring (descendant) — a theological paradox absent from the Hebrew. A back-translator from Greek would include 'and the offspring' (וְצֶאֱצָא), not the simple directional 'from the families.'

Greek adds ὁ ἀστὴρ ὁ λαμπρὸς ὁ πρωϊνός ('the bright morning star') — completely ABSENT from the Hebrew. This is one of the most recognizable phrases in Greek Revelation, and it is simply not in the Hebrew text.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: להראות לעדה ('to show to the congregation'). Greek: μαρτυρῆσαι ὑμῖν ταῦτα ἐπὶ ταῖς ἐκκλησίαις ('to testify to you these things for the churches'). 'Show' vs. 'testify'; singular 'congregation' vs. plural 'churches.'
Hebrew: 'the root from the families of David.' Greek: 'the root and the offspring of David.' Different claim.
Greek adds 'the bright morning star' — absent from Hebrew entirely.
translation_notes: 'Root' for shoresh (H8328) — Isaiah 11:10 uses the same word: 'the root of Jesse' (שֹׁרֶשׁ יִשַׁי). The claim is Davidic/Messianic.
'Congregation' for edah preserves the OT assembly concept without importing 'church' from the Greek.
textual_notes: Isaiah 11:1,10 — 'A shoot from the stump of Jesse, and a branch from his roots (שָׁרָשָׁיו) shall bear fruit... On that day the root of Jesse (שֹׁרֶשׁ יִשַׁי) shall stand as a signal for the peoples.' The shoresh/root claim is deeply Isaianic.

one_way_hebrew: NEAR-VERBATIM QUOTE from Isaiah 55:1: הוֹי כָּל צָמֵא לְכוּ לַמַּיִם... בְּלוֹא כֶסֶף וּבְלוֹא מְחִיר ('Ho, all who thirst, go to the waters... without silver and without price'). The Hebrew preserves Isaiah's exact phrasing: the plural imperative לְכוּ ('go!'), the compound negation בְּלוֹא כֶסֶף וּבְלוֹא מְחִיר ('without silver and without price'), and the specific word כֶסֶף ('silver' — not generic 'money'). Greek changes everything: ἐρχέσθω ('let him come' — singular, different verb), λαβέτω ὕδωρ ζωῆς δωρεάν ('let him take the water of life freely' — one word δωρεάν replaces the whole Isaiah phrase). A back-translator from Greek would NEVER reconstruct the full Isaiah 55:1 quotation.

Uses מַיִם חַיִּים (mayim chayyim — 'living waters') again, as in v1. Greek has ὕδωρ ζωῆς ('water of life'). The consistent Hebrew use of 'living waters' (flowing spring water) versus Greek 'water of life' (life-granting water) shows a systematic Hebrew idiom that a translator would not maintain.
Uses the plural imperatives לְכוּ... וּשְׁתוּ ('go ye... and drink ye') — addressing the thirsty masses. Greek uses singular. The Hebrew preserves Isaiah 55:1's plural address to the crowds.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: full Isaiah 55:1 quotation — 'go to living waters and drink without silver and without price.' Greek: 'let him come... let him take the water of life freely.' The Hebrew quotes Isaiah; the Greek paraphrases.
Hebrew: 'living waters' (mayim chayyim — flowing water). Greek: 'water of life' (ὕδωρ ζωῆς — life-granting water). Same systematic divergence as v1.
Hebrew: plural imperatives (לכו, שתו). Greek: singular (ἐρχέσθω, λαβέτω).
Hebrew: בלוא כסף ובלוא מחיר ('without silver and without price' — two-part negation). Greek: δωρεάν ('freely' — one word).
translation_notes: 'Bride' for kalah (H3618) — the standard Hebrew word for bride. This is the bride from 21:2,9.
'Silver' for kesef (H3701) — Hebrew uses 'silver' where English says 'money.' Kesef is both the metal and the currency.
'Price' for mechir (H4242) — the cost or payment for goods (2 Sam 24:24, 1 Kings 10:28, Lam 5:4).
textual_notes: Isaiah 55:1 (source text): הוֹי כָּל צָמֵא לְכוּ לַמַּיִם וַאֲשֶׁר אֵין לוֹ כָּסֶף לְכוּ שִׁבְרוּ וְאִכְלוּ וּלְכוּ שִׁבְרוּ בְּלוֹא כֶסֶף וּבְלוֹא מְחִיר יַיִן וְחָלָב. The Hebrew Revelation condenses Isaiah's invitation but preserves the key phrases verbatim: the thirsty, go to waters, without silver, without price.

one_way_hebrew: Uses the verb pair יוֹסִיף... יוֹסִיף (yosif... yosif — 'add... add', H3254) — a Hebrew word-play: if one ADDS to the scroll, YHWH will ADD plagues. This measure-for-measure (middah keneged middah) literary device is characteristic of Hebrew rhetoric and Torah law. Greek also uses the same verb (ἐπιθῇ... ἐπιθήσει) but the literary weight of the Hebrew word-play is native to the Semitic text.

Uses נְגָעִים (nega'im — 'plagues', H5061) — the same Levitical plague-word as in 21:9 (plagues of Egypt, Ex 11:1; priestly skin plagues, Lev 13-14). Greek has πληγάς ('blows/plagues' — generic). The Levitical term is consistent throughout the Hebrew text.
Uses יַהְוֶה (YHWH, H3068) as the agent who adds plagues. Greek has ὁ θεός ('God'). The Hebrew preserves the Tetragrammaton; the Greek substitutes a generic title.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: יהוה ('YHWH'). Greek: ὁ θεός ('God').
translation_notes: מֵעִיד (me'id — 'testifying/bearing witness', H5749) — from the root עוד (to testify). This is formal legal testimony, not casual assertion.
textual_notes: Deuteronomy 4:2 — לֹא תֹסִפוּ עַל הַדָּבָר אֲשֶׁר אָנֹכִי מְצַוֶּה אֶתְכֶם וְלֹא תִגְרְעוּ מִמֶּנּוּ ('You shall not ADD to the word that I command you, and you shall not DIMINISH from it'). Deuteronomy 12:32 repeats: לֹא תֹסֵף עָלָיו וְלֹא תִגְרַע מִמֶּנּוּ. Verses 18-19 together reproduce the Deuteronomic prohibition using the EXACT same Hebrew verb pair: יוסיף (add, H3254) in v18, יגרע (diminish, H1639) in v19.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses יִמְחֶה... שְׁמוֹ מִסֵּפֶר הַחַיִּים ('shall blot out his NAME from the scroll of life', H4229). Greek has ἀφελεῖ ὁ θεὸς τὸ μέρος αὐτοῦ ἀπὸ βίβλου τῆς ζωῆς ('God shall take away his PORTION from the book of life'). The Hebrew uses the verb מָחָה (machah — 'to blot out/wipe away') — the EXACT verb from Exodus 32:33 where YHWH says: מִי אֲשֶׁר חָטָא לִי אֶמְחֶנּוּ מִסִּפְרִי ('whoever has sinned against me, I will blot him out of my book'). And it is a NAME that is blotted — matching Deuteronomy 9:14 and 29:19. A back-translator from Greek's 'take away his portion' would use יסיר חלקו ('remove his share'), NOT the Exodus/Deuteronomy machah-from-the-book language.

Uses יִגְרַע (yigra — 'shall diminish', H1639) — the EXACT counterpart to יוסיף ('add', H3254) in v18. Together they reproduce the Deuteronomy 4:2 pair: תוסיפו / תגרעו ('add / diminish'). This verb pair is a Torah legal formula. The Greek uses different verbs (ἐπιθῇ / ἀφαιρῇ) that do not carry the Torah resonance.

Uses מִסֵּפֶר הַחַיִּים (mi-sefer hachayyim — 'from the scroll of life'). This is the OT concept from Psalm 69:29: יִמָּחוּ מִסֵּפֶר חַיִּים ('let them be blotted out from the scroll of the living'). Same verb (machah), same phrase (sefer chayyim). The Hebrew Revelation quotes the Psalms.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'shall blot out his NAME' (ימחה שמו — Exodus 32:33 language). Greek: 'shall take away his PORTION' (ἀφελεῖ τὸ μέρος αὐτοῦ). Different object — name vs. portion.
Hebrew: ימחה ('blot out' — the wiping/erasing verb). Greek: ἀφελεῖ ('take away' — the removing verb). Different action.

Greek adds: 'and from the holy city, and from the things written in this book' (καὶ ἐκ τῆς πόλεως τῆς ἁγίας, καὶ τῶν γεγραμμένων ἐν βιβλίῳ τούτῳ) — expanded consequences absent from the more concise Hebrew.
translation_notes: 'Blot out' for yimcheh — the verb of erasure. In ancient scrolls, text was physically wiped/scraped away. The image is YHWH personally erasing the person's name from the registered living.
'Scroll of life' for sefer hachayyim — a registry of the living, not a 'book' in the modern sense. See Psalm 69:29, Daniel 12:1, Exodus 32:32-33.
textual_notes: Exodus 32:32-33 — Moses says: 'blot me out (מְחֵנִי) from your scroll (מִסִּפְרְךָ).' YHWH replies: 'Whoever has sinned against me, I will blot him out (אֶמְחֶנּוּ) from my scroll.' The Hebrew Revelation uses this same Mosaic vocabulary for the ultimate threat against those who corrupt Scripture.

one_way_hebrew: Uses וְכֹה אָמַר (vekhoh amar — 'and thus said', H3541) — the PROPHETIC FORMULA. כֹּה אָמַר ('thus says') introduces divine speech throughout the prophets (Isa 7:7, 10:24, 28:16, 37:6; Jer 2:2, 4:3, 6:6; Ezek 2:4, 3:11, etc.). Greek has Λέγει ('he says' — present tense). A back-translator from Greek would write אוֹמֵר ('says'), not the formulaic prophetic koh amar.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: וכה אמר ('and thus said' — prophetic formula, past tense). Greek: Λέγει ('says' — present tense).
translation_notes: 'Lord' for adon (H113) — the human/relational title of authority, not the divine name. Calling Yeshua 'adon' parallels how subjects address their king (1 Sam 22:12, 2 Sam 14:9).

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses חֶסֶד (chesed — 'lovingkindness/covenant loyalty', H2617). Greek has χάρις (charis — 'grace'). These are NOT equivalent concepts. Chesed is YHWH's faithful love bound by covenant — the quality that drives his loyalty to Israel despite their failures (Ex 34:6-7, Ps 136, Mic 7:18-20). Charis is unmerited favor — a gift given without obligation. A back-translator from Greek χάρις would use חֵן (chen — 'grace/favor', H2580), the standard Hebrew equivalent, NOT chesed. The closing benediction of the Hebrew Revelation invokes covenant loyalty, not free grace — a fundamentally different theological framework.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: חסד ('lovingkindness/covenant loyalty'). Greek: χάρις ('grace'). Different theological concept for the closing benediction.
translation_notes: 'Lovingkindness' for chesed — no single English word captures this concept. It combines loyalty, love, faithfulness, and covenant obligation. Alternatives: 'loyal love,' 'covenant faithfulness,' 'steadfast love.'
'Anointed' for mashiach (H4899) — the Hebrew word Messiah, meaning 'one anointed with oil.' Greek Χριστός ('Christ') is a translation of this Hebrew term.
textual_notes: Psalm 136 uses חסד 26 times: כִּי לְעוֹלָם חַסְדּוֹ ('for his chesed endures forever'). The closing of the Hebrew Revelation invokes this same covenant quality — YHWH's enduring faithful love channeled through the Anointed One.

1.summary: Mark 1 in Hebrew uses distinctly Hebraic vocabulary throughout. Key one-way translation markers include: (1) קדוש השם ('Holy One of the Name') using the Jewish circumlocution HaShem where Greek has 'Holy One of God'; (2) ממלכות שמים ('kingdom of heaven') vs. Greek 'kingdom of God'; (3) כפרת ('atonement' — Yom Kippur language) where Greek has mere 'forgiveness'; (4) תשובה ('return') vs. Greek μετάνοια ('mind-change'); (5) נהגו ('led gently') vs. Greek ἐκβάλλει ('drove out') for the Spirit's action; (6) סגני הכהנים ('deputies of the priests') showing Temple bureaucratic knowledge; (7) שדים (shedim — Torah demons) vs. Greek 'unclean spirits'; (8) נס ('miracle/banner') vs. Greek 'word'; (9) משוטנים ('satan-possessed') as a uniquely Hebrew category; (10) חכמי הדת ('wise-ones of the law') vs. Greek 'scribes'; (11) מוסר ('Proverbs-style instruction') vs. Greek 'teaching.' The Hebrew consistently employs Levitical, priestly, and Torah-specific vocabulary where the Greek uses generic terms.

one_way_hebrew: Uses בשורה (besorah, H1309 — 'good tidings'), the OT herald-word for a messenger's good report (2 Sam 18:20,27; 2 Kgs 7:9; Isa 52:7). Greek εὐαγγέλιον is a semantic rendering of this Hebrew concept.

Uses אלוה (eloah, H433) — the singular form of God found primarily in Job (41 times) and in Deut 32:15,17; Hab 3:3. A back-translator from Greek θεοῦ would use the common אלהים (Elohim, H430), not this rare poetic singular.
greek_deviations: Some Greek manuscripts omit υἱοῦ τοῦ θεοῦ ('Son of God'). The Hebrew includes it.
translation_notes: 'Good-news' for besorah rather than 'gospel' — preserving the Hebrew word's OT meaning of a messenger's good report.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מלאכי (malachi — 'my messenger', H4397) — the word that forms the prophet Malachi's name. Quoting Malachi 3:1, the Hebrew preserves the possessive suffix that connects the messenger directly to the prophetic name. Greek ἄγγελόν μου ('my messenger/angel') obscures this wordplay.

Uses שיפנה (she-yifneh — 'who shall clear/turn', H6437) from the root פנה ('to turn/clear'). Greek κατασκευάσει ('shall prepare/construct') is a different concept — 'construct' vs. 'clear away obstacles.' A back-translator from Greek would use יכין ('shall prepare'), not יפנה.
greek_deviations: Both Hebrew and Greek attribute the combined quotation (Mal 3:1 + Isa 40:3) to Isaiah alone.
translation_notes: 'Clear' for yifneh captures the root פנה (to turn aside/clear) — the herald clears the road of obstacles, not merely 'prepares' it.
textual_notes: Malachi 3:1: הִנְנִי שֹׁלֵחַ מַלְאָכִי וּפִנָּה דֶרֶךְ לְפָנָי — 'Behold I send my messenger, and he shall clear the way before me.' The Hebrew Gospel preserves the Malachi text closely.

one_way_hebrew: Uses האדון (ha-Adon, H113 — 'the Master/Lord'), the human title of authority (Gen 18:12, 42:30), where the Masoretic Isaiah 40:3 has יהוה (YHWH). Greek κυρίου ('Lord') could represent either. The Hebrew Gospel's choice of Adon rather than YHWH allows the verse to apply to Yeshua as master without directly equating him with the divine name.

Uses ישרות (yesharot — 'straight things', from H3474 ישר) — the feminine plural adjective. Isaiah 40:3 has יַשְּׁרוּ (yashru — imperative 'make straight'). The Hebrew Gospel uses a variant form of the same root, confirming awareness of the Isaiah source but with independent word choice.
translation_notes: 'Master' for Adon (H113) — distinguishing this from YHWH. Adon is the title of human lordship and authority.
textual_notes: Isaiah 40:3: קוֹל קוֹרֵא בַּמִּדְבָּר פַּנּוּ דֶּרֶךְ יְהוָה יַשְּׁרוּ בָּעֲרָבָה מְסִלָּה לֵאלֹהֵינוּ — 'A voice cries in the wilderness: clear the way of YHWH, make straight in the desert a highway for our God.'

one_way_hebrew: Uses טובל (tovel — 'immerser', H2881) — from the root טבל describing full-body ritual immersion (2 Kgs 5:14 — Naaman 'dipped' seven times in the Yarden; Lev 14:6). The Hebrew term carries the full OT ritual-purity framework.

CRITICAL: Uses כפרת (kaparat — 'atonement', from H3722 כפר) — the Yom Kippur vocabulary. Greek ἄφεσιν ('forgiveness/release') is far weaker. The Hebrew frames immersion as atonement ritual; the Greek frames it as mere forgiveness. A back-translator from Greek would use מחילה ('pardon') or סליחה ('forgiveness'), not the Levitical atonement term כפרה.

Uses תשובה (teshuvah — 'repentance/return', H8666, from שוב — 'to return'). This is the Hebrew concept of turning back to God, not merely changing one's mind. Greek μετάνοια ('change of mind') focuses on mental transformation; Hebrew focuses on directional return.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'atonement of iniquities' (כפרת עונות). Greek: 'forgiveness of sins' (ἄφεσιν ἁμαρτιῶν). Different theological framing — Levitical atonement vs. legal remission.
translation_notes: 'Atonement' for kaparat — preserving the Yom Kippur connection. The immersion is framed as a priestly atonement act.
'Repentance' for teshuvah, though the Hebrew literally means 'return' — the act of turning back to God's path.

one_way_hebrew: Uses ממלכות יהודה ('from the kingdom of Yehudah', H4467) — a political-territorial designation. Greek πᾶσα ἡ Ἰουδαία χώρα ('all the Judean region'). The Hebrew frames Judah as a kingdom (malkhut), not a region (chora). A back-translator from Greek would use ארץ יהודה ('land of Judea') or מחוז ('district'), not 'kingdom.'

Uses מתודים (mitvadim — 'confessing', from H3034 ידה) — the Yom Kippur confession verb (Lev 16:21 — the priest 'confesses' all the iniquities of Israel over the scapegoat). Greek ἐξομολογούμενοι ('confessing') is a direct equivalent, but the Hebrew carries the Day of Atonement ritual context.
translation_notes: 'Kingdom' for malkhut preserves the political framing — Judah as a sovereign entity, not merely a geographic region.

one_way_hebrew: Uses עורות גמלים ('skins of camels', H5785) — meaning hides. Greek τρίχας καμήλου ('camel hair'). The Hebrew says 'skins' (hides); the Greek says 'hair.' A back-translator from Greek would write שער גמלים ('camel hair'), not עורות ('skins'). This may preserve a more primitive description of the prophet's garb.
Uses דבש מדבריי ('wilderness honey') — specifying the source. Greek μέλι ἄγριον ('wild honey') specifies the quality. Hebrew identifies the terrain; Greek identifies the category.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'skins of camels' (hides). Greek: 'camel hair.' Different material.
textual_notes: The description echoes Elijah in 2 Kings 1:8: אִישׁ בַּעַל שֵׂעָר וְאֵזוֹר עוֹר אָזוּר בְּמָתְנָיו — 'a hairy man with a leather belt around his waist.' Yochanan is portrayed as the returning Elijah (Mal 4:5).

one_way_hebrew: Uses לחלוץ (lachalutz — 'to loose/remove', H2502) — the same verb used in the levirate marriage ceremony where the widow removes (חלץ) the sandal (Deut 25:9-10, Ruth 4:7-8). Greek λῦσαι ('to untie') is generic. The Hebrew verb carries the legal overtone of the sandal-removal rite, implying Yochanan is unworthy even to perform this legal act for the Coming One. A back-translator from Greek would use להתיר ('to untie'), not the levirate-ceremony verb חלץ.
greek_deviations: Greek: κύψας λῦσαι ('stooping down to untie'). Hebrew has no 'stooping down' — only 'to loose.' The Greek adds the physical posture.
translation_notes: 'Loose' for chalutz preserves the sandal-removal ceremony connection.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses the preposition מ (min — 'from') in מהקדוש רוח ('from the Holy Spirit'). Greek ἐν πνεύματι ἁγίῳ uses ἐν ('in/with'). The Hebrew preposition implies the Spirit as the source of immersion; the Greek implies the Spirit as the medium. A back-translator from Greek would write ברוח הקדש ('in/with the Holy Spirit'), not מ ('from').

Word order הקדוש רוח ('the-Holy Spirit') differs from the standard OT construct רוח הקדש ('spirit of holiness', Isa 63:10-11, Ps 51:13). This adjective-before-noun pattern may reflect later Hebrew syntax.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'from the Holy Spirit' (מ — 'from'). Greek: 'in/with the Holy Spirit' (ἐν — 'in'). Different preposition, different theology.
translation_notes: 'From' for the preposition מ, preserving the Hebrew source-origin sense.

one_way_hebrew: Uses נצרי (Natsri — 'the Nazarene') as an epithet-title rather than a geographic origin. Greek ἀπὸ Ναζαρὲτ τῆς Γαλιλαίας ('from Nazareth of Galilee') treats it as geography. The Hebrew uses it as a title — 'Yeshua the Natsri' — similar to prophetic or clan designations.

Uses ונעשה (vena'aseh — 'and it came to pass', H6213) — a narrative formula using the root עשה ('to do/make') rather than the classical ויהי (vayehi — 'and it was'). This is a later Hebrew narrative style.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'from the city of Galil.' Greek: 'from Nazareth of Galilee.' The Hebrew omits Nazareth as a place name.

one_way_hebrew: Uses כדמות (kidmut — 'like the form/likeness of', H1823) — the same word from Genesis 1:26 ('in our likeness — דמות') and Ezekiel's throne visions (Ezek 1:5,10,22,26). Greek ὡς περιστεράν ('like a dove') is a simple comparison. The Hebrew word implies a visionary form — an Ezekiel-like apparition — not a simple simile. A back-translator from Greek would use כמו ('like'), not the theologically loaded דמות.

Uses נפתחו השמים ('the heavens were opened') — echoing Ezekiel 1:1 verbatim: וְנִפְתְּחוּ הַשָּׁמַיִם ('and the heavens were opened'). The Hebrew Gospel uses the identical passive form, connecting Yeshua's experience to Ezekiel's prophetic inauguration.
greek_deviations: Greek: σχιζομένους τοὺς οὐρανούς ('the heavens being torn/split'). Hebrew: השמים נפתחו ('the heavens were opened'). Different imagery — 'torn' (violent) vs. 'opened' (gentle). The Hebrew matches Ezekiel; the Greek is more dramatic.
translation_notes: 'Form' for demut preserves the Genesis/Ezekiel visionary language.
textual_notes: Ezekiel 1:1 — 'The heavens were opened (נפתחו השמים) and I saw visions of God.' The Hebrew Mark uses Ezekiel's exact inauguration formula.

one_way_hebrew: Uses ערב (arev — 'pleasing/sweet', H6149) — a sensory word describing sweetness to the senses (Ps 104:34 'May my meditation be sweet — יֶעֱרַב — to him'; Jer 31:26; Mal 3:4). Greek εὐδόκησα ('I am well-pleased') is cognitive. The Hebrew is sensory — the son is sweet/pleasing; the Greek is volitional. A back-translator from Greek would use רציתי ('I desired'), not the sensory ערב.
Uses אתהו (at'hu — emphatic 'you are he') — a uniquely Hebrew emphatic pronoun combining אתה+הוא. This emphatic identification has no Greek equivalent; Greek σὺ εἶ ('you are') is simpler.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'pleasing to me and beloved' (two qualities). Greek: ἐν σοὶ εὐδόκησα ('in you I am well-pleased'). Different structure — Hebrew gives two attributes; Greek gives one statement of approval.
translation_notes: 'Pleasing' for arev captures the sensory Hebrew quality rather than the cognitive 'well-pleased.'
textual_notes: Echoes Psalm 2:7 ('You are my son') and Isaiah 42:1 ('my chosen, in whom my soul delights'). The Hebrew combines both sources.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses נהגו (nahagu — 'led him', H5090) — a pastoral verb for leading flocks (Gen 31:18, Isa 11:6) and guiding gently (Isa 49:10). Greek ἐκβάλλει ('casts out/drives out') is violent — the same word used for casting out demons. A back-translator from Greek would use גרש ('drove out') or השליך ('cast'). The Hebrew Spirit gently leads like a shepherd; the Greek Spirit violently drives.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'led him' (gentle guidance). Greek: 'drives him out' (forceful expulsion). Fundamentally different portrayals of the Spirit's action.
translation_notes: 'Led' for nahag captures the pastoral Hebrew sense — the Spirit guides like a shepherd, not drives like an exorcist.

one_way_hebrew: Uses התענה (hit'aneh — 'fasted/afflicted himself', H6031) — from ענה, the Yom Kippur verb: 'you shall afflict your souls' (תְּעַנּוּ — Lev 16:29,31; 23:27,32). Greek πειραζόμενος focuses on temptation only. The Hebrew adds a Yom Kippur-style self-affliction absent from the Greek.

Uses משרתים (mesharetim — 'ministering', H8334) — the Levitical service verb used of priests and Levites serving in the sanctuary (Num 3:6, 1 Sam 2:11, Ezek 44:11). Greek διηκόνουν ('served/waited on') is generic table service. The Hebrew frames angelic ministry as priestly/Levitical service.
greek_deviations: Hebrew adds 'forty nights' (ומ' לילה) — matching the Moses template (Ex 34:28). Greek mentions only 'forty days.'
translation_notes: 'Fasted' for hit'aneh, though the Hebrew word means 'afflicted himself' — the broader Yom Kippur concept of self-denial.
textual_notes: The 'forty days and forty nights' directly parallels Moses (Ex 24:18, 34:28) and Elijah (1 Kgs 19:8). The Hebrew frames Yeshua's testing in the Torah/Prophets template.

one_way_hebrew: Uses אסור (asur — 'bound/imprisoned', H631) — from the root אסר, used of binding prisoners (Gen 42:24, Judg 16:21, 2 Kgs 25:7). Greek παραδοθῆναι ('was handed over/delivered up') carries theological weight of divine providence. The Hebrew is concrete and physical — Yochanan was bound in chains; the Greek is theological — he was delivered up. A back-translator from Greek would use נמסר ('was handed over'), not אסור ('was bound').
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the word of God' (דבר האל). Greek: τὸ εὐαγγέλιον τοῦ θεοῦ ('the gospel of God'). Different content description — 'word' vs. 'gospel.'

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses ממלכות שמים ('kingdom of heaven', H4467+H8064) — the circumlocution avoiding the divine name, identical to Matthew's consistent מלכות השמים. Greek has βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ ('kingdom of God'). Greek Mark NEVER uses 'kingdom of heaven'; only 'kingdom of God.' The Hebrew Gospel uses the Jewish reverence pattern. A back-translator from Greek would write מלכות האל, not מלכות שמים.
Uses עשו תשובה ('make repentance' — lit. 'do teshuvah'). The verb+noun combination is a native Hebrew idiom for the act of returning. Greek μετανοεῖτε ('repent/change your mind') is a single verb.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'kingdom of heaven.' Greek: 'kingdom of God.' The Hebrew uses the Jewish reverential circumlocution.
Hebrew: 'the word of God' (דבר האל). Greek: τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ ('the gospel'). Different object of belief.

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew: 'walking with others' (והולך ישוע ואחרים). Greek: 'passing alongside the Sea of Galilee' (παράγων παρὰ τὴν θάλασσαν). The Hebrew has Yeshua walking with companions already; the Greek has him alone by the sea. Different narrative setup.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'in Galil' (no mention of the sea in the itinerary). Greek: 'beside the Sea of Galilee.' Different framing of the scene.

one_way_hebrew: Uses לכו אחרי ('walk after me') — the Hebrew discipleship idiom הלך אחרי (halach acharei), used for following God (Deut 13:5, 1 Kgs 14:8) and prophets (1 Kgs 19:20-21 — Elisha 'went after' Elijah). Greek δεῦτε ὀπίσω μου ('come behind me') is less idiomatic. The Hebrew carries the Elijah-Elisha prophetic call pattern.
translation_notes: 'Walk after me' rather than 'follow me' preserves the Hebrew idiom of discipleship as walking in another's path.

greek_deviations: Greek adds μετὰ τῶν μισθωτῶν ('with the hired workers') — absent from Hebrew. The Hebrew scene is starker: the sons leave their father alone.

one_way_hebrew: Uses כפר נחום ('village of Nachum') — preserving the Hebrew meaning: כפר ('village') + נחום ('comfort'). Greek Καφαρναούμ is a transliteration that obscures the meaning.
Uses בית הכנסת ('house of assembly') — the full Hebrew construct phrase. Greek συναγωγή is a single compressed word that originates from this Hebrew concept.

Uses מוסר (musar, H4148 — 'instruction/discipline') — the Proverbs wisdom-word (Prov 1:2,7,8; 4:1,13; 8:33). Greek διδαχή ('teaching/doctrine') is generic. The Hebrew frames Yeshua's teaching as musar — ethical wisdom instruction in the Proverbs tradition.

Uses בעל כח ('master of power' — ba'al koach) — a compound phrase meaning 'one who possesses authority.' Greek ἐξουσίαν ἔχων ('having authority'). The Hebrew בעל (ba'al — 'master/owner', H1167) implies ownership — he possesses power as its lord.

Uses חכמי הדת ('wise-ones of the law/religion') for scribes. Greek γραμματεῖς ('scribes/copyists'). The Hebrew is honorific — 'sages of the law'; the Greek is functional — 'writers.' A back-translator from Greek would use סופרים (sofrim — 'scribes'), not the respectful 'wise-ones of the law.'
translation_notes: 'Instruction' for musar preserves the Proverbs wisdom-teaching framework.
'Wise-ones of the law' for חכמי הדת — a respectful Hebrew designation for Torah scholars.

greek_deviations: Greek specifies ἄνθρωπος ἐν πνεύματι ἀκαθάρτῳ ('a man with an unclean spirit'). The Hebrew says only 'a man, and he cried out' — leaving the nature of his affliction to be revealed in dialogue. The Hebrew narration is more restrained.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses קדוש השם ('the Holy One of the Name', H6918+H8034) — where השם (HaShem — 'the Name') is the standard Jewish circumlocution for YHWH used to this day. Greek has ὁ ἅγιος τοῦ θεοῦ ('the Holy One of God'). A back-translator from Greek would write קדוש האלהים ('the Holy One of God'). The Hebrew uses the distinctly Jewish reverential substitute השם, which no translator working from Greek would independently produce.

Uses להשמיד (lehashmid — 'to destroy/annihilate', H8045) — the total-destruction verb for annihilating nations (Deut 2:21-22; 9:3; Josh 7:7). Greek ἀπολέσαι ('to destroy/ruin') is weaker. The Hebrew implies utter annihilation — the demonic realm fears complete obliteration.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the Holy One of the Name' (HaShem). Greek: 'the Holy One of God.' Different divine reference.
translation_notes: 'The Name' preserves the Jewish circumlocution HaShem — the standard reverential way of referring to YHWH.

one_way_hebrew: Uses גערו (ga'aro — 'rebuked him', H1605) — the OT verb for divine rebuke over chaotic forces: YHWH rebukes the sea (Ps 106:9, Nah 1:4) and the adversary (Zech 3:2). The Hebrew places Yeshua's exorcism in the pattern of YHWH's cosmic authority.

greek_deviations: Greek: τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἀκάθαρτον ('the unclean spirit'). Hebrew: השטן ('the adversary/satan'). Different terminology — the Hebrew names the entity; the Greek describes its nature.
Hebrew places the crowd's astonishment here in v.26. Greek places it in v.27.

one_way_hebrew: Uses שדים (shedim — 'demons', H7700) — the specific OT term from Deut 32:17 ('they sacrificed to shedim, not to God') and Ps 106:37. Greek πνεύμασι τοῖς ἀκαθάρτοις ('unclean spirits'). A back-translator from Greek would write רוחות טמאות ('unclean spirits'), not the Torah-specific שדים.
Again uses מוסר (musar — 'instruction', H4148) — consistent Hebrew vocabulary maintaining the Proverbs wisdom framework.

translation_notes: שמו (shemo — 'his name/fame', H8034). In Hebrew, 'name' carries the sense of reputation and fame (Gen 6:4, 2 Sam 7:9).

one_way_hebrew: Uses לאכול ('to eat', H398) — stating the purpose of the visit. Greek has no stated purpose — they simply enter the house. The Hebrew adds the practical, communal reason (eating together after Shabbat assembly) — a natural Hebrew narrative detail absent from Greek.

Uses כיפא (Kefa — Aramaic 'rock') — switching from שמעון (Shimon) in v.29. This bilingual name-switching (Hebrew Shimon / Aramaic Kefa) is natural in a Hebrew-Aramaic milieu. Greek uses Σίμωνος ('Simon') consistently.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'she told him' (אמרה לו) — the mother-in-law speaks directly. Greek: 'they told him about her' (λέγουσιν αὐτῷ περὶ αὐτῆς) — others report her condition. Different agency.

one_way_hebrew: Uses ושרתם (vesheratem — 'and she served them', H8334) — again the Levitical ministry verb (שרת), used of priestly service in the sanctuary. Greek διηκόνει ('served/waited on') is generic. The Hebrew dignifies her act with priestly vocabulary.

Uses השמש נכנע ('the sun was subdued', H3665) — using the verb נכנע (nichna — 'was subdued/humbled'), the word for enemies being subdued before Israel (Deut 9:3, Judg 3:30, 1 Sam 7:13, 2 Chr 7:14). The sun 'submits' — a personification absent from Greek, which simply says ὅτε ἔδυ ὁ ἥλιος ('when the sun set'). No back-translator would choose this verb for 'setting.'

Uses משוטנים (meshotanim — 'satan-possessed') — a uniquely Hebrew term formed from שטן (satan), describing possession by the Adversary himself. Greek δαιμονιζομένους ('demon-possessed') uses a different concept entirely. The Hebrew category 'satan-possessed' does not exist in Greek vocabulary.
translation_notes: 'Satan-possessed' for meshotanim — a distinctive Hebrew coinage not found in the OT or in Greek.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מגרש (megaresh — 'drove out', H1644, from גרש) — the verb for Adam being driven from Eden (Gen 3:24) and driving nations from the land (Ex 23:28-31, Deut 33:27). The Hebrew connects exorcism to the Edenic/conquest expulsion pattern.
greek_deviations: Greek adds 'he did not allow the demons to speak, because they knew him' (οὐκ ἤφιεν λαλεῖν τὰ δαιμόνια). Hebrew gives only the reason: 'they recognized him.'

one_way_hebrew: Uses העמים (ha-amim — 'the peoples', H5971, plural) — implying multiple communities or ethnic groups. Greek πάντες ('everyone') is simply 'all.' The Hebrew plural 'peoples' may reflect the diverse population of Galilee.

Uses מדינות (medinot — 'provinces/districts', H4082) — the administrative term from Esther, Ezra, and Daniel for governmental regions. Greek κωμοπόλεις ('market-towns') is a uniquely Greek compound. A back-translator from Greek would use עיירות ('towns') or כפרים ('villages'), not the administrative מדינות.

greek_deviations: Greek: 'throughout all Galilee... and casting out demons' (general). Hebrew adds 'from the men' (מן האנשים) — specifying the source from which demons are expelled.
