one_way_hebrew: Uses מצורע (metsora, H6879) — the specific Levitical term from Torah purity laws (Lev 13-14). The metsora is a precisely defined legal status requiring priestly examination. Greek λεπρός ('leper') is a medical term lacking the Levitical legal framework.
Uses ויקוד (vayiqod — 'bowed down', H6915) — deep prostration used before God (Gen 24:26, Ex 4:31, 34:8). Greek γονυπετῶν ('kneeling') is less intense — kneeling vs. full prostration.

Uses תרצה (tirtseh — 'you desire/delight in', H7521, from רצה) — the verb of God's acceptance of sacrifices (Lev 1:4, Ps 44:4, 51:18). Greek θέλῃς ('you wish') is simple volition. The Hebrew frames the request in sacrificial-acceptance language.
translation_notes: 'Desire' for tirtseh — capturing the Hebrew verb's sacrificial overtone.

one_way_hebrew: Uses כמרחם (ke-merachem — 'having compassion', H7355, from רחם) — the womb-compassion verb (Isa 49:15 — 'Can a woman forget her nursing child, that she should have no compassion — מֵרַחֵם — on the son of her womb?'; Ps 103:13). Greek σπλαγχνισθείς ('moved in the intestines') uses a different body metaphor. Some Greek manuscripts read ὀργισθείς ('being angry') instead.

Uses שלח ידו ('sent out his hand') — the OT idiom for divine power in action (Ex 3:20 — 'I will send out my hand'; Ex 7:5, 9:15). Greek ἐκτείνας τὴν χεῖρα ('stretching out the hand') is merely physical. The Hebrew phrase echoes God's hand in the Exodus.

greek_deviations: Greek: ἐμβριμησάμενος αὐτῷ εὐθὺς ἐξέβαλεν αὐτόν ('having sternly warned him, he immediately sent him away'). The Hebrew preserves only the action, not the stern warning.
textual_notes: Brackets in the source indicate textual uncertainty or editorial reconstruction.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses סגני הכהנים ('deputies of the priests', H5461) — סגן is a Persian loanword for 'prefect/deputy' (Neh 2:16, 4:8,13; Jer 51:23,28,57). Greek τῷ ἱερεῖ ('the priest', singular). The Hebrew uses a specific Temple administrative title reflecting knowledge of the priestly bureaucracy. A back-translator from Greek would write הכהן ('the priest'), not 'deputies of the priests.'

Uses ותדור ('and vow', H5087, from נדר) — to make a vow. Greek προσένεγκε ('offer/bring near') means to present an offering. The Hebrew frames the cleansing requirement as a neder (vow) — a distinct OT institution (Lev 27; Num 30; Deut 23:22-24). A back-translator from Greek would use הקרב ('offer'), not תדור ('vow').

Uses לעדות בישראל ('for a witness in Yisrael') — the specifically national focus. Greek εἰς μαρτύριον αὐτοῖς ('for a testimony to them'). Different referent: 'in Yisrael' (the whole nation) vs. 'to them' (the priests).
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'deputies of the priests' (plural administrative title). Greek: 'the priest' (singular).
Hebrew: 'vow' (נדר — a legal commitment). Greek: 'offer' (προσφέρω — a sacrificial act).
translation_notes: 'Deputies' for seganim — preserving the specific Temple administrative title.
textual_notes: The cleansing rite is prescribed in Leviticus 14:1-32 — involving two birds, cedar wood, scarlet yarn, hyssop, and priestly examination.

one_way_hebrew: Uses נס (nes — 'miracle/sign/banner', H5251) — the OT word for a miraculous sign or rallying banner (Ex 17:15, Num 21:8-9, Isa 11:10). Greek τὸν λόγον ('the word/matter') is generic. The Hebrew identifies the healing as a nes — a sign in the Exodus tradition. A back-translator from Greek would write דבר ('word/matter'), not נס.

Uses בהחבא ('in hiding', from חבא — 'to hide', Gen 3:8,10). Greek φανερῶς εἰσελθεῖν ('to enter openly'). Hebrew: 'could not enter in hiding'; Greek: 'could not enter openly.' These are opposite conditions — the Hebrew says he sought concealment but couldn't achieve it.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the miracle' (הנס). Greek: 'the word/matter' (τὸν λόγον). Different content being publicized.
Hebrew: 'in hiding' (בהחבא — he tried to be hidden). Greek: 'openly' (φανερῶς — he tried to be open). Opposite perspectives.

2.summary: Mark 2 in Hebrew contains several striking deviations from the Greek text. The most significant are: (1) 'Son of the Virgin' (בן הבתולה, v.10) and 'Son of God' (בן האלוה, v.28) replacing Greek 'Son of Man' — entirely different christological titles that no back-translator would produce; (2) קללה ('curse', v.7) vs. Greek 'blasphemy' — framing the accusation in Torah legal terms; (3) לכפר ('atone', v.7) vs. Greek 'forgive' — Yom Kippur vocabulary; (4) עוגבים ('debauchees', v.15-16) vs. Greek 'tax collectors' — moral vs. professional categorization; (5) יגזל ('seized/robbed', v.20) vs. Greek 'taken away' — violent seizure of the bridegroom; (6) חיילותיו ('soldiers', v.25-26) — identifying David's companions with military precision; (7) שר הכהנים ('chief of the priests', v.26) vs. 'high priest'; (8) רבנכם ('your rabbi', v.16) absent from Greek. The chapter reveals a Hebrew text with its own theological vocabulary and christological framework independent of the Greek tradition.

greek_deviations: Greek adds καὶ ἐλάλει αὐτοῖς τὸν λόγον ('and he was speaking the word to them'). Hebrew omits this — the Hebrew narrative is more spare.

one_way_hebrew: Uses נטול (natul — 'taken/paralyzed') — a later Hebrew form from the root נטל ('to take/carry'), meaning one whose limbs have been 'taken' from him. Greek παραλυτικόν ('paralytic') is a medical term. The Hebrew is an organic Semitic formation; a back-translator from Greek would use the loanword פראליטיקוס or a biblical term like נכה ('stricken').
translation_notes: 'Paralyzed' for natul — literally 'taken,' meaning his limbs were taken from his control.

one_way_hebrew: Uses החריבוהו (hecherivuhu — 'they destroyed/broke through it', H2717, from חרב — 'to be desolate/destroy') — a strong verb implying structural demolition. Greek ἀπεστέγασαν ('they unroofed') merely describes removing the roof. The Hebrew implies a more violent breaking; the Greek a more controlled removal. A back-translator from Greek would use פתחו ('opened') or גלו ('uncovered'), not the destruction verb חרב.
greek_deviations: Greek adds ἐξορύξαντες ('having dug through') specifying the method. Hebrew says only 'broke through it' without specifying digging.

one_way_hebrew: Uses עונות (avonot — 'iniquities', H5771) consistently, not חטאים (chata'im — 'sins'). Greek ἁμαρτίαι ('sins') is generic. The Hebrew maintains the distinction: avon implies guilt and its consequences — a deeper concept than mere 'sin.'
Uses מחולין (mochalin — 'pardoned', from H4229 מחל — 'to pardon/wipe') — a later Hebrew form meaning full pardon. Greek ἀφέωνται ('are forgiven/released'). The Hebrew implies a complete wiping clean.
Again uses חכמי הדת ('wise-ones of the law') for scribes — consistent with Mark 1:22. This respectful Hebrew designation contrasts with the Greek functional term γραμματεῖς ('scribes/copyists').

CRITICAL: Uses קללה (qelalah — 'curse', H7045) for the scribes' accusation. Greek βλασφημίας ('blasphemy') is a Greek religious concept. The Hebrew uses the Torah word for curse (Gen 27:12-13, Deut 11:26-28, 21:23, 27:13). The accusation in Hebrew is that he has pronounced a curse (by usurping God's prerogative), not 'blasphemy' in the Greek sense. A back-translator from Greek would use a transliteration or גידוף (giduf — 'reviling'), not the Torah concept of curse.

CRITICAL: Uses לכפר (lechaper — 'to atone for', H3722) — again the Yom Kippur verb. Greek ἀφιέναι ('to forgive/release') is simply 'to let go.' The wise-ones frame the issue in atonement terms: who can perform the priestly act of kapparah? A back-translator from Greek would use למחול ('to forgive'), not לכפר ('to atone').
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'curse' (קללה — Torah concept). Greek: 'blasphemy' (βλασφημία — Greek religious concept).
Hebrew: 'atone for iniquities' (כפר — priestly act). Greek: 'forgive sins' (ἀφιέναι — legal release).
translation_notes: 'Curse' for qelalah preserves the Torah legal framework — the scribes see a Torah violation, not a Greek-style blasphemy.

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew explicitly attributes the perception to the Holy Spirit (בעד הקדוש רוח — 'through the Holy Spirit'). Greek says only τῷ πνεύματι αὐτοῦ ('in his spirit' — lowercase, his own spirit). The Hebrew elevates this to the divine Holy Spirit; the Greek attributes it to Yeshua's own perception. A back-translator from Greek would write ברוחו ('in his spirit'), not 'through the Holy Spirit.'
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'through the Holy Spirit.' Greek: 'in his own spirit.' Different source of knowledge.
Hebrew: 'carry it to your house and go' (expanded). Greek: 'take up your bed and walk' (simpler). Hebrew adds the destination.
translation_notes: מלה (milah, H4405 — 'word/utterance') — the poetic/wisdom word for speech (Job 4:2, 6:26; Ps 19:5), distinct from דבר (davar — 'word/matter').

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses בן הבתולה ('Son of the Virgin', H1121+H1330) where Greek has ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ('the Son of Man'). This is a completely different christological title. בתולה (betulah — 'virgin') is the Hebrew word for a young woman who has not known a man (Gen 24:16, Isa 7:14 LXX). No back-translator from Greek 'Son of Man' would produce 'Son of the Virgin.' This title connects directly to the virgin birth tradition (Isa 7:14) and is absent from all Greek Gospel manuscripts.

Uses לעזוב (la'azov — 'to release/abandon', H5800, from עזב) — meaning to let go, to release. Greek ἀφιέναι ('to forgive/release') is semantically close, but the Hebrew עזב carries the sense of abandoning/leaving behind — the iniquities are abandoned, not merely forgiven.
greek_deviations: MAJOR: Hebrew: 'Son of the Virgin' (בן הבתולה). Greek: 'Son of Man' (υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου). Entirely different christological title.
translation_notes: 'Son of the Virgin' — a christological title absent from all Greek manuscripts, connecting to Isaiah 7:14.
textual_notes: Isaiah 7:14: הִנֵּה הָעַלְמָה הָרָה וְיֹלֶדֶת בֵּן — 'Behold, the young woman is pregnant and bearing a son.' The LXX renders עלמה as παρθένος ('virgin'). The Hebrew Gospel uses the explicit בתולה ('virgin') rather than עלמה ('young woman').

one_way_hebrew: Uses וברכו את האל ('and they blessed God', H1288 — from ברך 'to bless'). Greek ἐδόξαζον τὸν θεόν ('they glorified God'). The Hebrew response is blessing — the standard Jewish liturgical response to witnessing God's power (the berakhah tradition). The Greek response is glorification. A back-translator from Greek would use כבדו ('glorified'), not ברכו ('blessed').

translation_notes: The phrase מראה וילונים is textually difficult. The sense from context and the Greek parallel (ἐδίδασκεν αὐτούς — 'he was teaching them') is that he was instructing the crowd.

one_way_hebrew: Uses תמשך אחרי ('draw yourself after me', H4900 from משך — 'to draw/pull'). Greek ἀκολούθει μοι ('follow me') is a simple command. The Hebrew verb meshekh carries the image of being drawn or pulled — as in Jeremiah 31:3: 'with lovingkindness I have drawn you' (משכתיך). The call is not mere following but being drawn by attraction. A back-translator from Greek would use הלך אחרי ('walk after'), not the magnetic משך.
Identifies Levi as מתתיהו (Mattityahu — 'gift of Yah', H4993). Greek does not make this identification in Mark (only in Matthew's Gospel). The Hebrew adds this cross-reference naturally.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'sitting at the table' (בשלחן — 'at the table'). Greek: καθήμενον ἐπὶ τὸ τελώνιον ('sitting at the tax office'). Completely different setting — a dining table vs. a tax booth.
Hebrew identifies Levi as Mattityahu. Greek Mark does not.
translation_notes: 'Draw' for timshekh preserves the magnetic-attraction metaphor of the Hebrew verb.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses עוגבים (ogvim — 'debauchees/lustful ones', from עגב — 'to lust/desire excessively'). Greek τελωνῶν ('tax collectors'). These are entirely different categories — moral debauchees vs. economic functionaries. No back-translator from Greek 'tax collectors' would produce 'debauchees.' The Hebrew categorizes these people by moral character; the Greek by profession.

Uses תלמידים (talmidim — 'students', H8527) — the native Hebrew term for disciples, from the root למד ('to learn'). Greek μαθηταί ('learners/disciples') is a semantic equivalent but the Hebrew word carries the full Torah-study tradition of the master-student relationship.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'debauchees and sinners' (עוגבים וחטאים). Greek: 'tax collectors and sinners' (τελωνῶν καὶ ἁμαρτωλῶν). Different first category.
translation_notes: 'Debauchees' for ogvim — from the root עגב meaning excessive desire/lust.

one_way_hebrew: Uses המאותתים (ha-me'otetim — 'the letter-workers') — apparently from אות/אותיות ('letter/sign'), describing scribes by their occupation with letters. Greek γραμματεῖς ('scribes') is from γράμμα ('letter') — a parallel concept but independently formed. The Hebrew creates its own occupational title from אות rather than borrowing the Greek term.
Uses רבנכם (rabbankhem — 'your rabbi/master') — a term of respect absent from Greek, which has only the pronoun 'he.' The Hebrew preserves the social dynamic of respectful address to a teacher.
Uses פרושים (Perushim, from H6567 פרש — 'to separate/distinguish') — the native Hebrew name meaning 'the separated ones.' Greek Φαρισαῖοι is a transliteration of this Hebrew word.
greek_deviations: Hebrew adds 'your rabbi' (רבנכם) — absent from Greek, which says simply 'he.'
translation_notes: 'Perushim' preserved untranslated — meaning 'the separated ones,' those who separate themselves for ritual purity.

one_way_hebrew: Uses רופא (rofeh — 'healer', H7495) — the OT word for a physician/healer (Gen 50:2, Ex 15:26 — 'I am YHWH your healer', 2 Chr 16:12, Jer 8:22). Greek ἰατρός ('physician') is the medical professional. The Hebrew carries the resonance of YHWH as Israel's healer.
greek_deviations: Greek adds εἰς μετάνοιαν ('to repentance') at the end. Hebrew has only 'to call the sinners' without specifying the purpose.

one_way_hebrew: Uses נישואין (nisuin — 'wedding/marriage', from H5375 נשא — 'to lift/carry') — the standard Hebrew legal term for the marriage ceremony. Greek νηστεύειν ('to fast') context has υἱοὶ τοῦ νυμφῶνος ('sons of the bridal chamber') — a Semitic idiom preserved in Greek. The Hebrew uses the native legal term for marriage rather than the Semitic idiom.

Uses קרובים לנישואין ('near to a wedding') — describing the wedding party. Greek 'sons of the bridal chamber' is a Hebrew idiom that the Greek preserves. The Hebrew text uses a different, more natural expression.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'those near to a wedding.' Greek: 'sons of the bridal chamber' (υἱοὶ τοῦ νυμφῶνος — a Semiticism). Different idiom for the same concept.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses יגזל (yigazel — 'shall be seized/robbed', H1497 from גזל — 'to rob/seize by force'). Greek ἀπαρθῇ ('shall be taken away') is a gentle removal. The Hebrew verb implies violent seizure — robbery (Gen 21:25, Lev 19:13, Deut 28:29, Mic 2:2). The bridegroom is not merely 'taken away' but forcibly seized. A back-translator from Greek would use ילקח ('shall be taken'), not the violent גזל. This foreshadows the violent arrest and crucifixion.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'seized' (גזל — violent robbery). Greek: 'taken away' (ἀπαίρω — gentle removal). Different characterization of the event.
translation_notes: 'Seized' for yigazel preserves the violence of the Hebrew verb — the bridegroom is robbed from them, not merely removed.

one_way_hebrew: Uses שובר (shover — 'breaks/tears', H7665) — the verb for breaking pottery, breaking bones, breaking covenants (Jer 19:10-11, Ex 12:46, Isa 24:5). Greek αἴρει ('takes away/tears off') is simpler removal. The Hebrew implies destructive breaking — the new tears the old apart.

Uses נאדות (ne'odot — 'wineskins', H4997) — the OT word for leather water/wine containers (Josh 9:4,13; Judg 4:19; 1 Sam 16:20; Ps 119:83). Greek ἀσκούς ('skins') is the direct equivalent. The Hebrew maintains the biblical vocabulary.

Uses קוצים (qotsim — 'thorns/stalks', H6975) — the word typically meaning 'thorns' but here referring to grain stalks or ears. Greek στάχυας ('heads of grain') is specific. The Hebrew word choice is unusual — either a dialectal usage or the author sees the grain differently than the Greek tradition.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'break off from the stalks' (לשבור מהקוצים). Greek: τίλλειν τοὺς στάχυας ('to pluck the heads of grain'). Different action — breaking vs. plucking.

one_way_hebrew: Uses חיילותיו (chaylotav — 'his soldiers/troops', H2428, from חיל) — specifically identifying David's companions as military personnel. Greek μετ' αὐτοῦ ('with those with him') is vague. The Hebrew reflects knowledge of the 1 Samuel 21 narrative where David's companions are indeed armed soldiers on a mission. A back-translator from Greek would write אותם שהיו עמו ('those who were with him'), not the military term.
textual_notes: Reference to 1 Samuel 21:1-6 where David comes to Nob and receives the showbread from Ahimelech the priest.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מקדש (miqdash — 'sanctuary', H4720) — the standard Hebrew term for the sacred precinct. Greek εἰς τὸν οἶκον τοῦ θεοῦ ('into the house of God'). The Hebrew uses the specific OT sanctuary term (Ex 25:8, Lev 12:4); the Greek uses a general 'house of God.'

Uses שר הכהנים ('chief of the priests', H8269+H3548) — using שר (sar — 'prince/commander') rather than כהן גדול ('great priest' / high priest). Greek ἀρχιερέως ('high priest'). The Hebrew title implies a military-administrative commander of the priestly corps. A back-translator from Greek would write כהן גדול.

Uses לחמי הקדש ('bread of holiness', H3899+H6944) — echoing 1 Samuel 21:5-7. Greek τοὺς ἄρτους τῆς προθέσεως ('the bread of the setting-forth/showbread'). The Hebrew preserves the 1 Samuel terminology; the Greek uses the Pentateuchal technical term.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the sanctuary' (מקדש). Greek: 'the house of God.' Different designation.
Hebrew: 'chief of the priests' (שר). Greek: 'high priest' (ἀρχιερεύς). Different title.
textual_notes: Historical note: 1 Samuel 21 names the priest as Ahimelech, not Abiathar (Evyatar). Both the Hebrew and Greek Mark name Abiathar — a shared tradition, possibly because Abiathar was Ahimelech's son who survived the Nob massacre (1 Sam 22:20) and became the more famous high priest.

one_way_hebrew: Uses האדם (ha-adam — 'the man/mankind', H120, with definite article) — echoing Genesis 1-2 where 'the adam' is the archetypal human. The Shabbat was made for 'the adam' — the same being for whom the entire creation was made. Greek τὸν ἄνθρωπον is merely 'man.' The Hebrew connects the saying to the creation narrative.
textual_notes: The Mekhilta on Exodus 31:13 contains a parallel: 'The Shabbat was given to you, not you to the Shabbat.' This Hebrew saying circulated in rabbinic tradition.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses בן האלוה ('Son of God', H1121+H433) where Greek has ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ('the Son of Man'). As in v.10 (which uses 'Son of the Virgin'), the Hebrew Gospel avoids the title 'Son of Man' entirely, using different christological titles. No back-translator from Greek would replace 'Son of Man' with 'Son of God.'

Uses אדון מכל מה שהוא בעולם ('master of all that is in the world') — an expansive claim far beyond the Greek's κύριος τοῦ σαββάτου ('lord of the Sabbath'). The Hebrew extends mastery to all creation, with the Shabbat as one example.
Again uses אלוה (eloah, H433) — the rare singular form, consistent with 1:1.
greek_deviations: MAJOR: Hebrew: 'Son of God' (בן האלוה). Greek: 'Son of Man' (υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου). Different christological title.
Hebrew: 'master of all that is in the world, and of the Shabbat.' Greek: 'lord of the Sabbath.' The Hebrew is far more expansive.

3.summary: Mark 3 in Hebrew contains major deviations from the Greek text and distinctly Hebraic features. Key markers include: (1) מארבים ('lying in ambush', v.2) using military vocabulary for the Perushim's hostility vs. Greek 'watching'; (2) ביום החג ('on the feast day', v.4) vs. Greek 'on the Sabbath' — different sacred day; (3) נקצף (divine wrath verb, v.5) for Yeshua's anger; (4) בעל זבוב (OT spelling, v.22) vs. Greek 'Beelzebul'; (5) בזולת החכמה ('without wisdom', v.24) vs. Greek 'divided against itself' — different proverb entirely; (6) נכבד ('honored', v.21) vs. Greek 'out of his mind' — opposite assessment; (7) מיתה נפשיית נצחיית ('eternal soul-death', v.29) vs. Greek 'eternal sin'; (8) the epithet meaning 'Son of the Most High God' (v.17) vs. Greek 'Sons of Thunder'; (9) אמתות ('truths', v.28) vs. Greek 'amen'; (10) consistent use of השם (HaShem — 'the Name') for God. The chapter shows a Hebrew text with its own proverb traditions, independent theological vocabulary, and fundamentally different narrative details.

one_way_hebrew: Uses יבשה (yeveishah — 'withered/dried', H3001) — the same verb used for the drying of waters (Gen 8:7,14), of vegetation withering (Isa 40:7-8; Joel 1:12), and of Jeroboam's hand withering (1 Kgs 13:4). Greek ἐξηραμμένην ('shriveled') is medical. The Hebrew connects to the Jeroboam episode, where a king's hand withered as divine judgment.
textual_notes: 1 Kings 13:4 — Jeroboam's hand 'withered' (וַתִּיבַשׁ) when he stretched it out against the prophet. Same verb, same body part.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מארבים (me'arvim — 'lying in ambush', H693, from ארב) — a military/predatory verb used for enemies setting an ambush (Josh 8:2,4,12; Judg 9:25,32; 1 Sam 22:8,13). Greek παρετήρουν ('they were watching closely') is passive observation. The Hebrew frames the Perushim as military ambushers; the Greek as careful watchers. A back-translator from Greek would use שומרים ('watching') or צופים ('observing'), not the violent ארב.

Uses שילשינוהו ('they might inform against him', from לשון — 'tongue') — meaning to use the tongue against someone, to denounce or slander. Greek κατηγορήσωσιν ('they might accuse') is a legal term. The Hebrew is more visceral — using the tongue as a weapon.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'lying in ambush' (military). Greek: 'watching closely' (observation). Different characterization of hostility.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses ביום החג ('on the feast day', H2282 from חג — 'pilgrimage feast/festival') where the context and Greek both have 'on the Sabbath' (ἐν τοῖς σάββασιν). The Hebrew uses חג (chag — the word for the three pilgrimage festivals: Pesach, Shavuot, Sukkot) rather than שבת (Shabbat). A back-translator from Greek would use בשבת, not ביום החג. This may reflect a different tradition about when this event occurred.

Uses הושיע (hoshi'a — 'save', H3467, from ישע) — the root of Yeshua's own name. The wordplay is only visible in Hebrew: 'Yeshua' (ישוע — 'salvation') asks about 'saving' (הושיע). Greek σῶσαι ('to save') cannot produce this name-pun.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'on the feast day' (יום החג). Greek: 'on the Sabbath' (σάββασιν). Different sacred day.
translation_notes: 'Save' for hoshi'a — the verbal root of Yeshua's name, creating an implicit wordplay.

one_way_hebrew: Uses נקצף (niqtsaf — 'was angered', H7107, from קצף) — the verb for divine wrath (Deut 1:34; 9:19; 2 Kgs 5:11; Isa 54:9; 57:16; 64:4). Greek περιβλεψάμενος αὐτοὺς μετ' ὀργῆς ('looking around at them with anger') is a description. The Hebrew uses the specific OT verb for God's fury — placing Yeshua's anger in the category of divine wrath. A back-translator from Greek would use כעס ('angry') or חרה ('burned'), not the divine-wrath verb קצף.
greek_deviations: Greek adds: συλλυπούμενος ἐπὶ τῇ πωρώσει τῆς καρδίας αὐτῶν ('grieving at the hardness of their hearts'). Absent from Hebrew.

one_way_hebrew: Uses שימיתוהו ('that they might kill him', H4191, from מות — 'to die/kill') — the legal execution verb. Greek ἀπολέσωσιν ('destroy/ruin') is broader. The Hebrew specifies judicial killing — putting to death.

Uses נמשכים (nimshachim — 'drawn/attracted', H4900, from משך) — the same magnetic-attraction verb from 2:14. The crowds are 'drawn' to Yeshua as by a force. Greek ἠκολούθησεν ('followed') is simply 'followed.' The Hebrew consistently uses this drawing/attraction metaphor.

Uses אדום (Edom, H123) — the biblical name for the region. Greek Ἰδουμαίας ('Idumea') is the Greco-Roman name. A back-translator from Greek would transliterate as אדומיה, not use the biblical אדום. The Hebrew preserves the patriarchal name from Genesis (Gen 25:30, 36:1).

Uses הפלאים (ha-pela'im — 'the wonders', H6381, from פלא) — the OT word for God's miraculous acts in the Exodus (Ex 3:20, 15:11; Ps 77:12,15; 78:12). Greek does not have a specific word here — merely ὅσα ἐποίει ('how much he was doing'). The Hebrew identifies Yeshua's acts as divine Exodus-type wonders.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'Edom' (biblical name). Greek: 'Idumea' (Greco-Roman name).
Hebrew: 'Surya' (Syria). Greek: Τύρου (Tyre). Different location.
Greek: Yeshua tells his students to have a boat ready so the crowd wouldn't crush him. Hebrew simply says they boarded a small boat.

one_way_hebrew: Uses לנגעו (linga'o — 'to touch him', H5060, from נגע) — the same root that yields נגע (nega — 'plague/affliction', used in Lev 13-14 for skin diseases). The people want to 'touch' (נגע) the healer using the very root that means 'plague.' This wordplay is only visible in Hebrew — the afflicted seek the touch of the one who removes affliction. Greek ἅπτεσθαι ('to touch') carries no such resonance.

Uses כרעו (kar'u — 'fell to their knees/bowed down', H3766) — the verb for kneeling before God (2 Chr 29:29, Ps 95:6) and for enemies falling in defeat (Judg 5:27, Ps 20:9). Greek ἔπιπτον ('fell down') is generic falling. The Hebrew verb implies defeat — the demons kneel in submission.
Uses בן האלוה ('son of God', H433 — eloah, singular) — again the rare singular form. Greek: υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ ('Son of God'). Consistent with 1:1 and 2:28.
greek_deviations: Greek has τὰ πνεύματα τὰ ἀκάθαρτα ('the unclean spirits'). Hebrew has המשוטנים ('the satan-possessed'). Different terminology, consistent with ch.1.

one_way_hebrew: Uses יגלוהו ('reveal him', H1540, from גלה — 'to uncover/reveal/exile'). Greek ἵνα μὴ αὐτὸν φανερὸν ποιήσωσιν ('that they should not make him known'). The Hebrew verb גלה carries the OT sense of prophetic revelation (Amos 3:7 — 'He reveals his secret to his servants the prophets'). The demons' knowledge is treated as unauthorized prophetic revelation.

Uses ישרו בעיניו ('were upright in his eyes', H3474+H5869) — the moral criterion of yashar ('straight/upright'), the same word used in Judges for doing what is 'right in one's eyes' (Judg 17:6, 21:25) and for the 'book of Yashar' (Josh 10:13, 2 Sam 1:18). Greek has οὓς ἤθελεν αὐτός ('whom he himself wanted'). The Hebrew gives a moral quality — uprightness — as the selection criterion; the Greek gives only desire. A back-translator from Greek would use רצה ('desired'), not the moral-judgment phrase ישרו בעיניו.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'those most upright in his eyes' (moral criterion). Greek: 'whom he himself wanted' (volitional criterion).
Greek: 'that they might be with him and that he might send them to preach' (ἵνα ὦσιν μετ' αὐτοῦ καὶ ἵνα ἀποστέλλῃ αὐτοὺς κηρύσσειν). Hebrew omits 'being with him' — only the sending to proclaim.
Greek: 'authority to cast out demons' (ἐξουσίαν ἐκβάλλειν τὰ δαιμόνια). Hebrew: 'power to heal the sick and the satan-possessed.' Hebrew frames it as healing; Greek as exorcism.

one_way_hebrew: Uses כיפא (Kefa — Aramaic 'rock/stone'). Greek Πέτρον ('Peter' — Greek translation of 'rock'). The Hebrew text preserves the Aramaic name rather than translating it, naturally bilingual. A back-translator from Greek would write פטרוס (Petros) or צור/סלע (tsur/sela — Hebrew 'rock').
CRITICAL: Hebrew names James (Yaakov) as אלעזר (Elazar — 'God has helped', H499). Greek has Ἰάκωβον ('James/Jacob'). The Hebrew uses a completely different name for one of the sons of Zavdi.

CRITICAL: The epithet's meaning is given as בן מהעליון אלוה ('son of the Most High God'). Greek has Βοανηργές, ὅ ἐστιν Υἱοὶ Βροντῆς ('Boanerges — Sons of Thunder'). The Hebrew provides a theological title; the Greek a meteorological one. These are irreconcilable — no back-translator would convert 'Sons of Thunder' into 'Son of the Most High God.' The Hebrew text may preserve a different tradition about the meaning of the name.
greek_deviations: MAJOR: Hebrew: 'Elazar' for Yaakov. Greek: 'Iacobon' (Jacob/James). Different name.
MAJOR: Hebrew: name means 'Son of the Most High God.' Greek: name means 'Sons of Thunder.' Entirely different etymology.
translation_notes: The bracketed [לסיים] ('to conclude') appears to be a textual gloss or scribal note. The text is partially corrupt.
textual_notes: Uses עליון (Elyon — 'Most High', H5945) — the divine title from Genesis 14:18-22 (Melchizedek's God) and Psalm 82:6, 83:19; Daniel 7:18,22,25,27. This is a theologically loaded OT divine name.

one_way_hebrew: Uses קני (Qani — 'zealous/jealous one') for Shimon's epithet. Greek Καναναῖον ('Cananean'). The Hebrew preserves the meaning — from קנא (qana — 'to be zealous', H7065), connecting to Phinehas's zeal (Num 25:11,13) and Elijah's (1 Kgs 19:10,14).

Uses שבגדו (she-bagdo — 'who betrayed him', H898, from בגד — 'to deal treacherously/betray'). This is the OT covenant-betrayal verb (Judg 9:23, Isa 21:2, 24:16, 33:1; Jer 3:20; Mal 2:10-16). Greek ὃς καὶ παρέδωκεν αὐτόν ('who also handed him over'). The Hebrew uses the covenant-treachery term; the Greek a neutral 'handing over.' A back-translator from Greek would use מסר ('handed over'), not the loaded בגד.

CRITICAL: Uses נכבד (nichbad — 'honored/important', H3513, from כבד — 'to be heavy/honored'). Greek ἐξέστη ('he has gone out of his mind'). The Hebrew says people honored him; the Greek says his family thought him insane. These are diametrically opposite assessments. No back-translator from Greek 'he's lost his mind' would produce 'he is honored.' This represents a fundamentally different tradition about public reaction.
greek_deviations: MAJOR: Hebrew: 'He is honored' (נכבד — positive assessment). Greek: 'He has gone out of his mind' (ἐξέστη — negative assessment). Opposite meanings.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses בעל זבוב (Baal Zevuv — 'Lord of Flies', H1176) — the exact OT name from 2 Kings 1:2-3,6,16, the god of Ekron. Greek Βεελζεβούλ ('Beelzebul' — 'Lord of the dwelling/dung') is a modified form. The Hebrew preserves the biblical orthography; the Greek has a variant. A back-translator from Greek would transliterate as בעלזבול, not use the OT spelling בעל זבוב.

Uses שר השטנים ('chief of the adversaries', H8269+H7854) — using the Hebrew military title שר ('commander/chief') and the plural 'adversaries' (שטנים). Greek ἄρχοντι τῶν δαιμονίων ('ruler of the demons'). The Hebrew frames the cosmic hierarchy in military terms — a general commanding forces.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'Baal Zevuv' (OT spelling). Greek: 'Beelzebul' (modified form).
textual_notes: 2 Kings 1:2 — Ahaziah sent to inquire of 'Baal-Zebub the god of Ekron.' The Hebrew Mark preserves this exact name.

one_way_hebrew: Uses משלים (meshalim — 'parables/proverbs', H4912) — the Hebrew genre-word for wisdom comparisons (Prov 1:1, 10:1, 25:1; Ezek 17:2, 24:3). Greek ἐν παραβολαῖς ('in parables') is a direct equivalent, but the Hebrew meshalim carries the full Proverbs/prophetic wisdom tradition.

CRITICAL: Uses בזולת החכמה ('without wisdom', H2451). Greek ἐφ' ἑαυτὴν μερισθῇ ('divided against itself'). Entirely different aphorism — the Hebrew says a kingdom without wisdom cannot stand; the Greek says a kingdom divided against itself cannot stand. These are independent proverbs. No back-translator from Greek 'divided against itself' would produce 'without wisdom.' The Hebrew reflects the Proverbs tradition (Prov 11:14, 24:6 — 'without counsel a nation falls').
greek_deviations: MAJOR: Hebrew: 'without wisdom.' Greek: 'divided against itself.' Different proverb entirely.
textual_notes: Proverbs 11:14: 'Without counsel (בְּאֵין תַּחְבֻּלוֹת) a people falls.' The Hebrew Gospel echoes this Proverbs pattern.

one_way_hebrew: Uses חלוקת הלב ('division of the heart', H2515+H3820) — the division is located in the inner being, the heart. Greek ἐφ' ἑαυτὴν μερισθῇ ('divided against itself') is external. The Hebrew internalizes the conflict — the house fails because the hearts within it are divided, not merely because the people are opposed.

Uses קץ (qets — 'end', H7093) — the eschatological/apocalyptic term from Daniel (Dan 8:17,19; 11:35,40; 12:4,9,13) for the final end of an age. Greek τέλος ἔχει ('has an end') is neutral. The Hebrew frames the Adversary's end in Danielic apocalyptic terms — this is THE end, not merely 'an end.'

Uses כלים (kelim — 'vessels/implements', H3627) — the OT word for Temple vessels (1 Kgs 7:45-51; 2 Kgs 25:14-16; Dan 5:2-3) and household goods (Gen 31:37). Greek σκεύη ('goods/vessels') is equivalent but the Hebrew kelim carries the Temple-vessel resonance — plundering the strong man's house evokes plundering a temple.

Uses קושרו (qoshro — 'binds him', H7194, from קשר — 'to bind/conspire') — the same verb used for conspiracies (1 Kgs 15:27, 16:9, 2 Kgs 15:10). Greek δήσῃ ('bind') is neutral. The Hebrew verb adds the overtone of conspiracy.
textual_notes: Isaiah 49:24-25: 'Can the prey be taken from the mighty (גבור)... Even the captives of the mighty shall be taken.' The strong-man parable echoes this Isaiah passage.

one_way_hebrew: Uses אמתות (amitot — 'truths', H571, plural of אמת) rather than the Greek amen formula. Greek ἀμήν ('amen') is itself a Hebrew loanword. The Hebrew text uses the full Hebrew word אמת in its plural form rather than the liturgical amen formula — suggesting the author writes from within Hebrew, not borrowing back a loanword.

Uses מכופרים (mechupparim — 'atoned for', H3722) — again the Yom Kippur verb כפר. Greek ἀφεθήσεται ('shall be forgiven'). The Hebrew consistently frames forgiveness as atonement — a priestly act — while the Greek consistently frames it as release.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'truths' (אמתות — plural noun). Greek: 'amen' (ἀμήν — liturgical formula). Different form of the solemn oath.
Hebrew: 'atoned for' (כפר). Greek: 'forgiven' (ἀφίημι). Priestly atonement vs. legal release.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses תקוה (tiqvah — 'hope', H8615) — 'there is no hope for him.' This phrase is absent from Greek entirely. The Hebrew adds a declaration of hopelessness with the OT word for hope (Jer 29:11, 31:17; Prov 23:18, 24:14). The concept of losing tiqvah (hope) is deeply OT.

CRITICAL: Uses מיתה נפשיית נצחיית ('eternal soul-death', H4194+H5315+H5331). Greek has ἔνοχός ἐστιν αἰωνίου ἁμαρτήματος ('guilty of eternal sin'). Completely different concept — Hebrew: eternal destruction of the soul; Greek: perpetual state of sin. The Hebrew implies ontological annihilation of the soul; the Greek implies an unresolvable moral condition. A back-translator from Greek would write חטא נצחי ('eternal sin'), not 'soul-death.'
greek_deviations: Hebrew adds 'there is no hope for him' — absent from Greek.
MAJOR: Hebrew: 'eternal soul-death' (מיתה נפשיית נצחיית). Greek: 'eternal sin' (αἰωνίου ἁμαρτήματος). Annihilation vs. perpetual guilt.
translation_notes: 'Soul-death' — the Hebrew concept of the soul itself dying, distinct from physical death. This touches on the Hebrew understanding of the soul's mortality or destructibility.

greek_deviations: Greek: 'he has an unclean spirit' (πνεῦμα ἀκάθαρτον ἔχει). Hebrew: 'he is satan-possessed' (משוטן). Consistent terminological difference.

one_way_hebrew: Uses קרוביו (qerovav — 'his relatives', H7138) — a broad kinship term. Greek ἀδελφοὶ αὐτοῦ ('his brothers'). The Hebrew uses the wider 'relatives'; the Greek specifies 'brothers.' A back-translator from Greek would use אחיו ('his brothers'), not קרוביו ('his relatives').
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'his relatives' (קרוביו). Greek: 'his brothers' (ἀδελφοί). Broader vs. specific kinship.
Greek adds ἀπέστειλαν πρὸς αὐτὸν καλοῦντες αὐτόν ('they sent to him, calling him'). Hebrew says only 'they desired him.'

one_way_hebrew: Uses רצון השם ('the will of the Name', H7522+H8034) — again using השם (HaShem — 'the Name') as the reverential substitute for YHWH. Greek τὸ θέλημα τοῦ θεοῦ ('the will of God'). Consistent with 1:24 (קדוש השם). A back-translator from Greek would write רצון האלהים ('the will of God'), not the circumlocution השם.
greek_deviations: Hebrew omits 'mother' from the final declaration — only 'brothers and sisters.' Greek includes 'brother and sister and mother' (ἀδελφός μου καὶ ἀδελφὴ καὶ μήτηρ).

4.summary: Mark 4 in Hebrew centers on parabolic teaching and the stilling of the sea, employing rich OT vocabulary throughout. Key one-way translation markers include: (1) סודות ('secrets/divine-council', v.11) vs. Greek 'mysteries' — prophetic admission to God's counsel; (2) מלכות שממיי/מלכות השם ('kingdom of heaven/the Name', v.11,26,30) consistently replacing Greek 'kingdom of God'; (3) תמונות ('images', v.33-34) — the second-commandment word — vs. Greek 'parables'; (4) שינוחו ('let them rest', v.39) — the creation/Shabbat verb — vs. Greek 'be muzzled!'; (5) דרדור ('thorn-bush', v.21) vs. Greek 'bushel basket'; (6) מנורה ('menorah', v.21) vs. Greek 'lampstand'; (7) חסרונות ('deficiencies', v.19) vs. Greek 'cares/anxieties'; (8) the Jonah parallel in v.38 (ירכתים — same word as Jonah 1:5); (9) v.12's ending where sins 'are atoned for' (positive) vs. Greek 'lest they turn and be forgiven' (negative prevention); (10) מבארו ('explained', v.34) using Moses' Torah-explanation verb from Deuteronomy 1:5. The Hebrew text consistently frames Yeshua's ministry in the categories of creation rest, Temple worship, prophetic council, and Mosaic Torah.

one_way_hebrew: Uses החיל (ha-chayil — 'the company/host', H2428) for the crowd. Greek ὄχλος ('crowd') is civilian. The Hebrew uses the military/organizational term for an assembled force — the same word for an army division or productive capacity (Ruth 4:11, 1 Sam 10:26). The audience is framed as an assembled host, not a random crowd.

Uses בשפת הים ('at the lip of the sea', H8193+H3220) — the OT idiom for the seashore (Gen 22:17, 41:3; Ex 2:3, 14:30; Josh 11:4; 1 Kgs 4:29). Greek παρὰ τὴν θάλασσαν ('beside the sea') is generic. The 'lip' metaphor personifies the sea — it has a mouth edge — which is a Semitic idiom absent from Greek.
translation_notes: 'Lip' for sfat — preserving the Hebrew body-metaphor for the shoreline.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מייסרם (meyasrem — 'disciplining them', H3256, from יסר — 'to discipline/chastise/instruct'). Greek ἐδίδασκεν ('was teaching') is neutral. The Hebrew verb יסר is the Proverbs discipline verb (Prov 9:7, 19:18, 29:17,19) — teaching through correction and moral formation. A back-translator from Greek would use מלמד ('teaching'), not מייסר ('disciplining').

Uses גרעינים (garginim — 'grains/kernels', H1715) — a specific word for individual seed kernels. Greek simply uses the implied subject from σπείρειν ('to sow'). The Hebrew specifies the physical form of the seed.

Uses עפר (afar — 'earth/dust', H6083) — the Genesis creation word (Gen 2:7 — man formed from afar). Greek γῆ ('earth/soil') is generic. The Hebrew uses the specific dust-of-creation word, giving the thin soil a Genesis resonance.

Uses הכהו (hikahu — 'struck it', H5221, from נכה — 'to strike/smite') — the OT verb for God striking enemies (Ex 3:20, 7:17,20; 12:12,29). The sun 'smites' the plant like a divine blow. Greek ἐκαυματίσθη ('was scorched') is meteorological. The Hebrew personalizes the sun as an active smiter.

Uses בטוב הארץ ('in the good of the earth') — 'the good of the land' echoes Genesis 45:18,20 where Pharaoh tells Joseph's family to eat 'the good of the land' (טוב ארץ מצרים). Greek εἰς τὴν γῆν τὴν καλήν ('into the good earth'). The Hebrew construct is a partitive — 'the goodness that belongs to the earth' — while the Greek is adjectival.
translation_notes: Numbers are abbreviated in the source text: ל'=30, ס'=60, ק'=100.

textual_notes: Echoes Deuteronomy 29:3 and Ezekiel 12:2 — the refrain about having ears but not hearing.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses סודות (sodot — 'secrets/counsels', H5475, from סוד — 'council/secret') — the OT word for being admitted to God's inner council (Amos 3:7: 'He reveals His secret — סוד — to His servants the prophets'; Ps 25:14; Job 15:8; Jer 23:18). Greek μυστήριον ('mystery') is a Hellenistic religious term for initiation secrets. The Hebrew concept is prophetic — admission to the divine council; the Greek concept is cultic — initiation mystery. A back-translator from Greek would transliterate as מוסטריון, not use the prophetic סוד.
Uses מלכות שממיי ('kingdom of heaven') — again the Jewish circumlocution, consistent with 1:15 and this chapter's v.26,30. Greek consistently has 'kingdom of God.'

Uses דמיונות (dimyonot — 'similitudes/likenesses', from H1819 דמה — 'to be like') — a different word from משלים ('parables', used in v.2). The outsiders receive dimyonot (visual likenesses); the insiders receive understanding. Greek uses παραβολαῖς for both.
translation_notes: 'Secrets' for sodot — preserving the prophetic divine-council concept.
textual_notes: Amos 3:7: 'Surely the Lord YHWH does nothing without revealing His secret (סוֹדוֹ) to His servants the prophets.' The students are admitted to the prophetic סוד.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: The Hebrew ending is בחטאתיהם שהם מכופרים ('in their sins that they are atoned for') — a positive statement that sins are atoned. Greek ends with μήποτε ἐπιστρέψωσιν καὶ ἀφεθῇ αὐτοῖς ('lest they turn and be forgiven') — a negative statement implying prevention of forgiveness. These are opposite conclusions. The Hebrew says the parables lead to understanding that sins are atoned; the Greek says the parables prevent understanding and forgiveness. Irreconcilable difference.
Again uses מכופרים (mechupparim — 'atoned for', H3722) — the consistent Yom Kippur vocabulary.
greek_deviations: MAJOR: Hebrew ending: 'understanding that their sins are atoned for' (positive). Greek ending: 'lest they turn and be forgiven' (negative prevention). Opposite theological conclusions.
textual_notes: The Isaiah source (Isa 6:9-10) in the MT also has a complex structure. The Hebrew Gospel appears to resolve the apparent cruelty of the Isaiah quotation by affirming atonement.

one_way_hebrew: Uses דמיון (dimyon — 'similitude/likeness', H1823) — different from both משל (mashal — 'proverb/parable', v.2) and the plural דמיונות (v.11). The Hebrew has multiple words for parabolic speech; Greek uses παραβολή throughout.

Uses מלבם ('from their heart', H3820) — the Adversary removes the word from the heart (the seat of understanding in Hebrew thought). Greek αἴρει τὸν λόγον τὸν ἐσπαρμένον εἰς αὐτούς ('takes away the word sown in them') — 'in them,' not specifically 'in their heart.' The Hebrew locates the spiritual battleground in the lev (heart).
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the words of God' (דברי האל). Greek: τὸν λόγον ('the word'). Hebrew specifies the divine source.
textual_notes: Verses 16-17 are absent from this Hebrew source. The explanation of the rocky-ground seed appears to be missing.

one_way_hebrew: Uses הדרשות (ha-derashot — 'the teachings/expositions', from H1875 דרש — 'to seek/expound') — the Hebrew term for Torah exposition, the root of 'midrash.' Greek τὸν λόγον ('the word') is generic. The Hebrew frames what they hear as derashot — formal Torah teachings.

Uses חסרונות העולם ('deficiencies of the world') for what chokes. Greek αἱ μέριμναι τοῦ αἰῶνος ('the cares/anxieties of the age'). The Hebrew says it is the world's lacks — its emptiness and insufficiency — that choke; the Greek says it is worries. Different diagnosis: deprivation vs. anxiety.

Uses אובדן העושרים ('the loss/destruction of riches', H6 from אבד — 'to perish'). Greek ἡ ἀπάτη τοῦ πλούτου ('the deceit of wealth'). The Hebrew says riches are lost/destroyed; the Greek says riches deceive. Different moral: impermanence vs. deception.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'deficiencies of the world.' Greek: 'cares of the age.' Different source of choking.
Hebrew: 'loss of riches.' Greek: 'deceit of riches.' Different moral about wealth.

one_way_hebrew: Uses ומשימין בפועל ('and put into practice' — literally 'place into action'). Greek uses καρποφοροῦσιν ('they bear fruit'). The Hebrew adds an action component absent from Greek — not merely bearing fruit passively but actively practicing what was heard. This reflects the Jewish emphasis on deed over belief.
The 'ears to hear' refrain is repeated from v.9 — the Hebrew places it at the end of the parable explanation, where Greek does not. This frames the explanation itself as requiring ears to hear.

CRITICAL: Uses דרדור (dardur — 'thorn-bush') where Greek has μόδιον ('bushel basket/measuring vessel'). A thorn-bush and a measuring basket are completely different objects. No back-translator from Greek would produce 'thorn-bush.' The Hebrew may preserve a different version of the saying rooted in the agricultural Palestinian landscape.

Uses מנורה (menorah, H4501) — the specific Temple lampstand (Ex 25:31-40, 37:17-24). Greek λυχνία ('lampstand') is generic. The Hebrew evokes the Temple menorah — the light is placed on the sacred stand, not a common household fixture.
greek_deviations: MAJOR: Hebrew: 'thorn-bush' (דרדור). Greek: 'bushel basket' (μόδιον). Different object.
Hebrew: 'menorah' (Temple lampstand). Greek: 'lampstand' (generic).
translation_notes: 'Menorah' for the lampstand — preserving the Temple connection.

one_way_hebrew: Uses a pair of near-synonyms: נסתר (nistar — 'hidden', H5641) and נעלם (ne'elam — 'concealed', H5956). Hebrew poetry characteristically pairs synonyms for emphasis. Greek has κρυπτόν... ἀπόκρυφον ('hidden... secret') — a similar pair, but the Hebrew verbs carry distinct OT connotations: nistar is used for God's hidden things (Deut 29:28), ne'elam for sins hidden from view (Lev 4:13, 5:2-4).

Uses באותה מדה שתמדדו באותה תקבלו ('with the measure you measure, with that you shall receive') — a Hebrew proverb known from the Mishnah (Sotah 1:7): במדה שאדם מודד בה מודדין לו ('with the measure a person measures, it is measured to him'). Greek ᾧ μέτρῳ μετρεῖτε μετρηθήσεται ὑμῖν ('with what measure you measure, it shall be measured to you'). Both reflect this proverb, but the Hebrew adds בהגדלה ('with increase') — God gives back more than what was measured. This addition is absent from Greek.
greek_deviations: Hebrew adds 'with increase' (בהגדלה). Greek adds καὶ προστεθήσεται ὑμῖν ('and more shall be added to you'). Similar concept but different phrasing.
textual_notes: Mishnah Sotah 1:7 contains the same proverb: 'With the measure a person measures, it is measured to him.'

one_way_hebrew: Uses יגזלו (yigzelu — 'they shall seize/rob', H1497, from גזל), consistent with 2:20. The violent robbery verb. Greek ἀρθήσεται ('shall be taken away') is a gentle passive removal. The Hebrew says what little remains will be violently seized — robbery, not mere loss.

Uses מלכות שממיי ('kingdom of heaven') — the consistent Jewish circumlocution. Greek βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ ('kingdom of God'). This is the fourth occurrence in Mark of this circumlocution (1:15, 4:11, 4:26, 4:30), consistently replacing Greek 'kingdom of God.'
Hebrew adds טוב ('good') to describe the seed. Greek has no qualifier — just σπόρον ('seed'). The Hebrew specifies the quality of the seed.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'good seed.' Greek: 'seed' (without qualifier).

one_way_hebrew: Uses ונח (ve-nach — 'and rests', H5117, from נוח — 'to rest') — the Shabbat/Noah rest verb. The sower rests while creation grows — an image of the creation Sabbath. Greek καθεύδῃ ('sleeps') is merely sleeping. The Hebrew adds theological rest — the sower participates in God's sabbatical pattern, resting while the earth does its work (Gen 2:2-3).

Uses שבולים (shibbolim — 'ears of grain', H7641) — the word from the Shibboleth episode (Judg 12:6), from Pharaoh's dream (Gen 41:5-7,22-27), and from the gleaning of Ruth (Ruth 2:2). Greek στάχυν ('ear of grain') is a direct equivalent. The Hebrew carries the full OT grain-narrative tradition.

Uses נשלם (nishlam — 'is complete/made whole', H7999, from שלם — 'to be complete/at peace'). Greek παραδοῖ ('yields/hands over'). The Hebrew implies the fruit reaches שלמות (shlemut — completion/wholeness); the Greek implies the fruit surrenders itself. Different metaphor — maturity vs. yielding.
textual_notes: Joel 4:13 (Hebrew 3:13): שִׁלְחוּ מַגָּל כִּי בָשַׁל קָצִיר — 'Put in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe.' The Hebrew Gospel echoes Joel's eschatological harvest imagery.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מלכות השם ('the kingdom of the Name', H4467+H8034) — again using השם (HaShem) as the reverential circumlocution for YHWH. Greek βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ ('kingdom of God'). Consistent with the Hebrew Gospel's pattern throughout Mark.

The double question אדמה...אדמהו echoes Isaiah 40:18: 'To whom then will you liken God? And what likeness (דמות) will you set alongside him?' and 40:25: 'To whom will you compare me (תדמיוני) that I should be equal?' The Hebrew frames Yeshua's parable introduction in the language of Isaiah's divine incomparability.
textual_notes: Isaiah 40:18: וְאֶל מִי תְּדַמְּיוּן אֵל — 'To whom will you liken God?' Same root דמה in the same rhetorical question pattern.

one_way_hebrew: Uses עופות השמים דרים בצל הענף ('the birds of heaven dwell in the shade of the branch') — echoing Ezekiel 17:23: 'Under it shall dwell all birds of every wing; in the shade of its branches they shall dwell' (בצל דליותיו תשכנה). Also Daniel 4:12,21. Greek κατασκηνοῦν ὑπὸ τὴν σκιὰν αὐτοῦ ('nest under its shadow'). The Hebrew uses the Ezekiel/Daniel world-tree imagery — the kingdom as a cosmic tree sheltering the nations.
textual_notes: Ezekiel 17:23: 'On the mountain of the height of Israel I will plant it, and it will bear branches and produce fruit and become a noble cedar. Under it every bird of every wing shall dwell; in the shade of its branches they shall dwell.'

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses תמונות (temunot — 'images/forms', H8544) — the same word from the second commandment: 'You shall not make any image — תמונה' (Ex 20:4; Deut 4:12,15,16,23,25). Greek παραβολαῖς ('parables'). The Hebrew calls the parables 'images' — the same word prohibited for idolatrous representation. Yeshua creates verbal תמונות (images) of the kingdom. A back-translator from Greek would use משלים ('parables'), not the laden תמונות.

CRITICAL: Hebrew says the purpose is שיבינו ('so they might understand'). Greek says καθὼς ἠδύναντο ἀκούειν ('as they were able to hear'). Different purpose: Hebrew = to enable understanding; Greek = as much as they could receive. The Hebrew is optimistic about the parables' function.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'images' (תמונות). Greek: 'parables' (παραβολαί). Different genre designation.
Hebrew: 'so they might understand.' Greek: 'as they were able to hear.' Different purpose.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מבארו (meva'aro — 'explained them', H874, from באר — 'to explain/make clear'). This is the verb from Deuteronomy 1:5: 'Moshe began to explain (באר) this Torah.' Greek ἐπέλυεν ('solved/resolved'). The Hebrew frames Yeshua's private explanations using the same verb as Moses explaining Torah. A back-translator from Greek would use פתר ('interpreted') or פרש ('explained'), not the Mosaic באר.
textual_notes: Deuteronomy 1:5: הוֹאִיל מֹשֶׁה בֵּאֵר אֶת הַתּוֹרָה הַזֹּאת — 'Moshe began to explain this Torah.' Same verb באר.

one_way_hebrew: Uses החיילות (ha-chaylot — 'the troops', H2428) for the crowd being dismissed. Greek τὸν ὄχλον ('the crowd'). Consistent with v.1 where the crowd is called חיל. The Hebrew consistently treats the audience as an assembled military-style host.

Uses הניחו (hinichu — 'they released/set down', H5117, from נוח — 'to rest') — they 'rested' the troops, i.e., dismissed them. Greek ἀφέντες ('leaving'). The Hebrew verb again uses the rest/shabbat root.

Uses רוח (ruach — 'wind/spirit', H7307) — the same word used throughout for 'the Holy Spirit.' The word's dual meaning creates a subtle tension: is this merely wind, or is it a spirit? Greek λαῖλαψ μεγάλη ἀνέμου ('a great windstorm') is unambiguous. The Hebrew ambiguity is natural to the language.

Uses בירכתים (be-yarketayim — 'in the far recesses/stern', H3411) — echoing Jonah 1:5: 'Jonah had gone down into the recesses of the vessel (ירכתי הספינה) and had lain down and fallen fast asleep.' The verbal parallel is striking — both Yeshua and Jonah sleep in the yarketei ha-sefinah during a storm. The Hebrew Mark deliberately evokes the Jonah narrative. Greek ἐν τῇ πρύμνῃ ('in the stern') is nautical; the Hebrew carries the Jonah echo.
Uses רבי (rabbi — 'my master/teacher') — the native Hebrew/Aramaic title. Greek διδάσκαλε ('teacher') is a translation. The Hebrew preserves the actual term of address.

Uses פונה ('turn', H6437, from פנה) — 'Do you not turn to us?' The verb implies turning one's face toward someone in attention. Greek οὐ μέλει σοι ('does it not concern you?') is an impersonal 'do you not care?' The Hebrew is personal — 'turn your face to us'; the Greek is abstract — 'are you not concerned?'
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'Do you not turn to us?' (personal). Greek: 'Do you not care?' (abstract).
textual_notes: Jonah 1:5: וְיוֹנָה יָרַד אֶל יַרְכְּתֵי הַסְּפִינָה וַיִּשְׁכַּב וַיֵּרָדַם — 'And Jonah had gone down to the recesses of the vessel and lay down and fell fast asleep.' Nearly identical scene: prophet asleep in the ship's back during a divine storm.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses שינוחו (she-yanuchu — 'that they should rest', H5117, from נוח) — the Shabbat/creation rest verb. Yeshua commands the wind and sea to enter into sabbatical rest. Greek σιώπα, πεφίμωσο ('be silent! be muzzled!') is violent silencing — the same word used for muzzling an animal. The Hebrew commands rest; the Greek commands silencing. The Hebrew verb is the one God uses when He rests on the seventh day (Gen 2:2-3). Yeshua exercises the Creator's authority to command rest. A back-translator from Greek would use שתוק ('be silent') or חדל ('cease'), not the creation-rest verb נוח.
greek_deviations: MAJOR: Hebrew: 'rest' (נוח — sabbatical rest). Greek: 'be silent! be muzzled!' (σιώπα, πεφίμωσο). Different command entirely — peaceful rest vs. forceful silencing.
translation_notes: 'Rest' for yanuchu — the creation/Shabbat verb, implying divine sovereignty over nature.
textual_notes: Psalm 107:29 — 'He made the storm be still (יקם סערה לדממה), and the waves of the sea were hushed.' The Hebrew Mark echoes this psalm about YHWH calming the sea.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מי חשבנו שיהיה זה ('who did we think this was') — an introspective question acknowledging prior underestimation. Greek τίς ἄρα οὗτός ἐστιν ('who then is this?') is a present question. The Hebrew looks backward — 'who did we THINK he was?' — implying their previous estimate was wrong. The Greek asks an open question; the Hebrew admits an error.

Uses שמעוהו (shema'uhu — 'they obey him', H8085, from שמע — 'to hear/obey'). Greek ὑπακούει ('obeys'). The Hebrew verb is the שמע of the Shema — the fundamental verb of Israelite identity (Deut 6:4). The wind and sea perform the שמע — they 'hear and obey' Yeshua as Israel is commanded to hear and obey YHWH.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'Who did we THINK this was?' (past tense — admitting prior error). Greek: 'Who IS this?' (present — open question).
textual_notes: Psalm 89:9-10 — 'You rule the raging of the sea; when its waves rise, You still them.' The disciples' awe reflects recognition that Yeshua exercises YHWH's authority over the sea.

5.summary: Mark 5 in Hebrew contains at least 15 strong one-way translation markers. The most striking: (1) מושטן/שטנים ('satan-possessed/satans') throughout — the Hebrew uses OT adversary-theology (שטן from Job 1-2, Zech 3:1) while Greek uses Hellenistic demonic categories (δαιμονιζόμενος), and no back-translator would replace 'demons' with 'satans'; (2) מספר ('Number') instead of 'Legion' — avoiding the Latin military loanword entirely; (3) חסד ('steadfast-love') instead of 'mercy' — the covenant-loyalty word appearing 248 times in the OT; (4) סגן ('deputy') for the assembly leader — a Temple administrative term from Nehemiah and Jeremiah; (5) טליתא glossed as בתולה ('virgin') not 'little girl' — connecting to Isaiah 7:14; (6) השם ('HaShem') for God — the rabbinic circumlocution; (7) משיח added to Yeshua's name where Greek lacks it; (8) הושיעך ('has saved you') creating a wordplay on Yeshua's own name (ישוע/ישע) that only works in Hebrew; (9) אנכי (archaic first person) in the woman's oath; (10) Two different divine names (אלוה/אל) in v7 where Greek has θεός for both. The chapter also shows consistent Hebrew theological framing: truth over power (v30), covenant-love over mercy (v19), and virginal purity over girlhood (v41).

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew says 'opposite Ginnesaret' (נגד גניסרת) — a geographic reference from the western shore's perspective. Greek TR has εἰς τὴν χώραν τῶν Γαδαρηνῶν ('to the region of the Gadarenes'). These are different place-naming systems: the Hebrew orients by relation to a known Galilean town; the Greek names the eastern region. A back-translator from Greek would write 'to the land of the Gadarenes,' not 'opposite Ginnesaret.'
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'opposite Ginnesaret.' Greek: 'the region of the Gadarenes/Gerasenes.' Entirely different geographic identification.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses מושטן (moshotan — 'satan-possessed'), from the root שטן (satan, H7854 — 'adversary'). Greek has δαιμονιζόμενος ('demonized'), from δαίμων. The Hebrew describes the condition through the OT adversary-theology of שטן (Job 1-2, Zechariah 3:1) — a prosecuting accuser in YHWH's court. Greek demonic cosmology derives from Hellenistic spirit-world categories entirely foreign to the OT. A back-translator from Greek would use a form from שד (shed — 'demon', Deut 32:17, Ps 106:37), NOT from שטן. This word appears throughout Mark 5 and is one of the most consistent one-way markers in the Hebrew Gospels.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'satan-possessed' (שטן-theology). Greek: 'demonized' (δαίμων-theology). Fundamentally different spiritual cosmologies.
Hebrew says the man came 'on the way' (בדרך). Greek says he came 'from the tombs' (ἐκ τῶν μνημείων). Different point of encounter.
translation_notes: 'Satan-possessed' for moshotan — preserving the שטן root. This is not equivalent to 'demonized'; it implies being under the power of the Adversary, the prosecuting angel of YHWH's court.

greek_deviations: Hebrew says the man was 'evil' (רע) — a moral characterization. Greek describes his dwelling and binding without moral judgment. Different framing of the condition.
translation_notes: שוכב (shokhev) literally means 'lying/dwelling' — the word used for lying in bed, in a grave, or dwelling in a place. The man's habitation among tombs makes him ritually impure (Num 19:16).

one_way_hebrew: Uses להשקיטו (lehashqito — 'to quiet him', from שקט H8252 — 'to be quiet/at rest'). This is the OT word for the land being at rest from war (Josh 11:23, 14:15, Judg 3:11,30, 5:31). Greek says δαμάσαι ('to tame/subdue'). A back-translator from Greek would use לכבוש (likhbosh — 'to subdue') or לרסן (to bridle), not the peace/rest verb שקט. The Hebrew implies the goal is peace and rest, not domination.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'to quiet him' (peace/rest). Greek: 'to tame him' (control/domination). Different objectives.
Hebrew: 'standing' (עומד) in the tombs. Greek: 'cutting himself' (κατακόπτων). The Hebrew adds 'standing' as posture; both mention self-harm.
translation_notes: צועק (tso'eq, H6817) — the specific OT word for crying out in distress to God (Ex 2:23, 14:10, Judg 3:9). The man's shrieking is described with the same verb Israel uses when crying to YHWH for deliverance.

one_way_hebrew: Uses והתפלל (ve-hitpallel — 'and he prayed', H6419). Greek has προσεκύνησεν ('worshipped/prostrated'). The Hebrew uses the hitpael of פלל — the specific verb for prayer in the OT (Gen 20:7, 1 Sam 1:10, 1 Kings 8:30, Dan 9:4). A back-translator from Greek would use השתחוה (hishtachaveh — 'bowed down/worshipped'), NOT the prayer verb. The Hebrew says the demoniac instinctively prayed to Yeshua — an extraordinary theological statement that even a satan-possessed man prays in the presence of the divine.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'prayed to him' (התפלל). Greek: 'worshipped him' (προσεκύνησεν). Prayer vs. prostration — different actions.

one_way_hebrew: Uses TWO different divine names in one verse: אלוה עליון (Eloah Elyon — 'God Most High', H433+H5945) and אל חי (El Chai — 'living God', H410+H2416). Greek uses θεός ('God') for both. A back-translator from Greek, seeing the same Greek word twice, would use the same Hebrew word both times. The Hebrew author distinguishes: Eloah (the singular poetic form, Job 3:4, 4:9) for the transcendent title, and El (the ancient Semitic divine name, Gen 14:18-22) for the oath formula. Two different names from two different OT traditions.

אל חי (El Chai — 'living God') is a specific OT oath formula: Joshua 3:10 ('by this you shall know that the living God is among you'), Psalm 42:3 ('my soul thirsts for God, for the living God'). The demon swears by this specific divine title. A back-translator from Greek τὸν θεόν would not independently reconstruct this OT oath formula.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: two different divine names (Eloah + El). Greek: θεός for both.
Hebrew: 'that you not afflict me' (תצערני). Greek: μή με βασανίσῃς ('do not torment me'). Hebrew צער is emotional distress; Greek βασανίζω is physical torture.
translation_notes: 'What have you to do with me' — a Hebrew idiom (מה לך...ממני) found in Judges 11:12, 2 Samuel 16:10, 2 Kings 3:13. The expression is native Hebrew, though Greek τί ἐμοὶ καὶ σοί is itself recognized as a Semitism.

one_way_hebrew: Uses רוח אינו נקי ('spirit not clean') — with נקי (naqi, H5355 — 'innocent/clean') rather than טמא (tameh — 'impure/unclean'). In the OT, נקי is a legal/moral term for innocence (Ex 23:7 'the innocent and righteous do not slay', Deut 19:10,13, 2 Kings 24:4). Greek has πνεῦμα τὸ ἀκάθαρτον ('the unclean spirit'). A back-translator from Greek ἀκάθαρτος would use טמא (the standard Levitical impurity word), NOT negate נקי. The Hebrew frames the spirit's condition as lack of moral innocence, not ritual impurity.
translation_notes: 'Not clean' rather than 'unclean' — preserving the Hebrew's distinctive negation structure (אינו נקי) rather than the single Greek word ἀκάθαρτον.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses מספר (mispar, H4557 — 'number/multitude'). Greek has Λεγιών (Legiōn — from Latin legio, a Roman military unit of ~5,000 soldiers). A back-translator from Greek would transliterate the Latin military term as לגיון, as Rabbinic literature commonly does (e.g., Midrash Rabbah). The Hebrew author uses a native Hebrew word, completely avoiding the Roman military loanword. This suggests the Hebrew author either (a) predates the Roman military presence that made 'Legion' a familiar term, or (b) deliberately chose a Hebrew equivalent. Either way, the direction Hebrew→Greek (translating mispar into the culturally resonant Latin term) is far more plausible than Greek→Hebrew.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: מספר ('Number/multitude'). Greek: Λεγιών ('Legion'). Entirely different names — native Hebrew vs. Latin military loanword.
translation_notes: 'Number' for mispar — the Hebrew word means both a count and a multitude (cf. Gen 34:30 'few in number'; 1 Chr 22:4 'without number'). The demon's name conveys 'we are a multitude' without Roman military imagery.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מלכות (malkhut, H4438 — 'kingdom'). Greek has χώρα (chōra — 'region/country'). A back-translator from Greek would use ארץ (erets — 'land') or מדינה (medinah — 'province'), not the theologically loaded מלכות. The Hebrew word implies a domain of royal authority — the demon begs not to be expelled from a 'kingdom,' a concept with messianic overtones (Dan 2:44, 7:27). The demon recognizes it inhabits a domain of spiritual authority.

Uses יגרשהו (yegarsheihu — 'drive him out', H1644). This is the verb used for God driving Adam from Eden (Gen 3:24), driving out the Canaanite nations (Ex 23:28-31, Deut 33:27), and divorcing a wife (Lev 21:7). It carries connotations of permanent expulsion from a domain. Greek ἀποστείλῃ ('send away') is milder.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'kingdom' (מלכות). Greek: 'region' (χώρα). Different conceptual framework.
Hebrew: 'drive out' (גרש — permanent expulsion). Greek: 'send away' (ἀποστέλλω — dispatch).

Hebrew has lacunae (brackets [ ] [ ]) — text is damaged. Greek specifies πρὸς τῷ ὄρει ('near the mountain') and ἀγέλη χοίρων μεγάλη ('a great herd of swine'). The Hebrew damage may explain missing details.
translation_notes: חזירים (chazirim, H2386) — swine are the paradigmatic unclean animal in Torah law (Lev 11:7, Deut 14:8). Their presence signals Gentile territory.

one_way_hebrew: Uses ונסוהו (ve-nisuhu — from נסה, H5254 — 'tested/tried him'). Greek has παρεκάλεσαν ('they begged'). The Hebrew root נסה is the word for testing/proving (Gen 22:1 God tested Abraham; Ex 15:25, 16:4 God tested Israel; Ex 17:2 Israel tested YHWH). A back-translator from Greek 'begged' would use בקש or חנן, not the testing verb. The Hebrew says the spirits tested Yeshua's authority — probing his power, not merely begging.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'tested/entreated him' (נסה). Greek: 'begged him' (παρακαλέω). Different relational dynamic.

one_way_hebrew: Uses השטנים (ha-satanim — 'the satans', PLURAL of שטן, H7854). Greek has τὰ πνεύματα τὰ ἀκάθαρτα ('the unclean spirits'). The Hebrew consistently uses שטן/שטנים (adversary/adversaries) terminology throughout this chapter, never שד/שדים (demon/demons). In the OT, שטן is a specific role in YHWH's court (Job 1-2, Zech 3:1, 1 Chr 21:1). The Hebrew author operates within OT adversary-theology; the Greek translator uses Hellenistic spirit-world categories. A back-translator from Greek would never independently replace δαιμόνια ('demons') with שטנים ('satans').

Uses הודהו (hodahu — from ידה, H3034 — 'acknowledged/consented'). The root ידה means both 'to confess/acknowledge' and 'to give thanks' (Gen 29:35, Ps 136). Greek has ἐπέτρεψεν ('permitted'). A back-translator would use הרשה (hirshah — 'permitted'), not the theologically weighted ידה.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the satans' (שטנים). Greek: 'the unclean spirits.' Different terminology throughout.
Hebrew: the swine 'cast themselves' (reflexive). Greek: the herd 'rushed' (ὥρμησεν). The Hebrew emphasizes self-destruction.
Hebrew: 'in the city' (singular). Greek: εἰς τὴν πόλιν καὶ εἰς τοὺς ἀγρούς ('into the city and into the fields'). Hebrew is more concise.

one_way_hebrew: Uses בטוב שכלם (be-tov sikhlam — 'in good understanding/wisdom', H7922). Greek has σωφρονοῦντα ('being of sound mind'). The Hebrew שכל (sekhel) is a wisdom term — the same word used of David's skillful understanding (1 Sam 18:14,30), of the Maskil psalms, and of divine wisdom (Prov 12:8, 16:22). A back-translator from Greek σωφρονέω would use בדעת טובה ('in sound knowledge') or in a phrase with שפיות ('sanity'), not the wisdom-tradition term שכל.
translation_notes: 'Good understanding' for tov sikhlam — sekhel implies not merely sanity but wisdom and discernment. The healed man gained wisdom, not just mental stability.
מעשה (ma'aseh, H4639 — 'deed/work') — the standard OT word for God's works and mighty acts (Ps 8:7, 19:2, 92:5). The miracle is classified as a divine 'deed.'

one_way_hebrew: Uses מנוכחו (mi-nokhecho — 'from his/their presence', from נכח H5227). This word denotes being 'in front of/in the presence of' — used of standing before God (Prov 4:25, Lam 2:19). Greek has ἀπελθεῖν ἀπὸ τῶν ὁρίων ('depart from their borders'). A back-translator from 'borders' (ὁρίων) would use גבול (gevul — 'border'), not the presence-word נכח. The Hebrew frames the request as 'leave our presence' — a personal/spiritual expulsion, not geographic.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'from their presence' (relational). Greek: 'from their borders' (geographic).

one_way_hebrew: Uses להתחנן (lehithchanen — 'to implore grace', from חנן H2603 — 'to be gracious'). This is the hitpael of the root that gives us חן (chen — 'grace/favor'). Greek has παρεκάλει ('begged'). A back-translator from Greek would use בקש (biqesh — 'sought/asked'), not the grace-root verb. The Hebrew says the healed man 'sought grace' from Yeshua — the vocabulary of divine supplication (1 Kings 8:33, 2 Chr 6:24, Ps 30:9).

CRITICAL: Uses חסד (chesed, H2617 — 'steadfast-love/covenant-loyalty'). This is arguably the most theologically significant word in the entire OT — appearing 248 times, it denotes God's faithful covenant love (Ex 34:6, Ps 136:1-26 where each verse ends 'for his chesed endures forever'). Greek has ὅσα ὁ κύριός σοι πεποίηκεν καὶ ἠλέησέν σε ('how much the Lord has done for you and had mercy on you'). A back-translator from ἠλέησεν ('had mercy') would use רחמים (rachamim — 'mercy/compassion'), NOT the covenant-loyalty word chesed. The Hebrew identifies the healing as an act of covenant faithfulness, not merely mercy.

Uses השם (HaShem — 'the Name') for God. This is the distinctly Jewish circumlocution for YHWH, used to avoid pronouncing the divine name. Greek has κύριος (kyrios — 'Lord'). A back-translator from κύριος would use אדון (adon — 'lord') or write the tetragrammaton, NOT the rabbinic reverence-form השם.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the steadfast-love' (חסד — one theological concept). Greek: 'how much... did... had mercy' (two separate verbs). The Hebrew condenses into a single covenant-theology term what Greek expresses as actions.
Hebrew: 'HaShem' (השם). Greek: κύριος ('Lord'). Different ways of referencing God.
translation_notes: 'Steadfast-love' for chesed — this translation attempts to capture both the steadfastness/faithfulness and the love dimensions. 'Mercy' or 'kindness' alone would lose the covenant dimension.
textual_notes: The chesed of YHWH as the content of testimony: the healed man is told to recount God's covenant-love, not merely the miracle itself. This parallels Psalm 107:1-2 — 'Give thanks to YHWH, for he is good, for his chesed endures forever. Let the redeemed of YHWH say so.'

one_way_hebrew: Uses דורש (doresh, H1875 — 'sought/expounded/proclaimed'). In the OT, דרש specifically means to seek God, inquire of a prophet, or expound Scripture (Ezra 7:10 'Ezra set his heart to darash the Torah of YHWH'; Ps 34:5, 105:4). Greek has κηρύσσειν ('to herald/proclaim'). A back-translator from Greek would use הכריז or קרא ('proclaim'), not the Torah-study verb דרש. The Hebrew says the man was 'expounding' — teaching and explaining — God's covenant-love.

בקבול החסד ('the receiving of the steadfast-love') — a unique Hebrew construction. The word קבול (receiving/acceptance) appears nowhere in Greek. The Greek simply says ὅσα ἐποίησεν ('how much he did'). The Hebrew adds the concept of actively receiving chesed — not merely being acted upon, but participating in covenant love.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'proclaiming/expounding the receiving of the steadfast-love.' Greek: 'proclaiming how much Jesus had done for him.' Entirely different content — covenant theology vs. miracle reporting.
Hebrew: 'HaShem.' Greek: ὁ Ἰησοῦς ('Jesus'). The Hebrew attributes the deed to God; the Greek to Jesus.
textual_notes: The Hebrew says the man proclaimed what HaShem (God) did. The Greek says he proclaimed what Jesus did. The Hebrew maintains the theological distinction between Yeshua as agent and HaShem as author of chesed.

one_way_hebrew: Uses שפת הים (sfat ha-yam — 'the lip of the sea', H8193). שפה literally means 'lip' and is the Hebrew idiom for shoreline (Gen 22:17 'sand on the lip of the sea', Ex 14:30, Josh 11:4). Greek has παρὰ τὴν θάλασσαν ('beside the sea'). A back-translator from Greek would use יד הים (yad ha-yam — 'hand of the sea') or על הים ('by the sea'), not the poetic 'lip of the sea' idiom.
translation_notes: 'Shore' for sfat — literally 'lip.' The Hebrew idiom 'lip of the sea' is a vivid image preserved throughout the OT.

one_way_hebrew: Uses בית הכנסת (beit ha-knesset — 'house of assembly'). This is the native Hebrew term for a place of gathering. Greek has ἀρχισυναγώγων ('rulers of the synagogue'), using the Greek loanword συναγωγή. A back-translator from Greek would likely transliterate or use a calque of the Greek. The Hebrew preserves the pre-Greek native designation.

Uses כרע (kara, H3766 — 'bowed/knelt'). This is the specific OT word for kneeling in worship or submission — used of bowing before God (1 Kings 8:54, 2 Chr 6:13), of animals kneeling (Gen 49:9, Num 24:9), and of falling in death (Judg 5:27). Greek has πίπτει πρὸς τοὺς πόδας ('falls at the feet'). A back-translator from 'falls' (πίπτει) would use נפל (nafal — 'fell'), not the worship-posture verb כרע.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'a leader from the house of assembly.' Greek: 'one of the rulers of the synagogue.' Different institutional language.
Hebrew: 'bowed on his knees' (deliberate worship posture). Greek: 'fell at his feet' (collapse/prostration).
translation_notes: Yair (יאיר, H2971) — 'he enlightens,' from the root אור ('light'). This is an OT name: Jair the judge (Judg 10:3) and a Manassite clan leader (Num 32:41, Deut 3:14, 1 Chr 20:5).

one_way_hebrew: Uses והנח (ve-hanach, from נוח H5117 — 'to rest/lay'). This is the root of Noah's name (Gen 5:29). The Hebrew says 'rest your hands upon her' — the laying-on of hands is described as an act of bestowing rest. Greek has ἐπιθῇς τὰς χεῖρας ('lay hands'). A back-translator would use שים (sim — 'put/place'), not the rest/Noah verb נוח.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'near to death' (קרובה למות). Greek: ἐσχάτως ἔχει ('is at an extreme/at the point of death'). The Hebrew is spatial ('near to'); the Greek is qualitative ('at the extreme').

one_way_hebrew: Uses רפיון דם (rifyon dam — 'weakness/flowing of blood'). The word רפיון derives from רפה (raphah, H7503 — 'to be weak/slack'). This is a Hebrew medical term describing the condition as physical weakness/laxity. Greek has ἐν ῥύσει αἵματος ('in a flow of blood'). A back-translator from Greek ῥύσις ('flow') would use זוב (zov — 'discharge', the Levitical term from Lev 15:19-25) or שטף (shetef — 'flood/flow'), NOT the weakness/laxity term רפיון. The Hebrew frames the condition as bodily weakness; the Greek merely describes the discharge.
translation_notes: A woman with a blood flow is ritually impure under Leviticus 15:25 and renders impure anyone she touches. Her act of touching Yeshua's garment (v27) is an act of desperation that violates purity law.

greek_deviations: Hebrew is concise: 'spent all on medicines, to no benefit.' Greek expands: πολλὰ παθοῦσα ὑπὸ πολλῶν ἰατρῶν ('having suffered much under many physicians'). Hebrew omits physicians entirely, mentioning only medicines (רפואות).

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: The Hebrew says ישוע משיח (Yeshua Mashiach — 'Yeshua the Anointed One'). Greek has only τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ('about Jesus') without 'Christ/Anointed.' The title משיח (Mashiach, H4899) is the OT designation for the anointed king (1 Sam 2:10, Ps 2:2) and the anointed deliverer (Dan 9:25-26). A back-translator from Greek would NOT add a title absent from the source text. The Hebrew author includes it as the woman's understanding of who Yeshua is — the Mashiach.

Uses נגעה (nag'ah, H5060 — 'touched'). This is the specific OT verb for contact that transmits ritual impurity (Lev 5:2-3, 11:8, 15:19, Num 19:11). A woman in her condition who 'touches' (נגע) renders the touched person unclean. The Hebrew author uses the Levitical purity-law verb to underscore the audacity and faith of her act. Greek ἥψατο is more neutral.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'Yeshua Mashiach.' Greek: just 'Jesus.' The Messianic title is absent from Greek.
Hebrew: 'the back of his garments' (אחורי מלבושיו). Greek: τοῦ ἱματίου αὐτοῦ ('his garment'). Hebrew specifies 'behind' — she touched from the rear.

one_way_hebrew: Uses אנכי (anokhi, H595) — the archaic/solemn first-person pronoun, then switches to אני (ani, H589) in the same verse. אנכי is the form used in the Ten Commandments (אנכי יהוה אלהיך, Ex 20:2) and in solemn divine/prophetic declarations (Gen 15:1, Ex 3:6). Greek has no equivalent distinction between pronoun registers. A back-translator would use the common אני throughout. The deliberate use of אנכי for the conditional oath ('if I am able') and אני for the result ('I shall be healed') marks the first clause as a solemn vow.

Uses בקרבה (be-qirbah — 'in her midst/inner being', from קרב H7130). This is the OT word for the interior of a person or the midst of Israel where God dwells (Ex 34:9, Num 14:14, Deut 23:15). Greek has ἐν ἑαυτῇ ('in herself'). The Hebrew carries the theological weight of 'in her innermost being' — the place where God's presence dwells.
translation_notes: 'Within herself' for be-qirbah — preserving the depth of the Hebrew, which implies more than inner thought; it implies the core of her being.

greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the flowing of the blood stopped' (passive — the flow ceased). Greek: ἐξηράνθη ἡ πηγὴ τοῦ αἵματος ('the fountain of the blood was dried up'). Different metaphor: Hebrew uses stoppage; Greek uses drying of a spring.
translation_notes: הגרת (ha-geret) — 'the flowing,' possibly from גרר (to drag/flow) or גרה (to provoke/stir). A rare Hebrew medical term for chronic blood flow.

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew says Yeshua knew 'the truth' (האמת, emet, H571) that from him [power] went out. Greek says ἐπιγνοὺς τὴν ἐξ αὐτοῦ δύναμιν ἐξελθοῦσαν ('perceiving the power going out from him'). The Hebrew substitutes 'truth' (אמת) for Greek 'power' (δύναμις/כח). A back-translator from Greek would write הכח (ha-koach — 'the power'), not האמת ('the truth'). The Hebrew frames Yeshua's awareness as knowledge of truth rather than perception of power — an epistemological rather than phenomenological description.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the truth that from him went out.' Greek: 'the power going out from him.' Truth vs. power.
Hebrew omits the word for 'power' entirely.
translation_notes: [Power] added in brackets to clarify what went out — the Hebrew leaves this implicit, saying only 'from him went out.'

one_way_hebrew: Uses עמך (amkha — 'your people'). The Hebrew says 'your people press you' — implying that the crowd belongs to Yeshua, that they are 'his people.' Greek has ὁ ὄχλος ('the crowd'). A back-translator from 'the crowd' would write ההמון or העם without the possessive. The Hebrew possessive 'your people' echoes God's relationship with Israel — 'my people' (עמי) throughout the prophets.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'your people' (possessive — relational). Greek: 'the crowd' (neutral).

one_way_hebrew: Uses הפלא (ha-pele, H6382 — 'the wonder'). This is the OT's specific word for divine wonder-working — the wonders of the Exodus (Ex 15:11 'doing wonders'), the wonders God performs (Ps 77:12,15, 78:12), and the prophetic 'Wonderful Counselor' title (Isa 9:5). Greek has no single equivalent here. A back-translator from Greek would not independently select the loaded OT term פלא.

Uses ונברכה (ve-nivrekhah — 'and she knelt/blessed', from ברך H1288). The root ברך means both 'to kneel' and 'to bless.' The woman simultaneously knelt and invoked blessing. Greek has προσέπεσεν ('fell before'). A back-translator would use נפלה (naflah — 'fell'), not the blessing/kneeling verb ברך.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the wonder done in her' (פלא). Greek: no equivalent noun — only implies it through context.
