one_way_hebrew: Hebrew adds הבין (hevin, H995 — 'he understood/discerned') before speaking. This is absent in Greek. The verb בין is the OT wisdom verb for discernment (Prov 1:2, Dan 9:2, Neh 8:8). The Hebrew shows Yeshua exercising prophetic discernment before pronouncing the healing.

Uses הושיעך (hoshi'akh — 'has saved you', from ישע, H3467). This is the root of the name ישוע (Yeshua). The wordplay only works in Hebrew: 'Yeshua says your faith has yeshua'd (saved) you.' Greek σέσωκεν (from σῴζω) does not carry this nominal wordplay. This Hebraic pun on the Savior's own name is a strong one-way marker.
greek_deviations: Hebrew adds 'he understood' (הבין) — absent from Greek.
translation_notes: 'Saved' for hoshi'akh rather than 'healed' — to preserve the wordplay with Yeshua's name and the full scope of ישע (which includes both physical and spiritual deliverance).
textual_notes: The name ישוע (Yeshua) literally means 'he saves' — from the root ישע (yasha, H3467). When Yeshua says 'your faith has saved you,' the Hebrew audience hears the name and the verb as one: 'Yeshua (Salvation) says your faith has yeshua'd (saved) you.'

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses סגן (segan, H5461 — 'deputy/officer'). This is the priestly/Temple administrative title used in Nehemiah 2:16, 4:8, 5:7, 7:5, Jeremiah 51:23,28,57. In Second Temple literature, the סגן הכהנים was the Temple captain, second only to the High Priest. Greek has ἀρχισυνάγωγος ('ruler of the synagogue'). A back-translator from Greek would use ראש בית הכנסת ('head of the synagogue') or translate ἀρχι- as שר ('officer'), NOT reach for the Temple administrative term סגן. The Hebrew author sees the local assembly leader through Temple-priestly institutional categories.

Hebrew: 'why do you trouble yourself today still' (מצטער...היום עוד). Greek: τί ἔτι σκύλλεις τὸν διδάσκαλον ('why do you still trouble the teacher?'). The Hebrew says the father troubles himself; the Greek says he troubles the teacher. Completely different objects. Also, Hebrew adds 'today' (היום) which is absent from Greek.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'trouble yourself.' Greek: 'trouble the teacher.' Different objects.
Hebrew: adds 'today' (היום). Greek: absent.
Hebrew: 'deputy' (סגן). Greek: 'ruler of the synagogue' (ἀρχισυνάγωγος). Different titles.
translation_notes: 'Deputy' for segan — preserving the Temple administrative connotation. This is not merely a 'ruler' but a specific rank in the priestly hierarchy.

one_way_hebrew: Uses המלמד (ha-melamed, H3925 — 'the teacher'). From למד (lamed — 'to learn/teach'). This is a specifically Jewish educational title — the same root gives us תלמוד (Talmud — 'learning') and תלמיד (talmid — 'student'). Greek has no title here; it simply says ὁ Ἰησοῦς ('Jesus'). A back-translator from Greek would not add a title absent from the source.

Hebrew: 'good faith in HaShem' (טובה אמונה בשם). Greek: μόνον πίστευε ('only believe'). The Hebrew specifies the object of faith — HaShem (God) — while the Greek leaves faith objectless. Additionally, the Hebrew qualifies the faith as 'good' (טובה), absent in Greek. A back-translator from Greek would write האמן בלבד ('only believe'), not independently add 'good faith in HaShem.'
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the teacher Yeshua.' Greek: just 'Jesus.'
Hebrew: 'good faith in HaShem.' Greek: 'only believe.' Different scope and object of faith.
Hebrew: only Keyfa and Yaaqov (two disciples). Greek adds Ἰωάννην τὸν ἀδελφὸν Ἰακώβου ('John the brother of James'), making three. The Hebrew is shorter.
translation_notes: כיפא (Keyfa) — Aramaic for 'rock,' the Hebrew equivalent of Peter. The Hebrew text preserves the Semitic form, not the Greek Πέτρος.
צעקות (tse'aqot, H6818) — 'outcries,' the same word used for Israel's cry under Egyptian oppression (Ex 3:7,9). The mourning cries are described with Exodus-deliverance language.

one_way_hebrew: Uses נבוכים (nevukhim, H943 — 'troubled/confused'). This echoes Exodus 14:3 where Pharaoh says the Israelites are נבכים (entangled/confused) in the land. Greek has θορυβεῖσθε ('make commotion/uproar'). A back-translator from Greek would use סוערים (stormy/riotous) or המונים (noisy), not the Exodus-specific bewilderment verb.
greek_deviations: Hebrew structures Yeshua's statement as a question: 'The girl — is she dead?' (with interrogative האם). Greek is declarative: 'the child has not died.' Different rhetorical form.

one_way_hebrew: Uses גרש (garash, H1644 — 'drove out'). This is the verb used for God driving Adam from Eden (Gen 3:24), driving out the Canaanite nations (Ex 23:28-31, Deut 33:27), and Hagar being driven out (Gen 21:10). It implies forceful, authoritative expulsion. Greek has ἐκβαλών ('casting out') which is strong but lacks the specific OT exile connotation.

CRITICAL: The Hebrew glosses טליתא (Talitha) as בתולה (betulah, H1330 — 'virgin'). Greek glosses it as κοράσιον ('little girl'). The Hebrew author interprets the Aramaic word through the lens of virginal purity — specifically the word used in Isaiah 7:14 (הנה הבתולה הרה — 'behold, the virgin is with child'). A back-translator from Greek κοράσιον would use נערה (na'arah — 'girl') or ילדה (yaldah — 'child'), NEVER בתולה. The Hebrew interpretation loads the resurrection of this twelve-year-old girl with Isaiah's virgin prophecy. The girl is restored in her virginal wholeness — a sign pointing to resurrection itself.

The Aramaic טליתא קומי is preserved in brackets as a foreign phrase, then explained in Hebrew. This is the same authorial practice seen in Revelation where foreign words are marked בלעז ('in a foreign tongue'). A Hebrew author explains Aramaic for Hebrew readers; a Greek author would not need to explain what is already rendered in Greek.
greek_deviations: Hebrew gloss of Talitha: בתולה ('virgin'). Greek gloss: κοράσιον ('little girl'). Fundamentally different interpretations of the Aramaic.
Hebrew preserves Aramaic in brackets and provides a Hebrew explanation. Greek transliterates the Aramaic and provides a Greek translation.
translation_notes: 'Virgin' for betulah — this is not merely 'girl' but carries the full weight of virginal purity. The twelve-year-old girl is at the age of betrothal, and betulah specifically denotes an unmarried young woman of intact purity.
textual_notes: Talitha (טליתא) is Aramaic feminine for 'young girl/lamb.' The Hebrew author's choice to gloss this as betulah rather than na'arah reveals a theological interpretation: the girl raised from death is a 'virgin' — a sign of innocence restored, death's power over the pure overturned.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מגודל הפלא (mi-godel ha-pele — 'at the greatness of the wonder'). This is a constructed Hebrew expression combining גודל (H1433 — 'greatness', as in Deut 3:24, 5:24, 9:26, 11:2) with פלא (H6382 — 'wonder'). Greek has ἐξέστησαν ἐκστάσει μεγάλῃ ('they were amazed with great amazement') — a cognate accusative construction. A back-translator from Greek would write תמהו תמיהה גדולה ('amazed with great amazement'), not independently construct 'the greatness of the wonder.'
translation_notes: The girl was twelve years old — the same duration as the woman's blood flow (v25). This numerical parallel connects the two miracles: twelve years of death-in-life (the woman) and twelve years of life-unto-death (the girl).

6.summary: Mark 6 in Hebrew contains numerous strong one-way markers. The most significant: (1) בן נפח ('son of a smith/forger') where Greek has 'carpenter' — entirely different professions, with נפח (Isa 54:16) being a metalworker; (2) קרוביו ('his relatives') where Greek has 'brothers' — using the broader kinship term; (3) מאתים ככרות לחם ('200 loaves of bread') where Greek has '200 denarii worth of bread' — Hebrew counts bread, Greek counts money; (4) מכרכרת ('twirling' — 2 Sam 6:14 David's dance term) for Herodias's daughter where Greek has generic 'danced'; (5) שרביט ('scepter' — Esther's royal term) where Greek has 'staff'; (6) חיילות ('military companies') for seating where Greek has 'banquet groups'; (7) ערפליי ('clouded' — Sinai's thick darkness) for the disciples' hearts where Greek has 'hardened'; (8) אני הוא ('I am He' — Isaiah's divine self-identification) on the sea; (9) חינות והודאות ('supplications and thanksgivings') for the blessing where Greek has single 'blessed'; (10) פשוטי כלי עץ ('simple wooden vessels') for the platter — halakhic terminology; (11) תשובה ('return') for repentance; (12) שטן-theology continuing throughout. The chapter also contains a verbatim OT quote (כמו צאן בלא רועה — 'like sheep without a shepherd,' Num 27:17) and multiple echoes of Exodus wilderness narratives in the feeding account.

one_way_hebrew: Uses נכחיותיו (nekhachiyotav — 'his locales/neighborhoods'), a noun formed from נכח (nokhach — 'opposite/in front of', H5227). This is a uniquely Hebrew-constructed word for familiar surroundings. Greek has πατρίδα ('fatherland/hometown'). A back-translator from Greek would use מולדתו (moladto — 'his birthplace') or ארצו (artso — 'his land'), not this unusual formation from נכח.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'his locales' (נכחיותיו). Greek: 'his hometown' (πατρίδα). Different concepts.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מוסרו (musaro — 'his instruction/discipline', from מוסר H4148). In the OT, מוסר is the wisdom-tradition term for instruction and moral discipline (Prov 1:2,7,8, 3:11, 4:1, 8:33, 12:1). Greek has simply διδαχῇ ('teaching'). A back-translator from Greek would use תורתו or למודו, not the loaded Proverbs-wisdom term מוסר. The Hebrew says the crowd was amazed at his wisdom-tradition instruction.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'strength that goes out from his hands' (כח מהידים יוצא). Greek: δυνάμεις τοιαῦται ('such mighty works'). The Hebrew localizes the power to his hands; Greek speaks of mighty works generally.
Hebrew: 'the wisdom given to him' (passive — wisdom received). Greek: ἡ σοφία ἡ δοθεῖσα τούτῳ (similar, 'given to this one'). Both acknowledge the wisdom comes from outside.
translation_notes: מוסר (musar, H4148) in Proverbs encompasses the full scope of wisdom training: moral correction, intellectual instruction, and character formation. It is far richer than generic 'teaching.'

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses בן נפח (ben napach — 'son of a smith/forger'). The word נפח (H5301) means 'to blow' (bellows) and refers to a metalworker/smith. Isaiah 54:16: 'Behold, I created the smith (נפח) who blows the coals in the fire.' Greek has τέκτων (tektōn — 'carpenter/craftsman/builder'). A back-translator from Greek τέκτων would use חרש עצים (charash etsim — 'worker of wood') or simply חרש (artisan). The word נפח specifically means a SMITH — one who works metal by blowing bellows at a forge. Entirely different trade from carpentry.

Uses קרוביו (qerovav — 'his relatives/near ones', from קרב H7138 — 'near'). Greek has ἀδελφοί ('brothers'). A back-translator from 'brothers' would use אחיו (echav — 'his brothers'). The Hebrew uses the broader kinship term קרובים, which encompasses cousins, kinsmen, and extended family — a significant theological distinction regarding the 'brothers of Jesus' question.

Uses נכשלים (nikhshalim — 'stumbled/were offended', from כשל H3782 — 'to stumble'). This is the specific OT verb for stumbling over an obstacle (Lev 26:37, Isa 8:14-15 'He shall be... a stone of stumbling'). Greek σκανδαλίζω may itself derive from the Hebrew concept of מכשול (mikhshol — 'stumbling block'). The Hebrew is the original; the Greek is the loan-concept.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'son of a smith' (נפח — metalworker). Greek: 'the carpenter' (τέκτων — woodworker). Different professions.
Hebrew: 'his relatives' (קרובים — broad kinship). Greek: 'his brothers' (ἀδελφοί — siblings).
Hebrew: 'son of a smith AND Miriam' — names both parents. Greek: 'the son of Mary' — names only the mother.
translation_notes: 'Smith' for napach — the Isaiah 54:16 usage confirms this is a metalworker, not a woodworker. The distinction between Yeshua's father as a smith vs. a carpenter has theological implications: a smith works with fire and metal (judgment, refinement); a carpenter with wood (building, construction).
'Relatives' for qerovim preserves the Hebrew's broader kinship term, which does not require biological siblingship.
textual_notes: Isaiah 54:16: 'Behold, I have created the smith (נפח) who blows the coals in the fire and brings out a weapon for its purpose.' The same word for Yeshua's father's trade.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מכיריו (makirav — 'his acquaintances/those who know him', from נכר H5234 — 'to recognize/know'). Greek has συγγενεῦσιν ('kinsmen'). A back-translator from 'kinsmen' would use קרוביו (qerovav — 'relatives') or משפחתו (mishpachto — 'family'). The Hebrew uses the recognition/knowledge verb — those who 'know' him can't see past their familiarity.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'his acquaintances' (מכיריו). Greek: 'his kinsmen' (συγγενεῦσιν). Familiarity vs. kinship.

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew says he 'did not wish' (לא רצה) to do wonders. Greek says οὐκ ἐδύνατο ('was not able'). The Hebrew ascribes unwillingness; the Greek ascribes inability. A back-translator from 'could not' would write לא יכול (lo yakhol), not לא רצה (lo ratzah — 'did not want'). The Hebrew protects divine sovereignty — Yeshua chose not to act, rather than being unable.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'did not wish' (לא רצה — choice). Greek: 'could not' (οὐκ ἐδύνατο — inability). Fundamentally different theology of miracles.

translation_notes: Uses both דורש (doresh — 'expounding', the Torah-study verb) and מלמד (melamed — 'teaching'). Two different Hebrew educational terms: דרש is interpretive exposition; למד is direct instruction.

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew gives the disciples authority over 'sick and satan-possessed' (חולים ומשוטנים). Greek specifies ἐξουσίαν τῶν πνευμάτων τῶν ἀκαθάρτων ('authority over unclean spirits'). Again, Hebrew uses שטן-theology where Greek uses spirit-impurity language. The Hebrew also pairs healing and deliverance as one commission.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: authority over 'sick and satan-possessed.' Greek: authority over 'unclean spirits' only. Hebrew has broader scope.

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew includes אבן (even — 'stone'). This may refer to a money-stone or weight used for transactions (cf. Deut 25:13 'you shall not have in your bag diverse stones/weights'). Greek has μὴ χαλκόν ('no copper/money'). A back-translator from 'money' would use כסף (kesef) or מעות (ma'ot), not אבן. The Hebrew preserves the ancient practice of carrying weight-stones for commerce.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'sack, bread, stone, belt.' Greek: 'bread, bag, money in belt' (ἄρτον, πήραν, χαλκόν εἰς τὴν ζώνην). Different items in different order.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses שרביט (sharvit, H8275 — 'scepter'). This is the royal scepter — the word used in Esther 4:11, 5:2, 8:4 for the king's golden scepter that grants audience and authority. Greek has ῥάβδον ('rod/staff'). A back-translator from Greek would use מטה (mateh — 'staff') or מקל (maqel — 'stick'), not the royal scepter term. The Hebrew says the disciples carried scepters — symbols of royal authority — not mere walking sticks.

Uses עור חי (or chai — 'living leather') — untanned leather from freshly slaughtered animals. This specific material designation has no Greek equivalent; Greek says simply σανδάλια ('sandals'). The Hebrew specifies the material quality; the Greek names only the footwear type.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'scepter' (שרביט — royal authority). Greek: 'staff' (ῥάβδον — walking stick).
Hebrew: 'sandals of living leather.' Greek: just 'sandals.' Hebrew specifies material.
translation_notes: 'Scepter' for sharvit — the Esther connection (the king's scepter extending mercy and authority) may be intentional: the disciples carry the King's authority as they go out.

one_way_hebrew: Uses תלינו (talinu — 'you shall lodge', from לין H3885 — 'to lodge/spend the night'). This is the specific OT word for overnight hospitality (Gen 19:2, Judg 19:4,9,11,20, Ruth 1:16). Greek has μένετε ('remain/stay'). A back-translator would use שבו (shevu — 'stay'), not the hospitality verb לין.

Uses תסעו (tis'u — 'you depart/journey', from נסע H5265 — 'to pull up stakes/journey'). This is the Exodus travel verb — Israel 'journeyed' (ויסעו) from station to station (Ex 12:37, Num 10:12, 33:1ff). Greek has ἐξέλθητε ('go out'). The Hebrew frames the disciples' mission as an Exodus-like journeying.

translation_notes: Shaking off dust of the feet: a symbolic act marking separation from an unbelieving place, treating it as Gentile territory whose very soil defiles.

one_way_hebrew: Uses תשובה (teshuvah — 'repentance/return', from שוב H7725 — 'to return'). The Hebrew concept of repentance is fundamentally about returning to YHWH — a physical and spiritual turning back (Deut 30:2, Isa 55:7, Hos 14:2, Joel 2:12). Greek μετανοέω means 'to change one's mind' — a cognitive reorientation. A back-translator from Greek 'change of mind' would use a cognitive verb, not the return/journey verb שוב. The Hebrew frames repentance as homecoming; the Greek frames it as mental revision.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'repentance/return' (תשובה — returning to God). Greek: μετανοέω ('change of mind'). Different root metaphors.
translation_notes: 'Repentance' for teshuvah — though conventional, this translation loses the movement inherent in שוב ('return'). Teshuvah is a journey back, not merely a changed opinion.
textual_notes: Hosea 14:2: 'Return (שובה), O Israel, to YHWH your God, for you have stumbled in your iniquity.' The same root שוב defines the prophetic call to Israel.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses מישחת שמן מבורך (mishchat shemen mevorakh — 'anointing of blessed oil'). The root משח (mashach) is the same root that gives us משיח (Mashiach — 'the Anointed One'). Greek has ἤλειφον ἐλαίῳ ('anointed with oil'). Greek ἀλείφω is a common word for rubbing/smearing; Hebrew משח is the priestly-royal anointing verb (Ex 28:41, 30:30, 1 Sam 10:1, 16:13). A back-translator from Greek would use סכו בשמן (sakhu be-shemen — 'rubbed with oil'), not the messianic-priestly anointing term.
The oil is described as מבורך (mevorakh — 'blessed'). Greek has no equivalent adjective. The Hebrew implies the oil was ritually consecrated — paralleling the holy anointing oil of Exodus 30:25.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'anointing of blessed oil' (priestly/messianic). Greek: 'anointed with oil' (generic).
Hebrew: adds 'blessed' (מבורך). Greek: no qualification of the oil.

one_way_hebrew: Uses טבול (tavul — 'the Immerser', from טבל H2881 — 'to dip/immerse'). This is the OT word for ritual immersion (2 Kings 5:14 where Naaman 'dipped' in the Jordan; Lev 4:6, 14:16). Greek has Βαπτιστής (Baptistēs — from βαπτίζω). A back-translator from Greek would transliterate as בפטיסטא. The Hebrew uses the native OT ritual-immersion vocabulary.

Uses פלאות (pela'ot — 'wonders', H6381) — the plural of the OT divine wonder-working term. Greek has δυνάμεις ('powers/mighty works'). A back-translator from Greek would use גבורות (gevurot — 'mighty deeds'), not the Exodus-wonder vocabulary.
translation_notes: 'Immerser' for tavul rather than 'Baptist' — preserving the Hebrew/OT ritual immersion concept rather than importing the Greek ecclesiastical title.

one_way_hebrew: Uses חתכתי (chatakhti — 'I cut off', from כרת H3772 — 'to cut off/cut a covenant'). The root כרת is the OT word for both cutting a covenant (Gen 15:18, Ex 24:8) and being 'cut off' from the people as divine punishment (Gen 17:14, Ex 12:15, Lev 7:20). Greek has ἀπεκεφάλισα ('I beheaded'). A back-translator would transliterate or use a straightforward word. The Hebrew verb carries overtones of covenant-cutting — Herod 'cut off' the prophet in a grim inversion of covenant-making.

Uses בית הסוהר (beit ha-sohar — 'house of imprisonment', H5470). This is the same term used for Joseph's prison in Genesis 39:20-23 (בית הסהר). Greek has φυλακή ('guard/prison'). A back-translator from Greek would use more likely כלא (kele — 'prison') or משמר (mishmar — 'guard-house'). The Hebrew echoes the Joseph narrative — the righteous man imprisoned unjustly.
textual_notes: Genesis 39:20: 'And Joseph's master took him and put him in the prison (בית הסהר), the place where the king's prisoners were confined.' The same construction for Yochanan's imprisonment.

one_way_hebrew: Uses אשת אחיך (eshet achikha — 'the wife of your brother'). This is verbatim Levitical language from Leviticus 18:16: 'You shall not uncover the nakedness of your brother's wife (ערות אשת אחיך)' and Leviticus 20:21. Greek uses the same construction (γυναῖκα τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ), but the Hebrew phrase carries the full weight of Levitical sexual prohibitions.
textual_notes: Leviticus 18:16, 20:21 — the prohibition against taking a brother's wife while the brother lives. Yochanan charges Herodos with violating Torah.

one_way_hebrew: Uses ואורבו (ve-orevu — 'and laid in wait for him', from ארב H693 — 'to lie in ambush'). This is the specific OT word for ambush (Deut 19:11, Josh 8:2,4, Judg 9:25, Prov 1:11,18). Greek has ἐνεῖχεν αὐτῷ ('held a grudge against him'). A back-translator from 'held a grudge' would use שנאה (hatred) or נטרה (grudge), not the military-ambush verb. The Hebrew says Herodis plotted like a military ambusher.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'laid in wait' (ארב — ambush). Greek: 'held a grudge' (ἐνεῖχεν — bore resentment). Different intensity.

one_way_hebrew: Uses קדוש וצדיק (qadosh ve-tsaddiq — 'holy and righteous') — the two great OT character attributes. Greek has ἄνδρα δίκαιον καὶ ἅγιον ('a righteous and holy man'). The order is reversed: Hebrew puts 'holy' first (God's attribute), then 'righteous' (human ethical attribute). Greek puts 'righteous' first. The Hebrew order mirrors OT priority where God's holiness precedes human righteousness.

Uses שרי האלפים (sarei ha-alafim — 'officers of the thousands'). This is the specific OT military rank from Moses' judicial system (Ex 18:21,25, Deut 1:15) and Israel's army structure (Num 31:14,48, 1 Sam 8:12, 22:7). Greek has χιλιάρχοις ('chiliarchs/tribunes'). While χιλίαρχος is a literal Greek calque, the Hebrew term carries the full weight of Israelite military-judicial tradition stretching back to Sinai.

Uses חג (chag, H2282 — 'feast/pilgrimage-festival'). This is the word for the three great pilgrimage festivals: Pesach, Shavuot, Sukkot (Ex 23:14, Deut 16:16). Greek has γενέσια ('birthday feast'). A back-translator from Greek would use a birthday-specific term. The Hebrew ironically labels Herod's debaucherous birthday as a chag — a sacred pilgrimage term.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'feast from his birth' (חג מלידתו — using the sacred festival term). Greek: γενέσια ('birthday celebration' — a Greco-Roman custom).

one_way_hebrew: Uses מכרכרת (mekharkheret — 'twirling/whirling', from כרכר H3769). This is the exact word used in 2 Samuel 6:14,16 for David dancing/whirling before the ark: 'David was twirling (מכרכר) before YHWH with all his might.' Greek has ὀρχησαμένης ('having danced'). A back-translator from 'danced' would use רקדה (raqdah — 'danced') or חוללה (chollelah — 'danced in circle'). The Hebrew author uses the David-specific dance term — creating a dark inversion where Herodias's daughter twirls before a corrupt king as David twirled before YHWH.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'twirling' (מכרכרת — David's dance term). Greek: 'danced' (ὀρχέομαι — generic dancing).
translation_notes: 'Twirling' for mekharkheret — preserving the 2 Samuel 6 connection.
textual_notes: 2 Samuel 6:14: 'And David was twirling (מכרכר) before YHWH with all his might.' The same rare verb creates a deliberate contrast between sacred and profane dance.

Echoes Esther 5:3,6, 7:2 where King Ahasuerus says to Esther: 'What is your request? Even to half the kingdom it shall be given you.' The Hebrew narrative frames Herod's oath in the language of the Esther story — but with inverted morality.

one_way_hebrew: Uses פשוטי כלי עץ (peshutei klei ets — 'simple wooden vessels'). Greek has ἐπὶ πίνακι ('on a platter/plate'). A back-translator from Greek would use קערה (qe'arah — 'dish/platter') or צלחת (tsalachat — 'plate'). The Hebrew specifies a crude wooden vessel — emphasizing the degradation and poverty of the instrument. The Hebrew vocabulary suggests Rabbinic legal language where פשוטי כלי עץ ('simple wooden vessels') is a halakhic category for vessels that do not receive impurity (Mishnah Kelim 15:1).
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'simple wooden vessel' (crude, ritually significant). Greek: 'platter' (πίναξ — serving dish). Different object.

one_way_hebrew: Uses חתוך הראשים (chatokh ha-rashim — 'cutter of heads') for the executioner. This is a Hebrew compound title. Greek has σπεκουλάτωρ (spekoulator — a Latin loanword from speculator, a military executioner). A back-translator from Greek would transliterate the Latin military term. The Hebrew uses a native descriptive title instead.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'cutter of heads' (native Hebrew title). Greek: σπεκουλάτωρ (Latin military loanword). The Hebrew avoids the Latin term.
Hebrew: 'his body' (גופו). Greek: τὸ πτῶμα αὐτοῦ ('his corpse'). Hebrew uses the neutral 'body'; Greek uses the stronger 'corpse/fallen body.'

one_way_hebrew: Uses נחו (nuchu — 'rest', from נוח H5117). Again the Noah/sabbath-rest verb. Yeshua calls his disciples to sabbath-rest in the wilderness — echoing Israel's wilderness rest (Ex 33:14 'My presence will go with you, and I will give you rest'). Greek has ἀναπαύσασθε ('rest yourselves'). The same general meaning, but the Hebrew verb carries Exodus and sabbath theology.

Uses מקום חרב (maqom charev — 'desolate/ruined place'). The word חרב (charev) means 'dried up/desolate/ruined' and is the root of חרבה (chorbah — 'ruin') and חרב (cherev — 'sword'). It implies destruction and waste. Greek has ἔρημον τόπον ('deserted/uninhabited place') — neutral. A back-translator would use שומם (shomem — 'desolate') or just מדבר (midbar — 'wilderness'), not the ruins/destruction word חרב.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'desolate/ruined place' (חרב — destruction connotation). Greek: 'deserted place' (ἔρημος — merely empty).

one_way_hebrew: Uses דרך ארץ לרגל (derekh erets la-regel — 'by way of land on foot'). This is a native Hebrew travel idiom. Greek has πεζῇ ('on foot'). The Hebrew triple construction (way + land + foot) is characteristically Hebraic phrasing that a back-translator would compress.

DIRECT OT QUOTATION: כמו צאן בלא רועה ('like sheep without a shepherd') — from Numbers 27:17 where Moses asks YHWH to appoint a successor 'that the congregation of YHWH may not be like sheep that have no shepherd' (כצאן אשר אין להם רעה). Also 1 Kings 22:17 / 2 Chronicles 18:16. Greek has ὡς πρόβατα μὴ ἔχοντα ποιμένα — a fair translation of the Hebrew, but the Hebrew IS the original OT text. The Hebrew author naturally uses the Numbers 27 language; a Greek translator rendered it into Greek.

Uses ריחם (richem — 'had compassion', from רחם H7355 — 'womb/compassion'). This is womb-compassion — the deep visceral love of a mother for her child (Isa 49:15 'Can a woman forget her nursing child, that she should not have compassion (רחם) on the son of her womb?'). Greek ἐσπλαγχνίσθη (from σπλάγχνα — 'intestines') carries a similar visceral metaphor but from a different body organ.
translation_notes: 'Had compassion' for richem — the womb-love verb. Yeshua's response to the crowd is maternal in its depth.
textual_notes: Numbers 27:17: 'Let YHWH... appoint a man over the congregation... that the congregation of YHWH may not be like sheep that have no shepherd.' Moses' prayer for a successor — Joshua/Yeshua (same name) was the answer. The Hebrew Yeshua fulfills the role Moses prayed for.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Hebrew says מאתים ככרות לחם (matayim kikrot lechem — 'two hundred loaves of bread'). Greek says δηναρίων διακοσίων ἄρτους ('two hundred denarii worth of bread'). The Hebrew gives a QUANTITY of bread (200 loaves); the Greek gives a PRICE (200 denarii). A back-translator from Greek would write 'bread of 200 denarii' using the monetary term דינר, not a count of loaves. The Hebrew counts bread; the Greek counts money. The Hebrew perspective is about provision; the Greek about cost.

ככרות (kikrot) — plural of ככר (kikkar, H3603). In the OT, ככר can mean both 'round loaf' (1 Sam 2:36, 10:3, Jer 37:21) and 'talent' (a weight/monetary unit, Ex 25:39). In context with לחם, it means 'loaves.' The word's monetary double-meaning may explain how the Greek came to render this as a monetary figure.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: '200 loaves of bread' (quantity). Greek: '200 denarii of bread' (price). Different measurement systems.

one_way_hebrew: Uses חיילות (chaylot — 'companies/troops'). The word חיל (chayil) is a military term for an army unit, force, or troop (Ex 14:4, 1 Sam 17:20, 2 Sam 24:4). Greek has συμπόσια ('banquet-groups/drinking parties'). A back-translator from Greek would use חבורות (chavurot — 'groups') or מסיבות (mesivot — 'circles'). The Hebrew organizes the crowd in military formations — an echo of the wilderness camp order of Numbers 2.

The text adds a botanical annotation: [נקרא פי] ('called pei') — identifying the specific type of grass. This kind of local botanical notation is characteristic of an eyewitness or local author, not a translator.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'companies' (חיילות — military groupings). Greek: 'groups' (συμπόσια — banquet parties). Different organizational metaphor.
Hebrew includes botanical name of the grass. Greek has only χλωρῷ χόρτῳ ('green grass').

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew order: fifties then hundreds. Greek order: hundreds then fifties (κατὰ ἑκατὸν καὶ κατὰ πεντήκοντα). Different ordering. The Hebrew matches the military organization of Exodus 18:21 where Moses appointed rulers of thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens — listed from smallest upward in Hebrew style.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: fifties then hundreds (small to large). Greek: hundreds then fifties (large to small). Reversed order.
textual_notes: Exodus 18:21: 'rulers of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties, and of tens.' The wilderness feeding mirrors the wilderness camp structure.

one_way_hebrew: Uses חינות והודאות (chinot ve-hoda'ot — 'supplications and thanksgivings'). חינות from חן (chen — 'grace/favor') — petitions for grace. הודאות from ידה (yadah — 'to give thanks/confess'). These are TWO distinct Hebrew liturgical acts. Greek has εὐλόγησεν ('blessed') — a single act. A back-translator from 'blessed' would write ברך (berakh — 'blessed'), not the double liturgical formula. The Hebrew preserves the two-part Jewish blessing structure: petition (bakashah) followed by thanksgiving (hodayah).
greek_deviations: Hebrew: two acts — 'supplications and thanksgivings' (חינות והודאות). Greek: one act — 'blessed' (εὐλόγησεν). Hebrew has fuller liturgical detail.

translation_notes: שבעו (save'u — 'were satisfied', from שבע H7646). This is the Deuteronomic promise word: 'you will eat and be satisfied' (Deut 6:11, 8:10, 11:15). The wilderness feeding fulfills the Deuteronomic covenant blessing.
textual_notes: Deuteronomy 8:10: 'And you shall eat and be satisfied (ושבעת) and bless YHWH your God for the good land he has given you.' The feeding miracle echoes the manna narrative.

translation_notes: Twelve baskets — one for each tribe of Israel. The surplus is a sign of covenant abundance.
ביתה צידה (beitah tsidah) — literally 'house of provision/hunting.' The Hebrew preserves the Semitic meaning of Bethsaida.

greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'when his disciples went up on the mountain, he prayed by himself.' Greek: 'having sent them away, he went up on the mountain to pray.' In the Hebrew, the DISCIPLES go up the mountain; in Greek, YESHUA goes up. Different subjects.
Hebrew: 'Yeshua alone entered' — ambiguous. Greek: Yeshua was 'alone on the land' (μόνος ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς). Different location.

one_way_hebrew: הולך על הים (holekh al ha-yam — 'walking upon the sea'). This echoes Job 9:8 where God alone 'treads upon the heights of the sea' (דורך על במתי ים). Also Psalm 77:20: 'Your way was through the sea, your path through the great waters.' By walking on the sea, Yeshua performs an act that the OT attributes exclusively to YHWH. The Hebrew reader immediately recognizes the divine action.
textual_notes: Job 9:8: 'Who alone stretched out the heavens and treads upon the heights of the sea (דורך על במתי ים).' Walking on the sea is a YHWH-exclusive prerogative in the OT.

one_way_hebrew: Uses רוח רעה (ruach ra'ah — 'evil spirit'). This is the specific OT term from 1 Samuel 16:14-16,23, 18:10, 19:9 — 'an evil spirit from YHWH' that tormented Saul. Greek has φάντασμα ('phantom/ghost'). A back-translator from Greek would use a word for ghost/apparition, not the 1 Samuel theological term. The Hebrew frames the disciples' fear through Saul's torment narrative.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'evil spirit' (רוח רעה — 1 Samuel term). Greek: 'phantom' (φάντασμα — Hellenistic ghost concept).

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses אני הוא (ani hu — 'I am He'). This is the divine self-identification formula from Isaiah: 'I, I am He' (אני אני הוא, Deut 32:39); 'I am He' (אני הוא, Isa 41:4, 43:10,13, 46:4, 48:12). YHWH uses אני הוא to declare his unique identity. Greek ἐγώ εἰμι also carries this weight (cf. John 8:58), but the Hebrew formula directly connects to the Isaiah/Deuteronomy declarations. Yeshua, walking on the sea (a YHWH act, Job 9:8), then declares 'I am He' (a YHWH formula). The Hebrew audience hears two interlocking divine claims.
translation_notes: 'I am He' for ani hu — preserving the divine self-identification formula. Not merely 'it is I' (self-identification) but 'I AM HE' (divine declaration).

'Stand firm in confidence' for imdu be-vitchah — the Hebrew doesn't merely say 'take courage' (θαρσεῖτε) but 'stand firm in trust/security.' The root בטח (H983) is the OT word for trusting in YHWH (Ps 4:6, 9:11, 21:8, 25:2).
textual_notes: Isaiah 43:10: 'You are my witnesses, declares YHWH, and my servant whom I have chosen, that you may know and believe me and understand that I am He (אני הוא). Before me no god was formed, nor shall there be any after me.'

one_way_hebrew: Uses ערפליי (arafliy — 'clouded/foggy'). The root ערפל (arafel) is the word for the thick cloud/darkness that surrounds God's presence on Sinai (Ex 20:18, Deut 4:11, 5:19, 2 Sam 22:10, Ps 18:10). Greek has πεπωρωμένη ('hardened/petrified'). A back-translator from 'hardened' would use מוקשה (muqshah) or מאובנת (me'ubenet). The Hebrew says their hearts were in arafel-darkness — the same darkness that shrouded Sinai. They stood in the presence of divine glory but could not see through the cloud.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'clouded' (ערפליי — Sinai-theophany darkness). Greek: 'hardened' (πεπωρωμένη — petrified). Different metaphors with different theological associations.
textual_notes: Exodus 20:18: 'And the people stood far off, while Moses drew near to the thick darkness (ערפל) where God was.' The disciples' clouded hearts echo Israel's inability to approach God's presence.

one_way_hebrew: Uses שפת מלבושו (sfat malvusho — 'the lip/edge of his garment', H8193). שפה means 'lip/edge/border.' This echoes Numbers 15:38-39 where God commands Israel to make fringes (ציצית) on the corners/edges (כנפי) of their garments. Greek has τοῦ κρασπέδου τοῦ ἱματίου ('the fringe/border of his garment'). The Hebrew term 'lip' (שפה) for the garment edge is a distinctly Hebrew construction.
translation_notes: This verse merges what Greek separates as vv55-56. The Hebrew source combines both verses into a single narrative unit.
textual_notes: The touching of the garment's edge recalls the woman with the blood flow (5:27-28) and connects to the tsitsit (fringes) of Numbers 15:38-39, which remind Israel of YHWH's commandments.

7.summary: Mark 7 in Hebrew is saturated with Rabbinic halakhic terminology that no back-translator from Greek would independently produce. The strongest one-way markers: (1) נטילת ידים ('ritual hand-washing') — the precise Rabbinic technical term from Mishnah Yadayim, where Greek requires explanation ('common/unwashed hands'); (2) גזירת הישישים ('decree of the ancients') — a rabbinic legal category (gezirah = enacted decree), not mere 'tradition'; (3) חכמי הדת ישנה ('wise-men of the old religion') for 'scribes'; (4) רמאים ('deceivers') for 'hypocrites' — different moral category; (5) Two different defilement words (טנף and לכלך) where Greek uses one (κοινόω); (6) תמונה ('image/theophanic form') for 'parable'; (7) בלבול לשונו ('confusion of the tongue' — Babel reversal) for 'bond of the tongue'; (8) Verbatim Torah quotes (Ex 20:12, 21:17) with Hebrew infinitive absolute מות יומת; (9) Decalogue-ordered vice list (adultery, murder, theft); (10) Isaiah 29:13 quoted from MT rather than LXX. The chapter reveals an author thinking entirely within Rabbinic legal categories and Torah vocabulary — the debate over purity law is conducted in Hebrew halakhic language that Greek can only approximate.

one_way_hebrew: Uses פרושים (perushim — 'Separatists/those who separate', from פרש H6504 — 'to separate/distinguish'). This is the HEBREW meaning of the word: those who separate themselves for purity. Greek has Φαρισαῖοι (Pharisaioi) — a transliteration of the Hebrew. A back-translator from Greek would simply re-transliterate back. The Hebrew preserves the original etymological meaning: they are 'the separated ones.'

Uses חכמי הדת ישנה (chakhmei ha-dat yeshanah — 'wise-men of the old religion/law'). Greek has γραμματεῖς (grammateis — 'scribes/writers'). A back-translator from 'scribes' would use סופרים (sofrim — 'scribes/writers'). The Hebrew term is entirely different: these are not mere writers/copyists but 'sages of the ancient tradition.' The word דת (dat, H1881) is the Aramaic/later Hebrew word for law/religion (Ezra 7:26, Esther 1:8,13,15,19, 3:8). The qualifier ישנה ('old/ancient') distinguishes this tradition.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'Separatists' (פרושים — etymological meaning). Greek: 'Pharisees' (Φαρισαῖοι — transliteration).
Hebrew: 'wise-men of the old religion' (חכמי הדת ישנה). Greek: 'scribes' (γραμματεῖς). Entirely different titles.
translation_notes: 'Separatists' for perushim preserves the Hebrew etymological meaning.
'Old religion' for dat yeshanah — דת is specifically the law/decree/religion, not merely 'tradition.' The qualifier 'old' distinguishes it.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses נטילת ידים (netilat yadayim — 'ritual hand-washing'). This is the specific RABBINIC HALAKHIC term for the ritual of hand-washing before meals — a technical term from Rabbinic Judaism that appears in the Mishnah (Yadayim, Berakhot) and Talmud. Greek has κοιναῖς χερσίν, τοῦτ᾿ ἔστιν ἀνίπτοις ('with common/defiled hands, that is, unwashed'). A back-translator from Greek would write בידים טמאות ('with impure hands') or בידים בלתי רחוצות ('with unwashed hands'). The Hebrew uses the precise halakhic technical term that only a Hebrew author immersed in Rabbinic practice would employ.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: נטילת ידים (precise halakhic term for ritual hand-washing). Greek: 'common/unwashed hands' (κοιναῖς χερσίν, ἀνίπτοις). The Hebrew has a single technical term; the Greek requires explanation.
translation_notes: 'Ritual hand-washing' for netilat yadayim — this is not merely washing dirty hands but a specific ritual purification act with prescribed amounts of water and methods.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses גזירת הישישים (gezirat ha-yeshishim — 'decree of the ancients/elders'). גזירה (gezirah, from גזר H1504 — 'to cut/decree') is the specific RABBINIC term for a rabbinical decree or enacted prohibition — as opposed to a Torah commandment. It implies a legally binding ruling issued by rabbinic authorities. Greek has τὴν παράδοσιν τῶν πρεσβυτέρων ('the tradition of the elders'). A back-translator from Greek would use מסורת הזקנים (masoret ha-zqenim — 'tradition of the elders'). The Hebrew distinguishes: a גזירה is a DECREE (legislative act); a מסורת is a TRADITION (handed-down custom). The Hebrew says these are not traditions but legally enacted decrees.

Uses הישישים (ha-yeshishim, H3453 — 'the ancients'). This is a different word from זקנים (zqenim — 'elders'). ישישים implies extreme antiquity and age (Job 12:12, 15:10, 29:8, 32:6). Greek πρεσβυτέρων ('elders') would normally back-translate as זקנים. The Hebrew author uses the rarer, more ancient-sounding term.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'decree of the ancients' (גזירה — enacted law; ישישים — the very ancient). Greek: 'tradition of the elders' (παράδοσις — handed-down custom; πρεσβυτέρων — elders). Different legal categories.
translation_notes: 'Decree' for gezirah — this is a rabbinic legal ruling, not merely a custom. The distinction matters: Yeshua is challenging not informal traditions but formally enacted rabbinic legislation.
'Ancients' for yeshishim — older and more authoritative than merely 'elders.'

one_way_hebrew: Uses חקים (chuqim, H2706 — 'statutes/enactments'). This is the specific OT word for God's statutes (Lev 18:4, Deut 4:1, 6:1). Greek has no equivalent here (the verse structure differs). The Hebrew ironically applies the Torah's word for divine statutes to human ritual regulations — the very confusion Yeshua will challenge.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'statutes' (חקים — Torah's word for God's laws). Greek: various (the verse structure in Greek differs considerably, with more detail about washing of cups, pots, and brazen vessels).

one_way_hebrew: Uses גזירות ישישי האבות (gezirot yeshishei ha-avot — 'decrees of the ancients of the fathers'). This triple-layered authority designation (decree + ancients + patriarchs) is a distinctly Hebrew/Rabbinic authority chain. Greek has τὴν παράδοσιν τῶν πρεσβυτέρων ('the tradition of the elders'). The Hebrew is far more elaborate in its institutional terminology.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'decrees of the ancients of the fathers' (triple authority chain). Greek: 'tradition of the elders' (single term).
Hebrew: 'eat bread all the day' (פת כל הים). Greek has no time reference. Hebrew adds the habitual 'all day' detail.

one_way_hebrew: ISAIAH QUOTATION: Hebrew quotes Isaiah 29:13 — 'this people honors me with speech, but their heart is far from me' (העם הזה...בפיו ובשפתיו כבדוני ולבו רחק ממני). The Hebrew preserves the Isaiah source with minor variations. Greek quotes the LXX version of Isaiah. The Hebrew retains the MT form.

Uses רמאים (rama'im — 'deceivers/fraudsters', from רמה H7411 — 'to beguile/deceive'). Greek has ὑποκριταί ('hypocrites' — actors). A back-translator from Greek would use צבועים (tsevu'im — 'hypocrites/painted ones'). The Hebrew says the Pharisees are not merely play-actors (Greek concept) but DECEIVERS — active fraudsters. The OT roots of רמה include Jacob deceiving Esau (Gen 29:25) and Delilah deceiving Samson (Judg 16:10,13).
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'deceivers' (רמאים — active fraud). Greek: 'hypocrites' (ὑποκριταί — theatrical pretense). Different moral characterizations.
Hebrew: 'honors me with speech' (מדבר — words). Greek: 'honors me with their lips' (τοῖς χείλεσίν). Different body part.
translation_notes: 'Deceivers' for rama'im — stronger than 'hypocrites.' These are not merely actors but deliberate fraudsters.
textual_notes: Isaiah 29:13 (MT): 'Because this people draws near with their mouth and with their lips they honor me, but their heart is far from me, and their fear of me is a commandment of men learned by rote.' The Hebrew Mark preserves the MT; Greek uses the LXX.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מוסרים (musarim — 'instructions/disciplines', plural of מוסר H4148). Again the Proverbs wisdom-tradition term. These are not merely 'doctrines' (Greek διδασκαλίας) but wisdom-tradition 'instructions' — the word implies the entire apparatus of Rabbinic moral discipline. A back-translator from Greek would use הוראות (hora'ot — 'teachings/doctrines').

Uses גביעים (gevi'im — 'cups/goblets', H1375). This is the specific OT word for Joseph's silver divination cup (Gen 44:2,12,16,17). Greek has no equivalent here (the verse structure differs). The Hebrew author uses the Genesis-Joseph cup vocabulary for the ritual washing vessels.

Uses שוברים (shovrim — 'breaking', from שבר H7665 — 'to shatter/break'). This is the word for breaking a vessel, a covenant, or a law violently (Ex 32:19 Moses broke the tablets; Jer 19:10 breaking the potter's flask). Greek has ἀθετεῖτε ('you set aside/nullify'). A back-translator from 'set aside' would use מבטלים (mevatlin — 'annulling'). The Hebrew says they SHATTER God's commandments — the violence of Moses smashing the tablets.
Again uses השם (HaShem — 'the Name') for God. Consistent with Hebrew authorship.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'break/shatter' (שבר — violent destruction). Greek: 'set aside/reject' (ἀθετέω — nullification). Different intensity.

one_way_hebrew: VERBATIM TORAH QUOTATION: כבד את אביך ואת אמך (Exodus 20:12 / Deuteronomy 5:16) and אשר יקלל אביו ואמו מות יומת (Exodus 21:17 / Leviticus 20:9). The Hebrew preserves the EXACT MT wording including the emphatic Hebrew infinitive absolute construction מות יומת ('dying he shall die' — 'shall surely die'). Greek renders this as θανάτῳ τελευτάτω ('let him die the death') — a close but not exact rendering. A back-translator from Greek would not independently reproduce the Hebrew infinitive absolute construction.
translation_notes: מות יומת (mot yumat — 'surely die') — the Hebrew infinitive absolute construction that intensifies the verb. This exact form appears 47 times in the Torah as the penalty formula.
textual_notes: Exodus 20:12 and 21:17 — Yeshua quotes Torah to challenge the Pharisees' oral law, using the exact Hebrew text.

one_way_hebrew: Uses נדר (neder, H5088 — 'vow'). This is the OT vow system (Num 30:3-16, Deut 23:22-24). The Hebrew discusses the corban/vow system using native vocabulary. Greek has Κορβᾶν (Korban — a Hebrew loanword transliterated into Greek), then explains ὅ ἐστιν δῶρον ('which is, a gift'). The Greek needs to explain the Hebrew term to its audience; the Hebrew uses it naturally.
greek_deviations: Greek explains Korban as a foreign term that needs translation. Hebrew uses the vow system naturally without explanation — suggesting Hebrew priority.

one_way_hebrew: שמעוני ותבינוני ('hear me and understand me') echoes the Shema pattern and the wisdom call. שמע + בין together appear in Deuteronomy 9:1 ('Hear, O Israel') and Proverbs 1:2 ('to know wisdom and instruction, to understand words of understanding'). The dual imperative form is characteristically Hebrew.

Uses two different words for 'defile': לטנפו (letanfo — 'to dirty/soil him') and מלכלכו (melakhlekho — 'to defile/dirty him'). The first (טנף) is a practical term for physical soiling; the second (לכלך) is specifically moral defilement. Greek uses κοινόω ('to make common/profane') for both. A back-translator from Greek, seeing the same word twice, would use the same Hebrew word both times. The Hebrew author distinguishes between external contamination and internal defilement.
greek_deviations: Hebrew uses two different defilement words (טנף and לכלך). Greek uses one (κοινόω) for both.

textual_notes: This formula echoes Deuteronomy 29:3 ('YHWH has not given you a heart to understand or eyes to see or ears to hear') and Ezekiel 12:2 ('who have eyes to see but do not see, ears to hear but do not hear').

one_way_hebrew: Uses התמונה (ha-temunah — 'the image/figure/likeness'). In the OT, תמונה (H8544) is the word for the form/likeness of God (Num 12:8 'the form (תמונת) of YHWH he beholds'; Deut 4:12,15,16). Greek has παραβολή ('parable'). A back-translator from 'parable' would use משל (mashal — 'parable/proverb'), not the theophany-word תמונה. The Hebrew says the disciples asked about 'the image/vision' — framing Yeshua's teaching as a divine revelation rather than a story.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'image/figure' (תמונה — theophanic term). Greek: 'parable' (παραβολή — teaching story). Different framing.

one_way_hebrew: Uses פתאים (peta'im, H6612 — 'fools/simpletons'). This is the Proverbs wisdom-tradition term for the naive/gullible (Prov 1:4,22,32, 7:7, 8:5, 9:4,6, 14:15, 22:3). Greek has ἀσύνετοι ('without understanding'). A back-translator from Greek would use חסרי בינה ('lacking understanding'). The Hebrew uses the specific Solomonic wisdom category.

greek_deviations: Greek adds καθαρίζων πάντα τὰ βρώματα ('purifying all foods') — a parenthetical remark often interpreted as declaring all foods clean. The Hebrew has simply מנקה ('cleansing') without this editorial expansion.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מתנועעים (mitno'a'im — 'stirring/shaking', from נוע H5128 — 'to shake/waver'). This is the verb used for the earth shaking (Isa 24:20), trees swaying (Isa 7:2), and wandering/vagrancy (Gen 4:12 Cain's sentence). Greek has ἐκπορεύεται ('goes out'). A back-translator would use יוצאים (yotzim — 'going out'). The Hebrew describes evil as stirring/shaking within the heart before erupting — a more vivid and dynamic image.

The vice list uses OT/Torah vocabulary: ניאופים (ni'ufim — 'adulteries', from נאף H5003, the Seventh Commandment); רציחות (retzichot — 'murders', from רצח H7523, the Sixth Commandment); גניבות (genevot — 'thefts', from גנב H1589, the Eighth Commandment). These are the exact verb roots of the Ten Commandments. The Hebrew author catalogs sins using Decalogue vocabulary.
greek_deviations: Hebrew list has 4 items. Greek list has 6 items (adds πορνεῖαι — 'fornications' and πλεονεξίαι — 'covetings'). Hebrew is more concise.
textual_notes: Exodus 20:13-15 (MT): 'You shall not murder (לא תרצח). You shall not commit adultery (לא תנאף). You shall not steal (לא תגנב).' The vice list follows the Decalogue order.

one_way_hebrew: Uses סכלות (sikhlut, H5531 — 'foolishness'). This is the Ecclesiastes/Proverbs wisdom-tradition term (Eccl 1:17, 2:3,12,13, 7:25, 10:1,13). Greek has ἀφροσύνη ('lack of sense'). A back-translator would use אולת or חסרון דעת, not the specific Qohelet term.
Uses כילאות (kila'ut — 'miserliness/stinginess'). This is a distinctly Hebrew term for hoarding/withholding. Greek has πονηρίαι ('wickedness') or similar. Different vice categories.
greek_deviations: Hebrew has 4 items. Greek has 7 items (adds βλασφημία — 'blasphemy', ὀφθαλμὸς πονηρός — 'evil eye', ὑπερηφανία — 'arrogance'). Different vice lists.

textual_notes: Genesis 6:5: 'YHWH saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually.' Yeshua's teaching echoes the Genesis diagnosis of the human heart.

one_way_hebrew: Uses אבה (avah, H14 — 'wished/consented'). This is a specifically Hebrew verb for willingness/consent that appears throughout the OT (Gen 24:5,8, Deut 2:30, 10:10, 25:7, Judg 19:25, 1 Sam 22:17, 26:23, 31:4). Greek has ἤθελεν ('wished'). While the meanings overlap, אבה is a verb with no exact Greek equivalent — it implies deep, considered consent/willingness.

greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'satan-possessed' (מושטנת). Greek: 'had an unclean spirit' (πνεῦμα ἀκάθαρτον). The שטן vs. δαιμόνιον pattern continues.

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew says she was 'from the family of Syria' (ממשפחת סוריא). Greek says she was Ἑλληνίς, Συροφοινίκισσα τῷ γένει ('a Greek, a Syro-Phoenician by birth'). The Hebrew does not call her 'Greek' at all — only Syrian. A back-translator from Greek would include the 'Greek' designation. The Hebrew identifies her by clan/family (משפחה, H4940 — the OT kinship unit, Josh 7:14, Judg 6:15) rather than by ethnicity/nationality.
Hebrew also adds that she was נאה (na'eh — 'fine/beautiful'). This detail is absent from Greek. The Hebrew author notes her appearance — an eyewitness-type detail.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'fine woman from the family of Syria.' Greek: 'Greek woman, Syro-Phoenician by birth.' Different ethnic identification.
Hebrew adds 'fine/beautiful' (נאה). Greek has no appearance detail.

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew frames the saying with חייב (chayyav — 'obligated'). This is a HALAKHIC term — a legal obligation. The Hebrew says it is legally obligatory to feed one's children first. Greek has ἄφες πρῶτον χορτασθῆναι τὰ τέκνα ('let the children first be satisfied'). The Hebrew frames this as Torah-obligation; the Greek frames it as sequence.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'a man is OBLIGATED to help his children' (legal duty). Greek: 'let the children first be satisfied' (priority of sequence).

one_way_hebrew: Uses גורי הכלבים (gurei ha-kelavim — 'the whelps/puppies of the dogs'). The word גור (gur, H1484) is the OT word for a young animal/whelp — used of lion cubs (Gen 49:9, Deut 33:22, Nah 2:12). Greek has κυνάρια ('little dogs/puppies'). A back-translator from Greek would use כלבים קטנים ('little dogs'), not the literary/zoological term גור. The Hebrew word choice gives the woman's response a more dignified, literary quality.

Uses האדונים (ha-adonim — 'the masters/lords', plural of אדון H113). This is the word used for God (אדני — 'my Lord') and for human masters. Greek has κυρίων ('lords'). The Hebrew woman addresses Yeshua as אדון and speaks of 'the masters' — the double use of the same root creates a theological echo: the crumbs from THE Master's table.
translation_notes: 'Whelps' for gurei — preserving the OT zoological term rather than the diminutive 'puppies.'

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew says 'for this word' (בעד דבר זה) your daughter shall be healed. Greek says 'for this saying' (διὰ τοῦτον τὸν λόγον). Similar meaning, but the Hebrew uses דבר (davar) which means both 'word' and 'thing/matter' — the woman's WORD becomes the THING that heals. This double meaning only works in Hebrew.
Hebrew says 'shall be healed' (תתרפא). Greek says 'the demon has gone out' (ἐξελήλυθεν τὸ δαιμόνιον). The Hebrew focuses on healing; the Greek on exorcism. Different priorities.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'your daughter shall be healed' (healing focus). Greek: 'the demon has gone out' (exorcism focus).
Hebrew: 'the satan' (השטן). Greek: 'the demon' (τὸ δαιμόνιον). שטן vs. δαιμόνιον again.

translation_notes: דכפוליס (Decapolis) — a Greek loanword preserved in brackets in the source, indicating the Hebrew author recognized it as a foreign term.

one_way_hebrew: Uses חרש ואלם (cheresh ve-ilem — 'deaf and mute'). The word חרש (cheresh, H2795) appears in Isaiah 29:18 ('the deaf shall hear the words of a book') and 35:5 ('the ears of the deaf shall be unstopped'). Greek has κωφόν καὶ μογιλάλον ('deaf and speech-impaired'). The Greek μογιλάλος appears only here in the NT and is likely a direct reference to Isaiah 35:6 LXX. Both traditions point to Isaiah, but the Hebrew uses the standard OT vocabulary.
Uses בתפלה (be-tefilah — 'in prayer', H8605). They brought the man 'in prayer' — the request was made as a prayer. Greek has no equivalent.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: they asked 'in prayer' (בתפלה). Greek: they 'begged' (παρακαλοῦσιν). Different register.
textual_notes: Isaiah 35:5-6: 'Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf (חרשים) shall be unstopped... and the tongue of the mute (אלם) shall sing for joy.' This healing fulfills Isaiah's messianic prophecy.

one_way_hebrew: The Hebrew glosses אפתח (Ephphatha — an Aramaic imperative) as פתחו (pitchu — 'be opened', from פתח H6605). The Hebrew author explains an Aramaic word in Hebrew — the same authorial practice seen in Mark 5:41. A translator working from Greek would not need to provide a Hebrew gloss of an Aramaic word already explained in Greek.

Uses מתאנח (mit'anech — 'groaning/sighing', from אנח H584). This is the specific OT word for sighing in distress and compassion (Isa 24:7, Lam 1:4,8, Ezek 9:4, 21:11). The groaning expresses visceral empathy.

Uses בלבול לשונו (bilbul leshono — 'the confusion of his tongue'). בלבול means 'confusion/mixing' — related to בבל (Babel, 'confusion', Gen 11:9). Greek has ὁ δεσμὸς τῆς γλώσσης ('the bond of the tongue'). A back-translator from 'bond' would use מוסר (moser — 'bond/chain') or קשר (qesher — 'knot'), not 'confusion.' The Hebrew says the tongue's CONFUSION (Babel) was loosed — an un-Babeling, a reversal of linguistic curse.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'confusion of the tongue' (בלבול — Babel/confusion). Greek: 'bond of the tongue' (δεσμός — chain/binding). Different metaphors.
textual_notes: The healing reverses the Babel curse (Gen 11:7-9) — the tongue's confusion is unbound. This is anti-Babel.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מגלה (megaleh — 'revealed/uncovered', from גלה H1540 — 'to uncover/reveal/exile'). This is the word for divine revelation (Amos 3:7 'YHWH does nothing without revealing (גלה) his secret to his servants the prophets'). Greek has μᾶλλον περισσότερον ἐκήρυσσον ('they proclaimed it even more'). A back-translator would use הכריזו (hikhirzu — 'proclaimed'). The Hebrew says the people REVEALED — using the prophetic revelation verb.

ISAIAH FULFILLMENT: 'He made the mute speak and the deaf hear' — echoing Isaiah 35:5-6 ('the ears of the deaf shall be unstopped... the tongue of the mute shall sing for joy'). The crowd's testimony is framed in Isaiah's messianic vocabulary. The Hebrew preserves the OT source; the Greek translates it.
textual_notes: Isaiah 35:5-6: 'Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf (חרשים) unstopped; then shall the lame leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute (אלם) sing for joy.' The crowd recognizes the Isaiah fulfillment.

8.summary: Mark 8 in Hebrew contains two of the most extraordinary one-way markers in the entire Hebrew Gospels corpus. (1) שתי וערב ('warp and woof') in v34 where Greek has 'cross' — the Hebrew uses the Levitical weaving terminology from Leviticus 13 (the inspection of garments for impurity). The cross-shape is inherent in weaving (vertical warp crossed by horizontal woof), but NO back-translator from Greek σταυρός would independently generate this Levitical textile term. The connection to priestly purity examination adds a layer of meaning absent from the Roman execution instrument. (2) בן הבתולה ('Son of the Virgin') in v38 where Greek has 'Son of Man' — a completely different Christological title that directly invokes Isaiah 7:14 rather than Daniel 7:13. This is perhaps the single most theologically significant divergence between the Hebrew and Greek traditions in all of Mark. Additional strong markers include: חיל (host/army) for the crowd; שכנגדי ('my adversary') instead of 'Satan' for Keyfa; הפרד ('separate' — Pharisee root) as Yeshua's command to Keyfa; the כפר (deny/atone) wordplay; באורו ('in his light') vs. 'in glory'; האומה ('the nation') vs. 'the generation'; and verbatim quotation from Jeremiah 5:21 / Ezekiel 12:2 ('eyes and do not see, ears and do not hear'). The chapter builds to a climactic revelation: the one called Mashiach (v29) is also the Son of the Virgin (v38) — the Isaiah 7:14 prophecy fulfilled.

one_way_hebrew: Uses חיל (chayil, H2428 — 'host/army/force'). This is the OT word for military strength, wealth, and force (Ex 14:4, Deut 8:17, Josh 1:14, Ruth 2:1 'mighty man of chayil'). Greek has ὄχλου πολλοῦ ('great crowd'). A back-translator from 'crowd' would use המון (hamon — 'multitude') or קהל (qahal — 'assembly'), not the military-wealth term חיל. The Hebrew frames the crowd as an 'army' — a host gathered around their commander.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'a great host of people' (חיל — military/force). Greek: 'a very great multitude' (ὄχλου πολλοῦ — neutral crowd).

one_way_hebrew: Uses רחמנות (rachmanut — 'compassion', from רחם H7356 — 'womb'). This is the visceral, maternal compassion — womb-love. Greek has σπλαγχνίζομαι ('moved in the bowels/intestines'). Both use visceral metaphors but from different body organs: Hebrew from the womb (feminine/maternal); Greek from the intestines (gender-neutral). A back-translator from Greek intestinal compassion would not independently choose the womb-compassion word.

Uses יתעלפו (yit'alefu — 'they will faint/swoon'). The root עלף appears in the OT for fainting/swooning (Isa 51:20, Amos 8:13, Jonah 4:8). Greek has ἐκλυθήσονται ('they will give out/collapse'). A back-translator would use יפלו (yiplu — 'they will fall') or ייעפו (yi'afu — 'they will tire'). The Hebrew verb carries overtones of heat exhaustion and physical collapse.

The phrase 'satisfied in the wilderness' (לשבוע...במדבר) directly invokes the manna narrative. שבע (sava — 'satisfied', H7646) + מדבר (midbar — 'wilderness', H4057) together echo Deuteronomy 8:15-16: 'who led you through the great and terrifying wilderness... who fed you with manna in the wilderness.' The disciples' question is framed in Exodus language — where will bread come from in the wilderness?
textual_notes: Deuteronomy 8:15-16: the manna feeding in the wilderness. The disciples fail to connect Yeshua's first feeding (ch. 6) with the wilderness provision pattern.

one_way_hebrew: Uses חנות (chanot — 'supplications/grace-seeking', from חן H2580 — 'grace'). Greek has εὐχαριστήσας ('having given thanks'). In the first feeding (6:41), the Hebrew had חינות והודאות ('supplications and thanksgivings'). Here only חנות — the grace-petition. A back-translator from Greek 'gave thanks' would use הודה (hodah — 'thanked'), not the grace-supplication verb.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'making supplications' (חנות — seeking grace). Greek: 'gave thanks' (εὐχαριστέω). Different liturgical acts.

translation_notes: Seven full baskets remaining — seven may symbolize divine completeness, contrasting with the twelve baskets of the first feeding (representing the twelve tribes).

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew preserves כפר נחום (Kfar Nachum — 'Village of Consolation/Nahum'). Greek has εἰς τὰ μέρη Δαλμανουθά ('to the region of Dalmanutha'). The Hebrew includes a specific destination (Kfar Nachum) that Greek lacks in this verse. The Hebrew place-name is meaningful: 'Village of Comfort' (from נחם — 'to comfort').
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'Kfar Nachum and Dalmanuta' (two destinations). Greek: 'the region of Dalmanutha' (one destination). Hebrew includes Kfar Nachum.

one_way_hebrew: Uses אות (ot, H226 — 'sign/omen/miraculous sign'). This is the OT word for God's signs: the rainbow (Gen 9:12), circumcision (Gen 17:11), the Exodus signs (Ex 4:8, 7:3, Deut 4:34). Greek has σημεῖον ('sign'). While similar in meaning, the Hebrew carries the full weight of OT sign-theology. The Pharisees demand an 'ot' — the kind of sign God gave Moses.

Uses נתוכחו (nitvakhechu — 'debated/argued', from יכח H3198 — 'to reprove/argue/reason'). This is the prophetic confrontation verb (Isa 1:18 'Come, let us reason together'; Job 13:3, 23:7). Greek has ἤρξαντο συζητεῖν ('began to dispute'). A back-translator would use התווכחו (hitvakhechu) or similar, but the Hebrew verb specifically invokes prophetic argumentation.

Uses סימן ההראות (siman ha-hera'ot — 'a sign of visions/showings'). This compound phrase means 'a visionary sign' — a sign that comes through divine vision. Greek has σημεῖον ('a sign'). The Hebrew is more specific: not just any sign, but a sign of prophetic vision. A back-translator from Greek would write simply אות ('sign'), not this elaborate visionary construction.

Uses אמת (emet, H571 — 'truth') where Greek has ἀμὴν (amēn — a Hebrew loanword transliterated). The Hebrew uses 'truth' as the introductory formula; the Greek transliterates the Hebrew אמן ('amen'). The Hebrew author says 'truth' (אמת); the Greek converts it to the liturgical 'amen.'
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'truly' (אמת — truth). Greek: 'amen' (ἀμήν — transliterated Hebrew). Different forms.
Hebrew: 'a sign of visions' (elaborate). Greek: 'a sign' (simple). Hebrew is more specific.

one_way_hebrew: Uses שאור (se'or, H7603 — 'leaven/sourdough'). This is the specific OT word for the leaven forbidden during Pesach (Ex 12:15,19, 13:7). Greek has ζύμη ('leaven'). While the meanings overlap, the Hebrew שאור specifically evokes the Passover prohibition — leaven as moral/spiritual contamination that must be purged. The Pesach context is immediate in Hebrew; in Greek it's merely metaphorical.
textual_notes: Exodus 12:15: 'Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread. On the first day you shall remove leaven (שאור) from your houses.' The Passover leaven purge is the background for Yeshua's warning.

one_way_hebrew: Uses עור לבבכם (iver levavkhem — 'blind is your heart', with עור H5787 — 'blind'). Greek has πεπωρωμένην... τὴν καρδίαν ('hardened heart'). In Mark 6:52, the Hebrew used ערפליי ('clouded'). Now it escalates to 'blind.' A back-translator from 'hardened' would use מוקשה (muqshah) or ערל (arel — 'uncircumcised/blocked'), not עור ('blind'). The Hebrew says the heart has eyes that have gone blind — a different metaphor from hardening.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'blind heart' (עור — visual metaphor). Greek: 'hardened heart' (πεπωρωμένη — petrification metaphor). Different images.

one_way_hebrew: VERBATIM OT QUOTATION: 'Eyes you have and do not see, ears you have and do not hear' — from Jeremiah 5:21 (עינים להם ולא יראו אזנים להם ולא ישמעו) and Ezekiel 12:2 (עינים להם לראות ולא ראו אזנים להם לשמע ולא שמעו). Also Deuteronomy 29:3 and Psalm 115:5-6 / 135:16-17. The Hebrew preserves the prophetic source text. Greek renders it as a translation. The Hebrew IS the source.

Adds אין לכם זכרון (ein lakhem zikaron — 'have you no memory/memorial?'). The word זכרון (zikaron, H2146) is the OT word for memorial/remembrance — the same word used for Passover (Ex 12:14 'this day shall be for you a memorial/zikaron') and the memorial stones of Joshua 4:7. Greek has οὐ μνημονεύετε ('do you not remember?'). The Hebrew asks about zikaron — the covenantal, liturgical act of remembrance.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'have you no memorial/remembrance?' (זכרון — covenantal memory). Greek: 'do you not remember?' (μνημονεύω — recall).
textual_notes: Jeremiah 5:21: 'Hear this, O foolish people without understanding, who have eyes and see not, who have ears and hear not.' Yeshua applies the prophetic rebuke of Israel to his own disciples.

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew uses two different words for 'basket': קופות (qufot) in v19 and סלים (salim, H5536) in v20. Greek also distinguishes: κοφίνων (large wicker baskets) in v19 and σπυρίδων (flexible hampers) in v20. Both Hebrew and Greek preserve a distinction between the two feeding miracles' baskets — suggesting independent witnesses to the same detail, not translation.
translation_notes: The two different basket words in both Hebrew and Greek independently preserve the same distinction between the two feedings.
בית צידה (Beit Tsaidah) — 'House of Hunting/Fishing.' The Hebrew preserves the Semitic meaning.

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew: 'spat on his face' (רקק לו בפניו). Greek: 'spit on his eyes' (πτύσας εἰς τὰ ὄμματα). Different target: face (פנים) vs. eyes (ὄμματα). The Hebrew is broader; the Greek more specific.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'on his face' (בפניו). Greek: 'on his eyes' (εἰς τὰ ὄμματα). Different target.

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew says 'I see the walking of the peoples, upright like trees' (הלוך העמים זקופים כמו אילנות). Greek says ὅτι ὡς δένδρα ὁρῶ περιπατοῦντας ('I see men walking like trees'). The Hebrew structure is different: he sees the peoples' movement, then describes them as upright like trees. The word זקופים (zequfim — 'upright/erect') emphasizes their vertical posture. The Hebrew perspective is more dynamic — he perceives movement and uprightness.

textual_notes: The two-stage healing is unique in the Gospels. It may symbolize the disciples' partial understanding — they see, but not yet clearly (cf. vv17-21).

one_way_hebrew: Uses משכיניך (mi-shekhenaikha — 'among your neighbors', from שכן H7934 — 'neighbor/one who dwells near'). Greek has μηδὲ εἰς τὴν κώμην εἰσέλθῃς ('do not enter into the village'). Completely different instructions: the Hebrew says don't tell your neighbors; the Greek says don't enter the village. A back-translator would not convert 'don't enter the village' into 'don't tell your neighbors.'
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'do not tell any man among your neighbors.' Greek: 'do not enter the village.' Different commands.

one_way_hebrew: Uses משיח (Mashiach, H4899 — 'the Anointed One'). This is the OT title for the anointed king (1 Sam 2:10, 24:7, 2 Sam 22:51, Ps 2:2) and the prophesied deliverer (Dan 9:25-26). Greek has ὁ Χριστός ('the Christ'). While Christos is the standard Greek translation of Mashiach, the Hebrew carries the full OT anointing theology — the oil poured on kings (1 Sam 10:1, 16:13) and priests (Ex 28:41). The Hebrew title is the original; the Greek is the translation.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: simply 'Mashiach' (the Anointed One). Greek adds τοῦ θεοῦ τοῦ ζῶντος ('of the living God') in Matthew's parallel, but Mark's Greek also has just ὁ Χριστός.
textual_notes: Psalm 2:2: 'The kings of the earth set themselves... against YHWH and against his Anointed One (משיחו).' Keyfa's confession identifies Yeshua with the Psalm 2 king.

one_way_hebrew: Uses נגוש (nagush — 'pushed/pressed/driven', from נגש H5065 — 'to oppress/drive/exact'). This is the word for the Egyptian taskmasters oppressing Israel (Ex 3:7, 5:6,10,13,14; Isa 3:12). Greek has ἀποδοκιμασθῆναι ('to be rejected'). A back-translator from 'rejected' would use נמאס (nim'as — 'rejected') or נדחה (nidchah — 'pushed away'). The Hebrew says Yeshua will be 'oppressed' like Israel in Egypt — an Exodus-suffering verb.

Uses שרי הכהנים (sarei ha-kohanim — 'officers/princes of the priests') and חכמי הדת (chakhmei ha-dat — 'wise-men of the religion'). Greek has ἀρχιερέων ('chief priests') and γραμματέων ('scribes'). The Hebrew uses different institutional titles throughout — never importing Greek terminology.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'pushed/oppressed to death' (נגש — Exodus oppression). Greek: 'rejected' (ἀποδοκιμάζω — official disapproval). Different verbs.
Hebrew: 'officers of the priests' and 'wise-men of the religion.' Greek: 'chief priests' and 'scribes.' Different titles.
textual_notes: Isaiah 53:7: 'He was oppressed (נגש) and he was afflicted.' The same verb נגש connects Yeshua's suffering prediction to Isaiah's Suffering Servant.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses שכנגדי (she-kenegdi — 'that which is against me/my adversary'). This is formed from כנגד (keneged — 'opposite/against/corresponding to'). The same root appears in Genesis 2:18 where God makes an עזר כנגדו (ezer kenegdo — 'a helper corresponding to him') for Adam. Greek has Σατανᾶ ('Satan'). A back-translator from 'Satan' would simply write שטן. The Hebrew does NOT use שטן here but a phrase meaning 'my adversary/opponent' — describing the ROLE (one who opposes), not the TITLE (Satan).

Uses שכל אלהיי...בשריי (sekhel elohiy...basriy — 'divine understanding...fleshly'). The contrast is between אלהיי (from אלהים — 'divine/of God') and בשריי (from בשר — 'flesh/carnal'). Greek has τὰ τοῦ θεοῦ... τὰ τῶν ἀνθρώπων ('the things of God... the things of men'). The Hebrew pairs divine understanding (שכל) with fleshly thinking — the contrast is intellectual/spiritual. The Greek pairs God's things with men's things — a more abstract contrast.

Uses הפרד (hipared — 'separate yourself/depart', from פרד H6504 — 'to separate'). This is the root of the Pharisees' name (פרושים — 'the separated'). Greek has ὕπαγε ('go away/get behind'). Yeshua tells Keyfa to 'separate' — ironically using the Pharisaic root. He becomes a 'Pharisee' (separator) by thinking fleshly thoughts.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'my adversary' (שכנגדי — descriptive). Greek: 'Satan' (Σατανᾶ — title/name). Different handling of the rebuke.
Hebrew: 'no divine understanding, but fleshly' (intellectual contrast). Greek: 'not minding God's things, but men's things' (orientation contrast).
Hebrew: 'depart/separate' (הפרד — same root as 'Pharisee'). Greek: 'get behind' (ὕπαγε).
translation_notes: 'Adversary' for she-kenegdi rather than 'Satan' — the Hebrew describes a role, not a title. Keyfa acts as an adversary to the divine plan, not as THE Satan.
The ironic use of הפרד (Pharisee-root) against Keyfa: 'Separate yourself from me' — you who oppose God's plan have become a Separator.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses שתי וערב (sheti va-erev — 'warp and woof'). These are the two sets of threads in weaving: the vertical (warp/שתי) and the horizontal (woof/ערב). Together they form the CROSS pattern of woven fabric. Greek has σταυρόν ('cross' — the Roman execution instrument). A back-translator from Greek σταυρός would use צלב (tselav — 'cross') or עמוד (amud — 'stake/post'). NO back-translator would EVER independently generate 'warp and woof' from 'cross.' This is one of the most extraordinary one-way markers in the Hebrew Gospels.

The phrase שתי וערב appears in Leviticus 13:48,49,51,52,53,56,57,58,59 as part of the laws of צרעת (tsara'at — 'leprosy/skin disease') in garments. The priest inspects the שתי או בערב ('warp or woof') for signs of disease. The warp-and-woof is connected to ritual purity examination. The Hebrew says: take your warp-and-woof (the place where impurity is found and examined) and follow me — a purification metaphor that only works in Hebrew/Levitical context.

Uses יכפור (yikhpor — 'let him deny/disavow', from כפר H3584 — 'to deny/lie/disown'). This root also means 'to cover/atone' (כפר, kaphar). The wordplay: deny (כפר) yourself = atone (כפר) for yourself. This double meaning only works in Hebrew.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'warp and woof' (שתי וערב — weaving/Levitical purity). Greek: 'cross' (σταυρός — Roman execution). Entirely different imagery with utterly different cultural contexts.
Hebrew: 'deny' (כפר — also 'atone'). Greek: 'deny' (ἀπαρνέομαι — renounce). Hebrew has double meaning.
translation_notes: 'Warp-and-woof' for sheti va-erev — the intersecting threads of a loom. The cross-shape is inherent in the weaving: vertical threads crossed by horizontal threads. The Hebrew preserves the original metaphor from which the Greek 'cross' derives its meaning in this context.

The Leviticus 13 connection: שתי וערב is the location in fabric where impurity manifests and must be examined by a priest. To 'take up your warp-and-woof' is to carry the site of impurity examination — to bear one's own purification.
textual_notes: Leviticus 13:48: 'whether in the warp (שתי) or the woof (ערב)... it is a leprous disease.' The warp-and-woof is where spiritual disease is diagnosed. Yeshua transforms the image: carry your warp-and-woof (the cross-pattern where sin is diagnosed and purged) and follow me.

one_way_hebrew: Uses הבשורה (ha-besorah — 'the good-news', from בשר H1319 — 'to bring good tidings'). This is the specific OT word for joyful proclamation: Isaiah 40:9 ('O bearer of good tidings to Zion'), 52:7 ('How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good tidings'), 61:1 ('YHWH has anointed me to bring good tidings'). Greek has εὐαγγέλιον ('gospel/good news'). While etymologically parallel, the Hebrew word carries the specific Isaiah context of messianic proclamation.
Again uses ישע (yasha, H3467 — 'to save') — the root of Yeshua's name. The wordplay: 'whoever loses his soul for Yeshua (ישוע) shall save (יושיע) it.' The salvation is embedded in the Savior's name.
translation_notes: 'Good-news' for besorah — preserving the Isaiah herald-proclamation sense rather than importing the ecclesiastical 'gospel.'
textual_notes: Isaiah 52:7: 'How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good tidings (מבשר), who publishes peace, who brings good tidings of good.' The besorah is the messianic herald's message.

translation_notes: Uses both נשמה (neshamah, v35 — 'breath-soul', the divine breath of Gen 2:7) and נפש (nefesh, v36 — 'living soul/life-force'). Hebrew distinguishes between these; Greek uses ψυχή for both.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses בן הבתולה (ben ha-betulah — 'the Son of the Virgin', H1121 + H1330). Greek has ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ('the Son of Man'). A back-translator from Greek 'Son of Man' would write בן אדם (ben adam) or בן אנוש (ben enosh) — the Daniel 7:13 title. The Hebrew says 'SON OF THE VIRGIN' — a completely different title that directly invokes Isaiah 7:14 (הנה הבתולה הרה וילדת בן — 'behold, the virgin is with child and bears a son'). This is among the most striking one-way markers in the entire Hebrew Gospels. No back-translator from Greek would EVER replace 'Son of Man' with 'Son of the Virgin.'

Uses האומה מנאפת חטאה ('this adulterous, sinful nation'). Hebrew uses אומה (ummah, H524 — 'nation/tribe') rather than the Greek γενεά ('generation'). A back-translator from 'generation' would use דור (dor — 'generation'). The Hebrew אומה implies a national entity, not a temporal generation.

Uses באורו (be-oro — 'in his light', from אור H216 — 'light'). Greek has ἐν τῇ δόξῃ τοῦ πατρὸς αὐτοῦ ('in the glory of his Father'). Hebrew: 'in his light.' Greek: 'in glory.' A back-translator from 'glory' would use בכבודו (be-khvodo), not באורו. Light (אור) is a more primordial divine attribute (Gen 1:3 'Let there be light') than glory (כבוד).
greek_deviations: MAJOR: Hebrew: 'Son of the Virgin' (בן הבתולה — Isaiah 7:14). Greek: 'Son of Man' (υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου — Daniel 7:13). Completely different Christological titles.
Hebrew: 'this adulterous, sinful nation' (אומה — national entity). Greek: 'this adulterous and sinful generation' (γενεά — temporal generation).
Hebrew: 'in his light' (אור — primordial light). Greek: 'in the glory of his Father' (δόξα — glory). Different divine attributes.
Hebrew: 'HaShem the Father' (השם האב). Greek: 'his Father' (τοῦ πατρὸς αὐτοῦ). Hebrew uses the divine Name circumlocution.
translation_notes: 'Son of the Virgin' for ben ha-betulah — preserving the Hebrew title exactly as it appears. This is NOT 'Son of Man' (ben adam). The Hebrew author uses a Christological title rooted in Isaiah 7:14's virgin prophecy, not Daniel 7:13's 'one like a son of man.'
'In his light' for be-oro — the primordial light of Genesis 1:3, the light that precedes sun and moon.
textual_notes: Isaiah 7:14: 'Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign: behold, the virgin (הבתולה) shall conceive and bear a son (בן), and shall call his name Immanuel.' The Hebrew title 'Son of the Virgin' directly combines Isaiah's הבתולה with the resulting בן — compressing the prophecy into a Christological title.

The presence of 'Son of the Virgin' where Greek has 'Son of Man' suggests the Hebrew tradition preserved an alternative or earlier Christological title. The Greek 'Son of Man' may reflect the Daniel 7 tradition while the Hebrew preserves the Isaiah 7 tradition.

9.summary: Mark 9 in Hebrew contains multiple critical one-way translation markers. The most striking are: (1) גן עדן ('Garden of Eden') vs. Greek 'life' — the Hebrew preserves the native Jewish eschatological destination (vv43,45,47); (2) ארסים ('venomous things') vs. Greek 'worm' — identifying Isaiah 66:24's creatures as serpentine rather than vermicular (vv44,46,48); (3) בן האלוה ('Son of God') where Greek has 'Son of Man' (vv12,31); (4) עב ('thick cloud') — the Sinai theophany term (v7); (5) יקר ('precious') vs. Greek 'beloved' for the divine son (v7); (6) משיחים ('anointed ones,' plural) vs. 'of Christ' (v41); (7) גיהנם paired with Garden of Eden creates a native Hebrew eschatological contrast absent from Greek. The chapter also shows consistent use of מראה (prophetic vision), סוד (secret counsel), מדה (measure/grade) for spiritual hierarchy, and חסד (covenant-love) — all Hebrew theological terms with no Greek equivalents.

one_way_hebrew: Uses האור (ha'or, H216 — 'the light') — bracketed in the source, suggesting editorial restoration. Greek has ἐληλυθυῖαν ἐν δυνάμει ('come in power'). A back-translator from Greek would write בא בכח ('come in power'), NOT 'the light.' The Hebrew frames the kingdom as a visible light — connecting to Isaiah 60:1 ('arise, shine, for your light has come') and Psalm 36:10 ('in your light we see light').
